World.title: Ebola: FG identifies 53 contacts, offers N100,000 weekly support
World.content:
Ali Pate, coordinating minister of health and social welfare

*Says emergency support to cover feeding, accommodation, family upkeep *Patient improves as DG warns against delayed precautions *Rivers suspected case tests negative *Lagos steps up airport surveillance, says no suspected case *Zamfara activates Ebola surveillance after passenger arrives airport with 38°C fever

By Chioma Obinna & Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja

The federal government has identified 53 contacts linked to Nigeria’s confirmed Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, up from the initial 44, as health authorities intensify efforts to prevent further transmission of the virus.

Read Also: Lagos govt on alert, says no Ebola case in state

It also announced the approval of an emergency payment of N100,000 per person weekly for individuals placed in isolation or quarantine as part of efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak in the Federal Capital Territory, FCT.

This came as Lagos State government weekend intensified Ebola surveillance at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport and strengthened public health preparedness, following the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja,.

The Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, NCDC, Dr. Jide Idris, disclosed this at a briefing in Abuja yesterday.

The government had initially announced 44 contacts, following the confirmation of the Ebola case in the FCT on October 20, 2026.

Idris said the contacts, including healthcare workers, the patient’s spouse, domestic staff and other individuals who might have been exposed to the virus, had been identified, categorised and placed under monitoring.

He explained that contact tracing was ongoing and that the number of contacts could change as investigations progressed and more information became available.

The NCDC chief maintained that Nigeria had recorded only one confirmed Ebola case, while two additional suspected cases had been investigated.

According to him, a suspected case in Rivers State tested negative, while investigations into another suspected case in the FCT were ongoing.

He added that no contact had tested positive for the virus and that the FCT remained the only state with a confirmed case.

“As of today, we have two suspected cases again. One in FCT, one in Rivers State. But we’ve tested the Rivers case; it’s negative.

“So there’s no red line. We have that confirmed case, that’s the patient in the hospital. Contacts with symptoms, none. Contacts positive, none. States affected, only FCT now. Now, that’s the summary,” he said.

The NCDC chief said the national incident management system had been activated at the highest level to coordinate the response, involving the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, FCT health authorities, other government agencies and technical partners.

He stressed that being identified as a contact did not mean that an individual had contracted the virus, explaining that public health officials needed to monitor such individuals to detect any possible infection early.

“Being identified as a contact does not mean that you have Ebola. It means that public health teams need to assess and monitor your health so that any possible infection can be identified early,” he said.

He urged Nigerians contacted by public health officials to cooperate fully and provide accurate information about their movements, contacts and any symptoms they might have experienced.

Samples collected

On laboratory investigations, Idris said samples collected from the confirmed patient on three occasions had remained positive, while a sample taken from her husband tested negative.

He added that genetic sequencing had been completed by two laboratory facilities to establish the genetic characteristics of the virus, with the findings being used to facilitate information-sharing with Ugandan health authorities.

The NCDC chief said the agency had also strengthened the country’s laboratory capacity, with between nine and 12 public and private laboratories equipped to test for Ebola.

He explained that testing for the confirmed case was being conducted at the National Reference Laboratory (NRL), adding that additional reagents and supplies had been positioned across the national laboratory network to improve preparedness.

On clinical management, Idris said the confirmed patient was receiving treatment at an isolation facility, while arrangements had been made to accommodate additional cases if necessary.

He disclosed that isolation and quarantine arrangements had also been established for contacts requiring closer monitoring.

According to him, the agency was providing accommodation and feeding for contacts placed in isolation or quarantine, alongside temporary financial assistance to help them cater for their families during the monitoring period.

He said the government had approved emergency payments of N100,000 per person weekly for contacts in isolation or quarantine.

“Just to douse the tension, we decided we would do this. We provide N100,000 per person per week just to maintain their comfort and feeding because they were complaining,” he said.

The NCDC chief further disclosed that the government had strengthened screening at the country’s international airports, with aviation authorities, immigration, customs and other relevant agencies working together to improve preparedness.

He said passenger screening measures had also been expanded following the confirmation of the case, with health declaration forms required for passengers travelling into Nigeria from all countries.

Idris called on public and private healthcare facilities to strengthen infection prevention and control measures, including patient screening, triage, hand hygiene, environmental cleaning, safe injection practices and proper medical waste management.

He urged healthcare workers to maintain a high index of suspicion when attending to patients with symptoms consistent with Ebola, particularly those with relevant exposure histories.

“Healthcare workers should not wait for laboratory confirmation before taking appropriate precautions. Protecting healthcare workers is essential to protecting the communities we serve,” he said.He also advised Nigerians to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid direct contact with the bodily fluids of suspected cases and promptly report possible exposure to public health authorities.

If you have symptoms…

According to him, anyone who develops symptoms following possible exposure should immediately contact public health officials and follow their instructions before visiting a healthcare facility.

Idris assured Nigerians that the response would continue to be guided by evidence, with surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory testing and preparedness activities reviewed as new information became available.

He urged the public to remain calm, cooperate with health officials and avoid spreading unverified information as the government intensifies efforts to prevent further transmission of the virus.

Lagos steps up airport surveillance, says no suspected case

Meanwhile, Lagos State government has intensified Ebola surveillance at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport and strengthened public health preparedness, following the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja.

The government, which also assured residents that no suspected case had been reported in the state, urged them not to panic but remain vigilant, promptly report possible exposure and seek medical assessment if they developed symptoms, particularly after travelling from areas reporting Ebola transmission.

The Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, disclosed this in a statement issued by the Lagos State Ministry of Health, saying the state was strengthening surveillance, risk communication and coordination with relevant agencies to ensure early detection and a rapid response to potential cases.

According to the statement, the ministry, through its Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, has conducted a strategic engagement and assessment at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport with airport management, Port Health Services and other aviation and public health stakeholders.

The engagement focused on passenger screening, information sharing, infection prevention and control, and coordination of emergency response measures.

The statement read: “Lagos State is ready to prevent, detect and respond to potential public health threats.”

It added that the government was intensifying public enlightenment on Ebola symptoms, transmission and prevention, while urging residents to rely on verified information rather than rumours.

“Ebola Virus Disease is a severe illness that can be fatal. It spreads primarily through direct contact with the blood and other body fluids of an infected person showing symptoms, contaminated materials, or the bodies of people who have died from the disease. Infection may also occur through contact with infected animals.”

The ministry listed symptoms to watch for as fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Unexplained bleeding or bruising may occur in some cases.

“Symptoms may develop between two and 21 days after exposure, the statement said, warning that early signs could resemble malaria and other common illnesses.”

Abayomi advised residents who develop fever to undergo a malaria rapid diagnostic test before taking antimalarial medicines, in line with the state’s fever-management policy.

Where the test is negative, a healthcare professional should assess other possible causes and determine appropriate treatment.

The government also urged travellers arriving from areas reporting Ebola transmission to cooperate with Port Health Services, provide accurate travel and health information when requested, and comply with applicable public health guidance.

“Anyone who develops symptoms during travel or after arrival should notify appropriate health personnel and seek guidance before visiting a healthcare facility.

The statement advised anyone who suspects exposure, particularly following contact with a suspected or confirmed case, to contact public health authorities promptly before visiting a healthcare facility.

Residents were urged to report suspected cases or relevant exposure concerns through the state’s emergency numbers, 112 or 767, or contact the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health on 0802 316 9485.

The government said it would continue to monitor developments, strengthen surveillance and response readiness, and provide verified updates as necessary.

It stressed that early detection and prompt reporting were critical to preventing the spread of the disease.

Zamfara passenger

Zamfara activates Ebola surveillance after passenger arrives airport with 38°C fever

Similarly, Zamfara State government has activated Ebola surveillance at Gusau airport and major motor parks after a passenger arriving from Saudi Arabia was found with a body temperature of 38 degrees celsius.

The Commissioner for Health, Nafisa Maradun, disclosed this weekend while leading a medical team to flag off passenger screening at the airport.

Maradun said the passenger, an indigene of Zamfara, was identified during screening and referred for further medical assessment.

The state government has deployed medical personnel at the airport, motor parks and other entry points to screen travellers and support the early detection of suspected cases.

Maradun said the surveillance measures were intended to prevent the virus from spreading to Zamfara, and urged residents to remain calm and cooperate with health officials.

The state’s ministry of health also directed public and private health facilities, disease surveillance officers and local government health authorities to strengthen preparedness, improve screening and promptly report suspected cases.

The government said it was working with relevant agencies, including the Nigeria Customs Service, NCS, and Nigeria Immigration Service, NIS, to strengthen surveillance at entry points.

Transport workers are also expected to help identify and report passengers who may require medical assessment.

World.title: FG: Era of Holding Nigeria’s Oil, Gas Assets as Souvenirs Over
World.content:
*Drill-or-drop policy: Operators returning assets voluntarily, says Lokpobiri

*Explains how exit of EPC firms pushed up project costs

*Kachikwu: How govt interference delayed decisions as NNPC GMD

*Ekpo: Nigeria’s 215TCF gas reserves must lead to higher domestic supply

*NEITI: NUPRC has brought greater openness to oil bid rounds

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The federal government has declared an end to the era of oil companies holding petroleum assets without developing them, insisting that operators must either invest in production or relinquish their licences under the drill-or-drop provisions of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA).



Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, said the policy has empowered the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) to recover undeveloped assets and make them available to investors willing and able to develop them.



Also, a former Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, and Group Managing Director of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), Prof. Ibe Kachikwu, has recalled how government interference and cumbersome approval processes delayed decisions and constrained investment during his tenure at the national oil company.



In the same vein, Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekperikpe Ekpo, said Nigeria must translate its 215 Trillion Cubic Feet (TCF) of proven gas reserves into higher domestic supply, stronger infrastructure and industrial growth over the next five years.

Similarly, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, has maintained that the PIA has brought greater calm and responsibility to oil-producing communities by giving them a clearer stake in petroleum operations through Host Communities Development Trusts (HCDTs).

They all spoke in a series of interviews published in ‘Upstream Gaze’, a special edition of a quarterly magazine by the NUPRC to mark its fifth anniversary.



Lokpobiri said the policy had helped make petroleum assets available for fresh investment, with 50 assets recently offered for bidding and another licensing round in the offing.

The drill-or-drop policy, provided for under the PIA requires oil and gas companies to develop their licensed petroleum assets within the stipulated period or risk losing them to the government. The policy empowers the regulator to revoke or recover licences for undeveloped assets and make them available to investors willing and capable of putting them into production.

Essentially, it is designed to discourage speculative ownership and the hoarding of oil blocks which has been the norm, accelerate exploration and development, attract fresh investment, increase crude oil and gas production, and help Nigeria achieve its production targets.



Lokpobiri said: “The drill-or-drop provision is one of the most consequential provisions of the PIA. It has kept operators on their toes. If you do not develop your assets within the provisions of the law, the NUPRC has the authority to recover those assets and make them available to investors that are willing and able to develop them.



“The era of holding assets as souvenirs or symbols of wealth is gone: you either drill or drop. Some operators are now willing to relinquish assets voluntarily because that may be preferable to regulatory recovery. Others are reassessing their portfolios and recognising that certain assets no longer fit their development plans.”

He also attributed the increase in active drilling rigs to reforms and improved regulatory activity, saying the number had risen from between 10 and 14 in 2023 to more than 60 currently.

However, the minister said the departure of major Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contractors, deep-offshore contractors and other service providers had contributed to higher project costs in Nigeria, following prolonged uncertainty before the passage of the PIA.



According to him, inadequate project activity had made it difficult for contractors to sustain their operations, prompting some to leave the country and reducing competition in critical areas of the industry.

“The cost of our projects became higher than in some other jurisdictions because there was limited competition and insufficient project activity. Contractors can only survive where there are projects to execute. If the project pipeline dries up, they will leave,” he said.

“Many contractors therefore left the country, leaving only one or two providers in some areas and contributing to prohibitive costs. That was a major challenge, but we are now working to bring them back.”



Lokpobiri said the government was engaging contractors in Europe and America to encourage their return, while pursuing fiscal, operational and regulatory reforms to improve Nigeria’s competitiveness.

He added that a recent presidential executive order was expected to help unlock almost $50 billion in deep-offshore investments, while the re-entry of shut-in wells following recent divestments was contributing to production growth.



He cited developments following Seplat Energy’s acquisition of ExxonMobil’s assets and Renaissance Africa Energy’s acquisition of Shell’s onshore assets as examples of efforts to revive previously inactive wells.

Looking ahead, Lokpobiri said Nigeria could significantly increase crude oil production over the next five years if investment commitments and development programmes materialised, projecting a potential output range of 3 million to 5 million barrels per day.

Kachikwu: Govt Interference Hobbled My Work as Minister

Also, former Group Managing Director of the NNPC and former Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, Prof. Kachikwu, has recalled how government interference and cumbersome approval processes delayed decisions and constrained investment during his tenure at the national oil company.



Kachikwu said the petroleum industry had suffered from excessive government control, which restricted managerial independence and made it difficult to implement decisions quickly, even when the commercial case for action was clear.

“The oil sector could be very frustrating because there was a great deal of government interference. In my case, I had the rare privilege of serving as both GMD of NNPC and Minister of State. Dealing with the investment process at NNPC was difficult because you could hardly do anything without government approval.



“The lack of independence constrained decision-making. The oil sector was run almost like a conventional government agency, which limited creativity. One of the things I tried to do when I came in was to bring more of a private-sector orientation into NNPC and the Ministry. It took quite a while for the system to adjust to new ways of doing things,” he explained.

He said the absence of clearly defined institutional powers under the old Petroleum Act meant investment decisions often depended on the initiative of individual officeholders, while the PIA had introduced greater clarity on responsibilities and institutional independence.

However, Kachikwu expressed concern that significant government control remained and that the new law had yet to deliver the scale of investment anticipated.



He noted that much of the investment recorded since the PIA’s passage involved domestic acquisitions, mergers and takeovers of existing assets, rather than the development of major new production platforms and floating production facilities at the expected pace.

Kachikwu also argued that Nigeria needed to raise its production ambitions beyond the federal government’s 3 million barrels per day target, saying the country had the potential to produce 4 million barrels daily by 2030.



“I think Nigeria could do four million barrels per day by 2030; targeting three million barrels may be underestimating our potential. We have to recognise that oil will not simply remain in the ground waiting for us indefinitely,” he said.

“The world is changing. Electric vehicles are expanding, solar power is growing, alternative energy systems are developing and new producing countries are entering the market. The world will not wait while we increase production gradually. We need a significant volumetric shift and we should sit down and ask what would it take to reach four million barrels per day,” he added.



He said Nigeria needed to identify the investments, projects, infrastructure and timelines required to achieve the higher target, warning that the country was competing with emerging oil producers, including Guyana and Namibia, for international capital.

Predictable fiscal terms, transparency, competitive project economics and timely government decisions, he stressed, were essential to attracting the investments required to increase production.

Ekpo: Enormous Gas Resources Must Benefit Nigerians

In the gas sector, the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekpo, said Nigeria must translate its 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves into higher domestic supply, stronger infrastructure and industrial growth over the next five years.

He reiterated that the country was targeting gas production of 10 billion standard cubic feet per day by 2027 and 12 billion standard cubic feet daily by 2030, but achieving the goals would require faster development of non-associated gas resources and sustained investment in processing and pipeline infrastructure.



“Over the next five years, Nigeria must convert its 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves into increased production, stronger infrastructure and sustainable industrial growth. Success must ultimately translate into reliable gas supply for power generation, fertiliser production, petrochemicals, manufacturing, Liquefied Petroleum Gas and Compressed Natural Gas, alongside sustained regional gas supply projects and Liquefied Natural Gas exports,” he said.



On the Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) initiative, introduced to provide a cheaper transport alternative following the removal of the petrol subsidy, Ekpo said the planned national network of refuelling stations was being expanded from 500 to 1,000.

He repeated that more than $2 billion had been catalysed in the CNG ecosystem since 2023, supporting 120,000 vehicle conversions, more than 400 certified conversion centres and over 90 operational refuelling stations.

He said the priority was to extend access beyond major cities and ensure that the lower cost of CNG translated into reduced transport expenses for Nigerians.

NEITI: NUPRC Has Improved Licensing Processes

Speaking on transparency in the upstream sector, the Executive Secretary of the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI), Musa Adar, commended the NUPRC for improving licensing procedures, disclosure and regulatory oversight since its establishment under the PIA.



Adar, who chaired the House Committee on Petroleum Resources (Upstream) in the Ninth National Assembly, said the law had created a clearer institutional and regulatory framework after years of concerns over transparency, accountability and disclosure.

“The NUPRC, as one of the institutions established under the Act, has helped to improve the licensing process, strengthen disclosure and provide more structured oversight of upstream operations. These are commendable developments,” he said.



On the 2025 licensing round monitored by NEITI, Adar said the organisation was awaiting its final report and would not pre-empt its conclusions, although preliminary feedback from field officers had not identified any material misalignment in the process.

He called for further improvements in disclosure, accountability and regulatory responsiveness, noting that investors valued regulators that were firm, fair, transparent and predictable.

Adar also argued that Nigeria’s ambitions should extend beyond crude oil production to greater domestic refining and petrochemical processing to retain more value within the economy and reduce exposure to imported refined products.

Olu of Warri: Indigenes Now Have Clearer Stake in Oil Sector

For his part, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, said the PIA had brought greater calm and responsibility to oil-producing communities by giving them a clearer stake in petroleum operations through Host Communities Development Trusts (HCDTs).

He said the framework had improved communities’ understanding of their entitlements and created incentives to protect petroleum infrastructure, although official data would be needed to establish the extent of any reduction in sabotage.

The PIA requires oil companies to contribute 3 per cent of their actual operating expenditure for the preceding financial year to the applicable HCDT.



“As someone who is on the ground, I would say that it has brought a sense of calm. There is also a clearer sense of direction and consideration. Before the PIA, these obligations were not set out in law in the same way. Today, the framework is captured in black and white and stakeholders have greater clarity about what is expected.

“When people know that a defined percentage is available, there can be better planning and consideration of development priorities. That goes a long way towards giving communities a sense of ownership and belonging,” he posited.

World.title: Nigeria’s Index Ebola Case Set for Medical Evacuation Abroad Today, Two Contacts Test Negative
World.content:
Quarantined persons may get N100,000 weekly upkeep

Ebola, brain drain top agenda as doctors in W/Africa meet in Abuja

Emmanuel Addeh and Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja

Nigeria’s index case of the Ebola virus disease is expected to be evacuated abroad for further medical treatment early Monday (today), a source familiar with the development told THISDAY last night.

The source said arrangements had been made to fly the 42-year-old woman out of the country by 6am, adding that a medical evacuation aircraft was already at the airport awaiting her arrival.

The fresh development came as the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said two suspected Ebola cases from the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) and Rivers State have tested negative, while 53 primary contacts of the confirmed index case have been identified and are being monitored.

The agency also said that based on complaints by the contacts in quarantine, the federal government was considering the payment of N100,000 per week.

However, NCDC said that the welfare arrangement was in the interim, as states were expected to take over maintenance of the contacts cases in their domain subsequently.

“The medivac plane is already at the airport waiting to evacuate her,” the source said, adding that the federal government was expected to announce the development after the patient had departed Nigeria.

The proposed evacuation is coming amid heightened surveillance and contact-tracing efforts by Nigerian health authorities to prevent further transmission of the disease.

Earlier, the Director General of the NCDC, Dr. Jide Idris, spoke at a press briefing in Abuja to provide an update on Nigeria’s Ebola disease response.

Idris said the search for other secondary contacts was ongoing, assuring Nigerians that the federal government through Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, NCDC, FCT health authorities and partners was fully committed to containing the outbreak.

“As previously announced, Nigeria has confirmed one case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus. The patient is currently receiving medical care under isolation, with infection prevention and control measures in place. Clinical teams continue to monitor and manage patient’s condition,” he said.

According to him, the 53 primary contacts comprise 44 personnel from the hospital where the index case is receiving treatment, while nine additional contacts from the index, three from Julius Berger office where she visited before coming down with symptoms, and three health workers who attended to index case.

He said samples collected from the husband of the index case tested negative, adding that two suspected cases in FCT and Rivers also tested negative, but will have more follow up.

Responding to a question about the true identity of the index case, the DG said she is from Uganda and married to a Swiss national, and the government is carrying out further investigations to establish her exact travel details. He said Nigerian officials will meet with Ugandan officials online to exchange information.

Idris explained that the case was detected through event-based surveillance after vigilant healthcare workers recognised clinical features that raised concern.

He said the response was being implemented through a structured Incident Management System coordinated by the Emergency Operations Centre under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Ali Pate, and Presidential Task Force on EVD.

Idris listed critical components as identifying and monitoring contacts for 21 days, ensuring safe clinical care, strengthening infection prevention and control across facilities, boosting surveillance and laboratory capacity, and community engagement.

The DG said the centre is being assisted by the Department of State Services (DSS) in tracking contacts, has expanded case definition for community surveillance, and is boosting genomic capabilities of 12 laboratories to test for Ebola.

He said the government has designated the University of Abuja Teaching Hospital as a special isolation centre and has fumigated premises of the index case.

On the welfare of contacts, Idris said the federal government was considering the payment of N100,000 per week for feeding and upkeep of each quarantined contact, while states are expected to take responsibility for contacts in their domain.

He appealed to Nigerians to cooperate with contact tracing teams, provide accurate information and adhere to public health advisories.

“An identified contact does not mean you have Ebola. It means public health teams need to assess and monitor your health,” he said, urging hand hygiene, avoiding contact with blood or body fluids of suspected cases and prompt reporting.

Idris commended healthcare workers whose vigilance led to detection and called on all public and private facilities to strengthen screening, triage and availability of personal protective equipment.

He recalled leading Lagos State response in 2014 as Commissioner for Health, saying experience taught lessons on leadership, coordination and public trust which are being deployed.

He warned against misinformation and stigmatisation, urging reliance on verified information from NCDC and Federal Ministry of Health.

“The government has worked hard to strengthen the surveillance system and boost capacities of disease testing laboratories. Success depends on the whole of society,” he said, noting that the patient is improving.

Meanwhile, to find solutions to major healthcare challenges facing West Africa, issues such as brain drain, infrastructure deficit and Ebola threat will be among key issues for deliberation as West African College of Physicians (WACP) marks 50 years anniversary with a summit in Abuja beginning on Monday.

The body had earlier visited President Bola Tinubu at State House Presidential Villa in Abuja where the president urged them to help find solutions to some of the daunting healthcare challenges facing the region.

Speaking at a press conference on Saturday, President of WACP, Dr. Mamadou Mourtalla, said the College will appraise developments in the health sector as it relates to new scientific discoveries, manpower training, infrastructure and infectious disease control.

“We’ll be discussing various perspectives, how to deal with the pandemic, an epidemic coming up in Africa which puts a lot of stress on our health system. We have over 70 scientific papers based on this theme. At the end, we usually issue a communique,” Mourtalla said.

He said implementation of resolutions is key, adding that the President of ECOWAS Commission, Director General of West African Health Organisation and President Tinubu who promised to send the Minister of Health will be present to make recommendations to leaders.

Assistant Secretary General of WACP, Dr. Habibu Galadanci, said the conference has scheduled deliberations on several key areas including brain drain, infrastructure deficit, rise in non-communicable diseases like kidney disease, hypertension, and infectious disease epidemics including current spread of Ebola.

“The scientific content will touch on several aspects of medicine, including disease conditions, health policies and contemporary medical issues,” he said.

On brain drain, he said the conference has a whole session that will look at push and pull dynamics.

“There are pull dynamics, push dynamics, and we are going to look at that and find solutions. When we saw President Tinubu, that was one main thing he charged us with, that we should discuss Japa syndrome and find solutions,” Galadanci said.

He said the conference will also look at use of artificial intelligence in medicine and ethical concerns in managing patients, maternal and reproductive health, access to safe healthcare for women and children, mental health priorities and development of balanced scorecards for improving performance of public sector hospitals.

Galadanci said the conference will be a landmark event that offers opportunity for stakeholders to pause and look at where College has come from in 50 years, achievements and pending issues.

“We still have a lot of problems, but we have come a long way, at least we can train our doctors. We have specialists, so many doctors that they poach them from outside because of how good we are,” he said.

Other areas include kidney disease epidemic, dementia which is creeping into society as population ages, and mental health often stigmatised and downplayed.

As part of its corporate social responsibility, members of College organised a medical outreach programme in Waru community, a suburb in Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja on Saturday, attracting a large crowd of men, women and children who benefited from free healthcare services.

The week-long summit in Abuja is expected to bring over 1,300 experts from across West Africa to propose solutions for the next 50 years.

World.title: FirstHoldCo Reports N911bn Profit Before Tax in 9 Months 2026; Reinforcing Profitability and Resilience
World.content:
First HoldCo Plc’s 9 months 2026 performance marks an important transition: the Group is moving from balance sheet repair toward a more resilient, capital-supported growth phase. The headline is compelling — profit before tax rose 60.8% year on year to N911.2 billion, while profit after tax advanced 65.1% to N744.5 billion; importantly, the quality of this growth is also improving.

First, earnings have broadened year on year and beyond the traditional interest income. Second, operating discipline has improved efficiency. Third, stronger capital and better asset-quality indicators are increasing the Group’s capacity to absorb risk and pursue selective growth. These factors support a more durable earnings profile and a stronger long-term shareholder proposition.

Profitability continues to strengthen

Gross earnings increased 8.8% to N2.87 trillion, but profitability expanded faster: profit before tax reached N911.2 billion and profit after tax reached N744.5 billion. Post-tax return on average equity improved to 27.7% from 24.7% in the previous year, while return on average assets rose to 3.3% from 2.6% in 9M 2025 showing that balance sheet growth is generating stronger returns.

This growth was supported by a more diversified revenue mix. Non-interest income surged 143.5% to N722.9 billion, supported by a 48.1% increase in net fee and commission income to N316.4 billion. Transaction-led revenues, including electronic banking, funds transfers and credit-related services and other non-interest income contributions are giving the Group more diversified avenues for earnings growth.

Operating leverage is becoming visible

Operating income rose 10.3% even as operating expenses declined 8.1% to N866.6 billion. The resulting cost-to-income ratio of 43.7%, down from 52.4%, is a strong indicator of improving operating leverage and cost discipline particularly in a 15.39% inflationary environment. The result suggests that management is not relying on balance-sheet expansion alone; it is extracting more value from the franchise while containing the cost base.



Core margins present a compelling earnings-upside opportunity. Although net interest income moderated by 16.0% to N1.26 trillion and net interest margin adjusted to 8.7% from 11.3% amid softer asset yields, the improvement in cost of funds to 4.5% from 4.9% demonstrates effective funding discipline and provides a strong foundation for margin recovery. Enhanced risk-adjusted pricing and a more efficient funding mix offer credible levers for margin expansion and sustainable returns, while maintaining rigorous credit standards and asset quality.



A balance sheet with greater strategic capacity

The balance sheet provides greater capacity for disciplined growth. Total assets increased 18.1% from year-end 2025 to N32.20 trillion, while customer deposits grew 21.3% to N22.91 trillion. Group equity rose 17.0% to N3.86 trillion. In contrast, net customer loans expanded by a deliberate and measured 4.8% to N9.39 trillion. This combination of strong funding growth, firmer equity and selective lending reflects disciplined capital deployment rather than indiscriminate risk-taking.

FirstBank’s capital adequacy ratio improved to 18.6% at September 2026 from 16.7% at half-year. The stronger capital buffer increases resilience supports regulatory confidence and provides greater flexibility to finance attractive opportunities. Importantly, capital is strengthening while profitability is accelerating, improving the Group’s capacity to compound value internally.

Asset-quality repair is gaining traction

Asset-quality repair is also advancing. The Group’s non-performing loan ratio declined to 10.4% from 13.9% at H1 2026 while NPL coverage, including regulatory reserves, increased to 98.8%. Impairment charges declined 28.3% to N207.1 billion and recoveries reached N94.3 billion.

These figures show broad-based progress: stronger coverage, reduced impairment charges and meaningful recoveries to date. Although the NPL ratio remains above management’s desired level, the downward trajectory improves protection and loss-absorption capacity.

To further strengthen asset quality by year-end, management could combine targeted restructuring of viable exposures, negotiated settlements and intensified recoveries with ongoing legal actions. These asset-quality measures are supported by more than N850 billion already held in regulatory risk reserves, providing a substantial prudential buffer against identified credit risks. Accordingly, subject to applicable accounting and regulatory treatment, additional impairment charges recognised in the books would be broadly capital-neutral, enabling management to accelerate the resolution or write-off of fully provided loans with limited recovery prospects without materially weakening regulatory capital, while recovery efforts continue. These measures should further reduce the NPL ratio, reinforce coverage and underscore the strength of the balance sheet.

Diversification strengthens the earnings growth outlook

Commercial Banking remains the Group’s principal earnings subsidiary, generating gross earnings of N2.70 trillion and profit before tax of N784.7 billion. Its scale, deposit franchise and broad customer relationships underpin recurring revenue.

Alongside this core franchise, Investment Banking and Asset Management is becoming more significant. The segment generated gross earnings of N120.1 billion, up 85.5%, and profit before tax of N85.7 billion, up 133.6%. This high-growth, capital-light platform broadens the Group’s exposure to advisory, asset management, trusteeship, brokerage and securities activities, reducing reliance on traditional banking spreads.

Why the investment case is strengthening

FirstHoldCo’s investment case is increasingly persuasive because improvement is visible across several reinforcing dimensions: faster earnings growth, better operating efficiency, expanding transaction-led revenues, stronger capital, disciplined loan growth and an improving asset quality position. These are not isolated gains; they describe a franchise becoming more resilient and better positioned to convert scale into sustainable returns.

The Group is well positioned to unlock the next phase of value creation by building on its current momentum. Continued progress toward a single-digit NPL ratio, sustained coverage, recovery in net interest margin, disciplined deployment of deposits, and greater fee income contribution provide clear pathways to stronger, more resilient earnings. Consistent execution should improve earnings quality and deepen market confidence.

Enhanced dividend policy reinforces the shareholder-value proposition

The market is already recognising this stronger proposition: as of 23 October 2026, FirstHoldCo’s 200.84% year-to-date share-price gain had delivered the highest total shareholder return in 2026 among its banking peers, signaling strong investor confidence in the Group’s earnings momentum and outlook.

Reinforcing these market gains, FirstHoldCo earlier this year reaffirmed its commitment to shareholder returns through an enhanced dividend policy. Under the policy, the Board approved a minimum annual distribution of 60% of profit after tax, commencing with the 2027 accounts. The policy gives shareholders a clearer route to participate in earnings growth and signals confidence in the Group’s profitability, capital and cash-generation.



The timing is strategically important. Beginning with the 2027 accounts allows FirstHoldCo to consolidate capital strength, further improve asset-quality and fund disciplined growth before the higher payout takes effect. Subject to distributable reserves, regulatory approvals and prevailing financial conditions, the policy offers a credible path to stronger shareholder returns.

Outlook: Disciplined growth with meaningful optionality

FirstHoldCo enters the final quarter of 2026 with a stronger balance sheet, improving credit metrics and enhanced operating leverage. Its N22.91 trillion deposit base provides substantial funding capacity, while the improved capital position creates room for selective expansion. Targeted investment in technology, innovation and customer experience can deepen transaction volumes and strengthen the durability of non-interest revenue.



The investment story therefore extends beyond stronger earnings. Capital strength, franchise depth, cost discipline and diversified capabilities make performance more sustainable. Margin pressure and the remaining NPL stock still require attention, but each also presents a defined opportunity for improvement.

Overall, the 9Months 2026 results show a Group regaining strategic flexibility and converting reform into measurable progress. Continued improvement in asset quality, margin recovery and disciplined capital allocation provide a credible path to resilient earnings and durable long-term value

World.title: Investors Rush for Dangote Refinery Shares as Offer Closes on 27 October
World.content:
Peter Uzoho

Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has reported a sharp increase in investor subscriptions as its landmark Initial Public Offering (IPO) enters its final days, with retail and institutional investors accelerating participation ahead of the closing date of October 27.

The company confirmed, in a statement yesterday, that the IPO will close on Tuesday, October 27, as scheduled.

The company said, “This is the final deadline, and no further extension will be granted. Investors wishing to participate must complete their subscriptions before the offer closes.”

The surge in demand follows the refinery’s recently released nine-month financial results, which showed exceptional growth in revenue, profitability, and cash generation, reinforcing investor confidence in the company’s long-term prospects.

Dangote Refinery reported revenue of $22.5 billion and net profit of $4.73 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, representing a significant turnaround from a loss recorded in the corresponding period of 2025.

Revenue increased by 144 per cent year-on-year, while Earnings, Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation (EBITDA) rose to $5.5 billion, reflecting higher refining throughput, improved operational reliability and stronger refining margins.

The company also strengthened its balance sheet, moving from a net debt position to a net cash position during the period.

It said the strong financial performance, combined with the refinery’s strategic importance to Africa’s energy security and industrial development, has continued to attract broad-based interest from individual investors, pension funds, institutional investors, asset managers, professionals, business owners and members of the African diaspora.

The statement said, “The level of investor interest we are seeing reflects growing confidence in our business and in the strong financial results we have delivered.

“Investors are recognising both the quality of our earnings and the long-term value creation opportunity represented by the refinery.”

According to the refinery, the IPO has become more than a capital-raising exercise, evolving into an opportunity for Africans and international investors to participate directly in the ownership of one of the continent’s most significant industrial enterprises.

It stated that subscriptions had been received from across Nigeria, other African countries and international markets, underscoring the refinery’s growing reputation as a world-class industrial asset.

The company stated, “Investors recognise that this refinery is not merely an energy asset. It is a platform for industrial growth, foreign-exchange generation, regional trade, energy security and economic development across Africa.

“The strong response to the offer reflects confidence in the future of African industry and in our ability to continue generating sustainable returns for shareholders.”

The company also reiterated its commitment to broad-based ownership, emphasising that the IPO has been structured to ensure that ordinary investors can participate alongside institutional investors in the refinery’s future growth.

It advised prospective investors who had not yet completed their subscriptions to do so immediately through their stockbrokers and approved distribution channels before the deadline.

It stated, “This is the final opportunity for investors to participate in this historic offer.

“We encourage all interested investors to complete their applications before the subscription window closes on 27 October.”

Dangote refinery expressed appreciation to regulators, issuing houses, stockbrokers, financial institutions, fintech partners, investor associations, market operators, and the investing public for their support throughout the offer period.

The company added that the strong demand recorded so far demonstrated growing investor confidence in African-owned industrial enterprises and highlighted the increasing capacity of African capital markets to support large-scale transformational investments.

The statement said, “History is being made. The remarkable investor response is a powerful vote of confidence in Africa’s future, in African enterprise, and in the long-term value that world-class industrial projects can create when opened to public ownership. We remain committed to delivering sustained growth and enduring value for all shareholders.”

World.title: Lula Stages Historic Comeback to Beat Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s Presidential Poll
World.content:
Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.

With nearly 99 per cent of votes counted this morning, the 80-year-old leftist received 51.75 per cent of the vote to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.25 per cent.

Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, has the first round runner-up won the second vote, the Guardian UK reported.

But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following the count, and at the hotel where he was watching the count.

As the result was confirmed, Reginaldo Lopes, a key Lula ally, told the Guardian: “I feel incredible … This is Brazil telling the world that the extreme right is fascist, that the extreme right is against black people, is against the poor, against the state, against gay people … We are going to reorganise the democratic forces (in this country).”

The incumbent, who had lost by 2.2 million votes three weeks ago, has now won by 4.3 million.

The 81-year-old leftist appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out. After a record abstention rate of 21.08 per cent in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live farther from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21 per cent.

For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s, the Guardian UK report added.

After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002.

Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup.

Lula’s win is bad news for Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed.

It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally. The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina.

Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count.

Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo.

World.title: Pipeline Security Claims Raise Bigger Questions
World.content:
Tracing the Reform Dividend from Fiscal Savings to Public Spending, Social Protection and Measurable Results

There is a legitimate national conversation to be had about the cost, structure, transparency and effectiveness of Nigeria’s pipeline surveillance architecture. There is also a legitimate argument about whether communities in the Niger Delta should derive greater economic value from the protection of the natural resources extracted from their environment.



When that conversation is reduced to ethnic insinuations, unverified figures and an apparent attempt to justify one contractor by attacking another, the country risks losing sight of the bigger issue: energy security is a national security matter, not a tribal entitlement.



That is where Asari Dokubo appears to have missed the point. In a video circulating this week, the Niger Delta activist questioned why Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, has faced criticism over pipeline surveillance while, according to him, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, and Dr. Osahon Okunbo were receiving as much as N2.7 trillion annually for protecting pipelines.

Dokubo initially referred to the amount as monthly before correcting himself to annual. Importantly, however, no documentary evidence was presented in the video to substantiate the N2.7 trillion figure, and reports carrying the allegation have expressly treated it as unverified.



That distinction is not cosmetic. It is fundamental. A claim of N2.7 trillion annually for pipeline surveillance is so extraordinary, that it demands concrete documentary evidence. Contracts, procurement records, payment schedules, scope of work, contracting entities and government approvals would have to be placed before the public.



Without such evidence, the figure remains an allegation – Not a fact. That is perhaps the first thing Dokubo missed.

The mathematics of the allegation in public domain – Therein is another problem where Dokubo’s allegation appears to collapse different entities, individuals and contractual relationships into one giant financial arrangement.



Osahon Okunbo is associated with Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL), where he has served in senior executive capacity. The Olu of Warri has also been publicly associated with PINL’s leadership structure. The relationship between a monarch, a company and a pipeline surveillance contract cannot simply be translated into a claim that the monarch personally receives the entire value of a corporate contract.



Indeed, this is not a new controversy. In 2022, reporting on the pipeline surveillance arrangement specifically recorded a denial that the Olu of Warri personally owned PINL, while identifying PINL alongside Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited and Maton Engineering Nigeria Limited among companies awarded pipeline surveillance contracts.



More recent reporting identifies Osahon Okunbo as a key executive of PINL, with the company operating on critical pipeline infrastructure.

The distinction matters because corporate contract value is not automatically personal income.

What Dokubo Gets Right

To be fair, there is a legitimate question beneath Dokubo’s provocative presentation. If several companies are receiving public money to protect critical national infrastructure, Nigerians are entitled to know how much each contractor receives, what kilometres of infrastructure each is responsible for, what performance indicators apply and what results have been achieved.



That is a serious governance question – So too is Dokubo’s broader argument that the Niger Delta should benefit economically from the protection and development of its natural resources.

That argument should lead to a conversation about transparent procurement, community participation, local employment, measurable security outcomes and accountability – Not ethnic arithmetic(s).



Pipeline security cannot become a competition over whether an Ijaw, Itsekiri, Bini or any other Nigerian is entitled to a particular contract.

Nigeria’s oil infrastructure belongs to Nigeria. The responsibility to protect it is therefore national priority – This is where Osahon Okunbo becomes relevant.

Perhaps the greatest irony in Dokubo’s intervention is that he appears to have overlooked what the emerging pipeline-security model represented by PINL is actually trying to do.



Okunbo has publicly argued that sustainable infrastructure security cannot depend on force alone. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, he emphasised inclusion, community engagement and indigenous partnerships as critical to securing energy infrastructure. He has also spoken about the importance of patient capital and community buy-in to Nigeria’s energy future.



In a public account of PINL’s operations, Okunbo described an approach built around traditional institutions, youths, local leadership, surveillance technology and continuous stakeholder engagement.



That is a materially different proposition from simply putting men on boats and around pipelines. Modern energy security involves intelligence, technology, community relations, rapid response, environmental protection, infrastructure maintenance and the creation of incentives for communities to protect – Not destroy the assets around them.



Indeed, host-community groups have publicly credited PINL’s engagement model with improved pipeline security and community relations, although such claims should themselves be assessed against independently verifiable production and security data.

The Tompolo question is legitimate to an extent, but the comparison is wrong. Tantita’s role in pipeline surveillance is itself an important part of Nigeria’s evolving security architecture. Reports have put the company’s annual contract value at about N48 billion, following a federal government award reported in 2023.



The appropriate question, therefore, is not whether Tompolo deserves a contract, while somebody else does not. The appropriate question is whether every contractor is delivering value commensurate with public expenditure.

That standard should apply equally to Tantita, PINL and every other contractor. If Dokubo believes the Federal Government is paying too much for pipeline security, let the contracts be published.



If he believes one company is receiving preferential treatment, let procurement records establish it. If he believes Niger Delta communities are being short-changed, let the data demonstrate it.

If he believes there is corruption, the appropriate institutions can investigate, but once the argument moves from evidence to ethnicity, the substance begins to disappear.



Energy security is bigger than Dokubo’s quarrel, as Nigeria has spent decades paying the price for oil theft, pipeline vandalism, illegal refining and production disruptions. Every barrel prevented from reaching the market affects government revenue, foreign exchange, investment confidence and the capacity of the country to finance development.

Pipeline security is therefore not merely about who gets a contract. It is about whether Nigeria can secure the infrastructure through which its economic lifeblood flows.



That is the point Asari Dokubo appears to have missed. His intervention could have opened a valuable national debate about procurement transparency and the economics of Niger Delta security.

Instead, by advancing an extraordinary N2.7 trillion allegation without documentary proof and framing the matter partly through ethnic identity, he risks turning a serious national-security conversation into another quarrel over who owns the Niger Delta.



Nigeria needs more accountability, not more suspicion; more evidence, not more allegations; more collaboration, not more ethnic polarisation. The pipelines do not know the ethnicity of the men protecting them.

In a nutshell, the Nigerian economy does not either need such distraction(s) – What matters is whether the infrastructure is secure, whether oil production is protected, whether communities benefit, whether public money is properly spent and whether every contractor, regardless of name or origin, can account for the value delivered.



That is the conversation worth having and that is precisely why energy security should never be twisted on its head.

•Ayoola Ajanaku is a Communications and Advocacy Specialist based in Lagos, Nigeria

World.title: Despite Cut in MPR, Average Maximum Lending Rate Rises to 32.62%
World.content:
Kayode Tokede

Despite the reduction of the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) to 23 per cent by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) in its last meeting, the banking sector’s average maximum lending rate increased to 32.62 per cent in September 2026 from 29.20 per cent in August 2026.

Maximum lending rate refers to the highest permissible interest rate that lenders can charge borrowers. The rate is crucial for ensuring fair lending practices and protecting borrowers from excessive interest rates.

According to the CBN Money Market Indicators, the average maximum lending had opened January 2026 at 32.68 per cent when MPR was at 27 per cent, and reached a peak of 35.17 per cent in March 2026 as MPR stood at 26.50 per cent.

An investigation by THISDAY revealed that most Nigerian banks’ maximum lending rate remained flat between September and October 9, 2026 amid the 350 basis points MPR cut by MPC.

Specifically, between September 4, 2026 and October 9, 2026, “Manufacturing sector” maximum lending rates of Access Bank, Alpha Morgan Merchant Bank, Coronation Merchant Bank and Ecobank remained flat at 32.28 per cent, 35.00 per cent, and 35 per cent respectively.

FCMB Bank, Fidelity Bank Plc, First Bank of Nigeria also posted 41.40 per cent, 36 per cent and 36 per cent, respectively between September 4, 2026 and October 9, 2026…

In the period under review, Citi Bank saw its Manufacturing sector maximum lending rate drop to 19 per cent from 20 per cent, while Quest Merchant Bank Manufacturing sector maximum lending rate moved to 30 per cent from 35 per cent.

In June 2026, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had expressed that Nigerian banks are quick to raise lending rates when the CBN tightens monetary policy, but slow to reduce borrowing costs when rates are eased.

The Washington-based institution said the country’s monetary policy transmission mechanism has strengthened since the unification of the foreign exchange (FX) market in June 2023, although distortions within the banking system still persist.

According to the IMF, interest rate transmission in Nigeria follows what economists describe as a ‘rockets-and-feathers’ pattern, where banks rapidly increase lending rates during tightening cycles but are reluctant to reduce them when policy conditions soften.

The report stated that a 100 basis-point increase in the MPR typically pushes treasury bill and lending rates up by about 175 to 180 basis points almost immediately. However, a similar rate cut results in only a 25 to 30 basis-point decline in borrowing costs.

“This asymmetry — statistically significant — implies that banks transmit tightening rapidly and even amplify it but adjust much more slowly during easing cycles,” the IMF said.

The institution noted that interbank rates respond more evenly to both tightening and easing, while deposit rates remain largely unresponsive in either direction.

The IMF attributed the weak response in deposit rates to limited competition among banks for customer deposits and the existence of what it described as ‘captive depositors’ with limited investment alternatives.

CBN data revealed that the average prime lending rate also rose to .19.04 per cent in September 2026 from 17.86per cent in August 2026. In January 2026, the average prime lending rate was at 19.54 per cent, making it the highest so far since 2006.

The prime lending rate indicates the possible rate offered to the most creditworthy customers by Nigerian banks.

Nigeria’s average prime lending rate reached an all-time high of 19.66 per cent in November 2009 and a record low of 11.13per cent in March 2021.

The steady increase in interest rate reflected in the average prime lending rate last year as the CBN intensified its effort to tackle inflation rate and stabilize the local currency at the foreign exchange market.

Reacting, Investment Banker & Stockbroker, Tajudeen Olayinka stated that Nigerian banks are not compelling to adjusted lending rate to MPR, but to use it as a guide to pricing and repricing loans and advances, plus other financial instruments, in a manner that gives credence to risk/return framework associated with different loan applicants.

“You’ll recall MPR was adjusted to 23per cent, to make it aligned with what the market is asking for. Only prime borrowers will receive an interest rate that is close to MPR or risk-free rate. It is also a function of demand and supply,” he said.

Also, the Vice President, Highcap Securities, David Adonri stated that the increase in lending rate in the Nigerian banking sector means there was tight money supply in the credit market in September 2026 despite massive cuts in MPR.

Cordros Research in a report stated that it expected the market performance to be shaped by the extent to which the policy adjustment translates into lower market yields, improved liquidity and reduced corporate financing costs.

“Continued macroeconomic stability, particularly in inflation and the exchange rate, will also remain important to investor sentiment. Against this backdrop, 2026FY earnings and dividend announcements, foreign and domestic portfolio flows, corporate actions and company-specific developments are likely to be the key drivers of the market performance in Q4-2026,” the firm had explained.

However, analysts have predicted a further increase in the average maximum lending and primer lending rate amid steady ease in inflation figures.

World.title: KPMG: Economic Uncertainty, AI Readiness Will Shape Next Phase of African Investment
World.content:
Emma Okonji

African business leaders remain confident about growth, but converting that confidence into sustained performance will depend on how effectively organisations navigate economic uncertainty, geopolitical disruption, technological change and structural constraints, according to the 2026 KPMG Africa CEO Outlook.

The Outlook examined the priorities shaping business leadership across the continent, from investment and growth expectations to emerging risks, Artificial Intelligence (AI), talent and sustainability.

According to the report, while 66 per cent of African CEOs are confident in the global economy, broadly in line with the global benchmark of 65 per cent, confidence in their domestic economies stood at 72 per cent. A further 79 per cent are confident in the growth prospects of their own organisations.

The confidence is supported by recent performance, with 86 per cent of African CEOs reporting revenue growth in their latest financial year. However, only 58 per cent expect annual earnings growth of at least 2.5 per cent over the next three years, compared with 68 per cent globally, suggesting that translating revenue gains into sustained profitability remains a priority.

According to the findings, cybersecurity and data security, alongside supply-chain resilience, are the leading threats to growth among African CEOs, each cited by 31 per cent of respondents.

According to the KPMG Outlook, about 45 per cent of African CEOs are increasing investment in cybersecurity and digital-risk resilience, 36 per cent in regulatory compliance and reporting, and 31 per cent in AI integration.

The findings suggested that resilience was no longer simply about protecting organisations against disruption. It is increasingly a condition for growth, enabling businesses to adapt to changing market conditions, protect critical operations and make investment decisions with greater confidence.

For businesses operating across diverse African markets, this requires balancing immediate operational pressures with longer-term investment in infrastructure, technology, governance and capabilities, the outlook said.

Giving details about the outlook, Senior Partner & CEO at KPMG One Africa, Tola Adeyemi, said: “African businesses are demonstrating confidence in their ability to grow, but the next phase of growth will require more than ambition. Leaders must make deliberate choices about where to invest, how to strengthen resilience and how to build organisations that can adapt to disruption. The opportunity is to translate the continent’s resources, markets and entrepreneurial capacity into more productive, competitive and sustainable businesses.”

On sustainability shifts towards measurable business value, the report explained that African CEOs were increasingly approaching sustainability through the lens of commercial performance, operational resilience and reporting readiness.

According to the outlook, almost half, or 48 per cent, report embedding sustainability more deeply into core business strategy, compared with 63 per cent globally, adding that 40 per cent are narrowing their focus to sustainability issues most critical to business performance, against 21 per cent globally.

Taken together, the findings presented a picture of African business leaders who remain optimistic but face increasingly complex decisions about where and how to invest.

“Economic and geopolitical uncertainty is reinforcing the importance of resilience, while AI adoption, skills development and sustainability are placing new demands on organisational capabilities. For Africa, the challenge extends beyond individual business performance. Converting the continent’s resources, demographic potential and expanding markets into sustained growth will require investment in infrastructure, local value chains, skills and competitive business environments,” the report further said.

World.title: LATEST on ‘early’ SASSA Old-Age Grants in November 2026
World.content:
SASSA Old-Age Grants in November 2026 will take place earlier than initially scheduled. In a change intended to prevent disruption around the local government elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026, some disbursements have been moved to this week.

Specifically, four-million recipients of SASSA Old-Age Grants in November 2026 will now receive their money on Friday 30 October 2026. While that’s good news for now – a 28-day wait (down from 32 days) – it does mean a longer run into next month’s December disbursements just before the Christmas holidays.

SASSA OLD-AGE GRANTS IN NOVEMBER 2026

The South African Social Security Agency confirmed the revised schedule after consulting stakeholders and securing National Treasury approval. Disability and the three Children’s grants were also brought forward, but not to this week:



Old-Age Grant: Friday 30 October 2026.

Disability Grant: Monday 2 November 2026.

Children’s grants: Tuesday 3 November 2026.

‘Fourth’ date for grants under review: Thursday 5 November 2026.

SASSA has urged beneficiaries to avoid unnecessary visits to its offices. Once the funds have been deposited, recipients can access them through their usual payment channels.

HOW MUCH ARE SASSA OLD-AGE GRANTS IN NOVEMBER 2026?

Date clashes with local government elections in November forced SASSA and the National Treasury’s hand. Image: File

Current monthly grant amounts are unchanged after zero October top-ups were approved:

Old-Age Grant: R2 400 (60-74) and R2 420 for 75 and older.

(60-74) and for 75 and older. War Veterans Grant: R2 420 .

. Disability Grant: R2 400 .

. Child Support Grant: R580 per child.

per child. Foster Care Grant: R1 300 per child.

per child. Chile Care Dependency Grant: R2 400 .

. Grant-in-Aid: R580 for eligible recipients.

STRICTER BIOMETRIC AND FRAUD PREVENTION

The revised payment calendar comes as Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana delivered his 2026 Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS). In the address on Wednesday 21 October, he also confirmed that the R370 Social Relief of Distress (SRD) grant would be extended for another year, to March 2028. However, the minister did not announce a definitive timetable for transforming the temporary SRD grant into permanent Basic Income Support.

Government says it will continue working to connect beneficiaries with employment, training and enterprise opportunities through its MzansiXchange data platform. And Treasury is also pursuing stronger biometric verification and fraud prevention to generate savings.

Try contact SASSA directly here if you have any queries:

SASSA toll-free line: 0800 601 011

World.title: Cats to burps: The Kiffness trolls President Trump [video]
World.content:
The Kiffness has spoofed President Donald Trump's burp. Images via YouTube screenshot

The Kiffness has done it again with another catchy jingle after by putting his unique spin on viral sound – this time poking fun at President Donald Trump burping mid-sentence.

The quirky artist has amassed millions of views with his samples of everything from animal sounds to singing children.

THE KIFFNESS TROLLS TRUMP’S BURP

The Kiffness’s latest music offering has poked fun at viral video of President Donald Trump burping mid-sentence.



The US leader was speaking at a campaign rally in South Carolina, in which he supported a local senator.

During his address, the 80-year-old appeared to loudl belch. Without excusing himself, he continued talking.

The video quickly went viral with many expressing disgust and concern.



Adding his spin was Cape Tow muso, The Kiffness who managed to turn the president’s ill-mannered actions into a catchy tune.

The “remix” was posted on Facebook, receiving hundreds and thousands of views, and almost 10 000 comments.

EATING THE CATS

It’s not the first time, The Kiffness has spoofed comments made by Trump.



Last year, the outspoken muso raised nearly R2 million for an SPCA shelter in the US from the proceeds of his catchy song Eating The Cats, featuring the then President-elect.

The song sampled the incoming statesman’s viral comments about immigrants, particularly Haitian people, whom he claimed eat domesticated animals.

An official music video has over 14 million YouTube views and many more millions on other streaming sites.

World.title: Storms batter Europe hitting power supplies, flights and phones
World.content:
PARIS - Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday, killing a man, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes and disrupting travel and phone networks.

A man died when a tree fell on him in southwestern Scotland, while a runner in a marathon in northern France was injured when a tree was felled by strong winds during the race.

More than 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany had power cuts inflicted by the passage of storms Boelo and Austen within 24 hours of each other, authorities in the countries said.

In the Argyll and Bute region of western Scotland, winds of up to 84 miles (135 kilometres) an hour were recorded. Trees and power cables brought down by the storm blocked roads and rail lines across Scotland and northern England.

Britain's Energy Networks Association said more than 400,000 homes had lost power at some stage during the storms.

Part of the pier at Brighton on the southern England coast, unused since a fire in 2003, blew away in Storm Austen on Friday.

The powerful winds also battered northern France across the Channel as Europe battled its first big autumn storms of the year. Experts have warned of more extreme weather events because of global warming.

Authorities warned of flood risk in regions in Scotland and England.

A runner was lightly injured in the northern French city of Lille near the start of the city's marathon, which was being staged for the first time in 31 years.
