World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.

03

What to See & Do

MONDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — ART IN THE RAIN Pinacoteca de São Paulo, Luz The Pinacoteca is open today from 10am to 6pm in Luz. It is the best wet-weather move in the centre: Brazilian collection, high ceilings and proper quiet. Entry costs R$40, and you can reach it on Linha 4-Amarela, Luz station. Spend ninety minutes with the 19th-century Brazilian portraits and then take the covered walkway to the contemporary annexe. Photography is allowed in most galleries without flash. Afterwards, walk two minutes to Mercado Municipal, open Monday to Saturday from 6am to 6pm. Lunch at the mezzanine counters avoids the heaviest crush. This is the committed choice: art in the morning, market lunch, then a metro back west before the evening rain picks up.

OUTDOORS — SHORT FLAT WALK Parque Ibirapuera, gate 5 The park stays open until midnight and costs nothing, but today’s rain window is best used between 11am and 3pm. Stick to the paved loop near the lake. Enter at the Pedrosa gate, buy a coffee at the central kiosk, and keep the route under 45 minutes so you can reach shelter quickly. The ground will be wet and leaf-slick.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — VILA MADALENA Desk weather Head to Coffee Lab in Vila Madalena, open from 9am, for serious espresso and tables that welcome laptops on weekdays. Wi-Fi is reliable and the back room stays quiet. If you need a formal desk, WeWork Paulista in Jardins offers day passes with call booths and fast internet. Book before noon because rain pushes more people indoors.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — OPEN-AIR WALK Beco do Batman alley For the opposite mood, walk the Beco do Batman in Vila Madalena between showers. The open-air street art is always open and free, and today it will be almost empty. Carry an umbrella and skip the side streets if the rain turns heavy. The cobbles drain poorly and the alleys feel quiet in wet weather.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Pinheiros, low-key Stay in Pinheiros once the rain settles. Start with a glass of natural wine at Bar Balcão on Rua Fidalga, a neighbourhood room with easy weeknight flow. For the second stop, Pirajá on the same strip serves cold chope and good appetisers until late. It offers covered seating and screens on slow news nights. No big match or headline concert tonight, so this is a conversation-and-food evening rather than a crowd night. Book a table at Bar Balcão for any group above two.

ALSO ON TODAY Sala São Paulo guided visit — Centro — guided visits today, free admission for visits; tickets hour-by-hour Mercado Municipal walk-through — Centro — Mon–Sat 6am–6pm, free entry, closed Sunday after 4pm MASP — Jardins — CLOSED today; reopens Tuesday 10am–8pm, R$85 (free Tuesday) Japan House (closed today; open Tue-Sun) São Paulo — Jardins — CLOSED today; reopens Tuesday 10am–6pm, free Museu do Ipiranga — Ipiranga — CLOSED today; reopens Tuesday 10am–5pm, R$30 (free Wednesday)

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

The single-journey metro fare is R$5.40. Lines 1-Blue, 2-Green, 4-Yellow and 5-Lilac run the normal Monday service, with the usual afternoon peak crowding from 5:30pm to 7pm.

Rodízio today: vehicles with plates ending 1 or 2 cannot circulate in the expanded centre from 7am–10am and 5pm–8pm. Ride apps are the dry option across town.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Mercado Municipal in Centro for mortadella sandwiches and pastel, around R$40–70 with a drink. Alternatively, a quieter plate at Balaio, near Paulista, for R$65–90.

Dinner: Bar Balcão in Pinheiros for petiscos and wine, R$90–140 per head. Pirajá next door does good bolinho de arroz and cold chope closer to R$70–100.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a compact umbrella, a thin waterproof layer and your phone battery pack. Cards and Pix accepted widely; keep R$30 in cash for market stalls and small counters.

Book museum tickets at the door for Pinacoteca, but reserve ahead only if you are bringing a group. Most bars around Pinheiros take cards and Pix.

In the rain, watch your bag on the Luz station footbridge and keep phones inside your jacket rather than in back pockets around Santa Cecília.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

For newcomers, the Expats São Paulo WhatsApp thread usually shares weather-day coffee plans; ask around Vila Madalena cafés after 4pm. The city is quieter this Monday due to the runoff result.

Digital nomads tend to gather at Coffee Lab or WeWork Paulista on wet weekdays. Arrive before 11am for the best seats near power outlets.

08

Game Day

THE WEEK AHEAD

No major São Paulo club match falls on this Monday. The quiet part of the calendar is why the city’s bars are tuned to news and NFL-style weeknight screens.

Keep an eye on Corinthians, Palmeiras and São Paulo FC fixture pages this week; the next big match-day crowd will form near Vila Madalena and Itaim Bibi.Olímpico bar in Pinheiros and The Blue Pub in Moema remain the safe choices when a local derby appears.Call ahead for table bookings on match nights.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Brazil’s real strengthened 1.3% on Friday to R$4.98 per US$ and the Ibovespa, the main stock index, rose 0.5% to 205,083 before the runoff. The market board above carries the settled Friday session because markets stayed shut over the weekend.

Brazil’s mid-month inflation gauge, the IPCA-15, rose 0.32% in October against a 0.43% forecast (previous 0.70%), and the annual rate reached 4.62% against a 4.73% forecast (previous 4.47%). Source: RT economic calendar (RT).

The central bank’s target is 3 percent with a tolerance band of 1.5 percentage points either side.This week’s global focus shifts to the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan decisions, plus big tech earnings.For expats earning in dollars or euros, any signal on US rates will matter more than the day-to-day exchange-rate print.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD MON 26 — Pinacoteca, coffee in Vila Madalena, dinner in Pinheiros TUE 27 — MASP (closed today; open Tue-Sun) reopens, free Tuesday, dry and milder WED 28 — Museu do Ipiranga (closed today; open Tue-Sun) free day, mostly dry THU 29 — Heavy rain likely, plan indoors FRI 30 — Check club fixtures, reserve sports-bar table early

Background: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight: Iron Maiden, Rain, Runoff Night.

Background: São Paulo Daily Brief.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

What is actually open for indoor sightseeing on Monday?

Pinacoteca de São Paulo in Luz is open today from 10am to 6pm, R$40. Sala São Paulo has guided visits, free for the visit-only option. Mercado Municipal is open Monday 6am–6pm and free to enter. MASP (closed today; open Tue-Sun), Japan House, Museu do Ipiranga and Sesc Pompeia are closed today.

Which metro line is easiest for a rainy day in the centre?

Take Linha 4-Amarela to Luz station for Pinacoteca, Sala São Paulo and Mercado Municipal. The single-journey metro fare is R$5.40. Keep the transfer at Luz to Linha 1-Blue if you head toward Vila Madalena from América station.

Do I need cash or can I use card and Pix?

Cards and Pix are accepted across most cafés, museums and bars. Keep R$30 in cash for small market stalls and the street vendors. At the Pinacoteca ticket desk, debit and credit cards are accepted. At Mercado Municipal, some fruit stalls and pastel counters prefer cash.

The headline today is the free, air-conditioned Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil in Centro, open from 9am to 8pm and ideal for a wet day.

On the business front, Lula won Sunday’s runoff and Brazilian markets reopen today; the board shows Friday’s close.

Your one-line day: stay central or indoors, work from a café in Botafogo, and save the beach for Wednesday.

03

What to See & Do

MONDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — INDOOR CULTURE Spend the wet hours at CCBB, free in Centro Make Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil your anchor today. It is free and open from 9am to 8pm on Mondays. You will find rotating exhibitions inside a handsome 1906 building. Check the programme desk on arrival for current shows. The centre is at Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro. Take Metrô Line 2 to Uruguaiana and walk three blocks. Afterwards, stroll under cover to Real Gabinete Português de Leitura on Rua Luís de Camões, free and open until 5pm. It is one of Rio’s most beautiful reading rooms. Monday suits it well with fewer visitors.

OUTDOORS — RAINY-DAY GARDEN Jardim Botânico works even in drizzle If you want greenery between showers, head to Jardim Botânico. It opens daily at 8am and closes at 5pm. Entry is R$40 for residents and R$80 for foreigners. The palm avenues and orchid house offer partial cover. Carry an umbrella and wear shoes that can handle wet paths. It is a 30-minute ride from Copacabana by taxi.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — BOTAFOGO Set up in Botafogo for reliable wifi and good coffee Start at Slow Bakery in Botafogo, which opens early and has good pastries plus stable wifi. Aim for a window seat. For a longer work session, try Curto Café on Voluntários da Pátria. It is laptop-friendly and busy with freelancers by 10am. Both are walking distance from Botafogo metro. Rainy Mondays make them calmer than usual.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — SANTA TERESA A moody afternoon in the hills If the weather clears briefly, ride the bondinho to Santa Teresa. The old tram leaves from Carioca in Centro. Even under cloud, the neighbourhood rewards wandering. Parque das Ruínas has wide views and free entry, open Tuesday to Sunday though — check before you go. For today, the safer option is a late lunch at a Santa Teresa restaurant with covered seating. Bar do Mineiro opens in the afternoon.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Keep it local, low-key and close to home Monday night in Rio is quiet by design. Most live music rooms in Lapa stay shut until Thursday. Meet friends for pizza in Ipanema at Ferro e Farinha, which opens on Monday evenings. It is casual and good value. For a drink after 9pm, try Canastra Bar in Ipanema. The crowd is mixed local and expat, and the kitchen runs late. Avoid long walks on Avenida Atlântica after dark in the rain. Take a taxi or ride app between spots.

ALSO ON TODAY Museu do Amanhã — Centro — CLOSED today; opens Tuesday to Sunday 10am–6pm, free on Tuesdays; a rainy-day science museum Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR) — Praça Mauá — free on Tuesdays; check its opening days before you go Real Gabinete Português de Leitura — Centro — free, open 10am–5pm Monday to Friday Parque Lage — Jardim Botânico — free, open 8am–5pm; good for a green pause Museu Nacional de Belas Artes — Centro — closed today; opens Tuesday to Sunday 10am–6pm

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô Lines 1, 2 and 4 run normally today. The single-journey fare is R$7.90.

Expect bus and VLT delays if rain intensifies after midday. Ride apps may surge during the evening rush.

The seafront ciclovia is open but slippery in the wet. Use the boardwalk with care if you cycle.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: For a working lunch, try TT Burger in Botafogo for a quick, under-R$60 meal. Or go to Comuna in Botafogo for a coxinha and coffee near the metro.

Dinner: Start with pizza at Ferro e Farinha in Ipanema, around R$60–80 per person. For something quieter, try Satsuma in Ipanema for Japanese small plates.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a small umbrella, a dry bag for electronics, and cash or Pix. Many small restaurants still prefer Pix for payments.

Book a table for dinner if you plan to eat after 8pm — Monday options are fewer and fill with locals.If walking in Centro after rain, use well-lit streets near the metro and avoid the empty side lanes around Uruguaiana.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Digital nomads often cluster at Curto Café in Botafogo on Monday mornings. It is an easy place to meet other remote workers.

Look for the Rio Expats WhatsApp group or Internations meetups. Monday is usually quiet, so plan a bigger social outing for Thursday night.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

No Flamengo or Fluminense match falls on Monday. The local football week stays quiet until midweek cup fixtures.

For live sport at a bar, wait until Wednesday when Copa do Brasil ties usually land. Botafogo and Vasco fans often gather at Bar da Frente in Botafogo.

If you want a Monday night game on screen, ask at Blue Agave in Ipanema. It shows international football and has good wings.

Check Tuesday’s fixture list before committing. Monday is a rest day for most Carioca clubs.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Brazil’s real strengthened 1.3% on Friday to R$4.98 per US$, and the Ibovespa, the main stock index, rose 0.5% to 205,083, before Sunday’s runoff.Brazil’s mid-month inflation gauge, the IPCA-15, rose 0.32% in October against a 0.43% forecast (previous 0.70%), and the annual rate reached 4.62% against a 4.73% forecast (previous 4.47%).

Source: RT economic calendar (RT).Lula won a fourth term on Sunday, so the first test is whether the dollar stays below R$5.00 when B3, the São Paulo stock exchange, reopens.

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

I only have today free in Rio. What should I actually do?

Go to CCBB in Centro. It is free, opens 9am to 8pm, and gives you real Brazilian culture without weather risk. Then walk to Real Gabinete Português de Leitura nearby. It closes at 5pm and is free. End in Botafogo for coffee and a long lunch — Slow Bakery or Curto Café work well.

Is the beach worth it today?

No. Rain is likely all day, so the beach is a poor choice. Save Ipanema or Leblon for Wednesday, the driest day this week. Today is for indoor culture or café work.

How do I pay for things around Rio on a Monday?

Pix is the easiest and most accepted method. Keep R$50–100 in cash for small stalls. Cards work at most restaurants and museums. Use a ride app for longer trips rather than hailing taxis in the rain.

World.content:
Brazil wakes to a narrow Lula win and a furious Bolsonaro camp while its neighbours watch. A psychogram of how Latin America is feeling today.

Rio Times · Latin America

Key Facts —Brazil A mood of contested relief as Lula wins a fourth term and Flávio Bolsonaro, the defeated candidate, says he will seek to annul the result. —Argentina Watchful as a political fight next door raises worries about regional risk, with the extra yield on Argentine bonds near 700 points. —Mexico Calm and celebratory as Club América pays tribute to goalkeeper Memo Ochoa, and President Claudia Sheinbaum hails a democratic win in Brazil. —Chile Warmly welcoming as President José Antonio Kast congratulates Lula, framing the moment as a chance for a stronger bilateral future. —Colombia Business-minded amid corporate expansion news, while the region’s political drama plays out next door. —Peru Focused on domestic sport, with Universitario winning the first stage of the national volleyball league.

Latin America woke up to a Brazil split almost down the middle: Lula won a fourth term, and the loser says he will not accept it.

The Continent’s Mood Today

The dominant feeling across Latin America this morning is a nervous exhale. Brazil finally has a declared winner, but the result is too close, and the defeated side too angry, for anyone to truly relax.

Across the region, the story is Lula’s 51.79% to 48.21% win and Flávio Bolsonaro’s vow to seek an annulment. The anxiety is political rather than financial for now: investors are asking whether the dispute will drag through the courts.

Brazil – Relief, Fury and a Test for the Real

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s 80-year-old president, won Sunday’s runoff with 51.79% of the vote to 48.21% for Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, with all ballots counted, according to the electoral court (TSE). It is Lula’s fourth term.

But the victory arrived with an immediate wound. Flávio Bolsonaro said late on Sunday that he did not recognise the result and would ask for the election to be annulled.

Argentina – Watching a Neighbour’s Fever

Argentina is watching its neighbour’s political fight with a familiar, queasy recognition. The worry is a knock-on effect on Argentine bonds if the dispute drags on.

The specific fear is that a Brazilian political crisis will raise risk premiums across the region. Argentina’s country risk, the extra yield investors demand to hold its bonds, has already climbed to around 700 points, its highest level in a year, and a regional wobble could push it higher.

Underneath this is a deeper memory. Argentines know what it feels like to have a polarised election end in a disputed, economically painful aftermath.

For an Argentine holding assets, the practical point is stark: keep an eye on the real, because when Brazil sneezes, Buenos Aires still catches a cold.

Mexico – Football, Democracy and a Warm Nod North

Club América hosted Pachuca on Sunday evening in round 14 of the Liga MX Apertura, as league leaders. The night was also a tribute to Guillermo ‘Memo’ Ochoa, the goalkeeper with the most appearances in the club’s history.

The mood was meant to be celebratory and nostalgic: a night to honour Ochoa’s long career between the posts, with nothing to do with politics.Politically, Mexico’s response to Brazil was warm.President Claudia Sheinbaum posted on X that democracy had won and the people of Brazil had won, congratulating Lula on his victory.The deeper sentiment is relief that a fellow leftist leader has survived a tough fight.For a foreigner in Mexico City, this means a week of normal life, with the Formula 1 Mexican Grand Prix on 30 October–1 November, which Canaco, the Mexico City chamber of commerce, expects to bring in MXN 22.2 billion (about US$1.2 billion), and Day of the Dead preparations under way.

Chile – A Hand Extended Across the Andes

Chile’s mood is one of courteous, slightly formal satisfaction. President José Antonio Kast spoke with Lula to congratulate him, saying that Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead and that the two countries will work on economic integration and the fight against organised crime.

There is also a personal note: Lula turns 81 on Tuesday, one day after Brazil’s markets reopen.

For a Chilean businessperson, the practical meaning is that Santiago wants a stable, predictable Brazil. Kast’s call signals that Chile intends to keep working with its largest South American neighbour.

Colombia – Corporate Confidence, Political Distance

Colombia is doing what it often does during regional political storms: talking business. Scanntech, a Uruguayan retail-data company that already operates in Colombia, raised US$180 million this month to expand its network across Latin America.

This is not obliviousness; it is insulation. The local angle is not ideological but commercial: will Brazilian instability hurt Colombian exports or investment flows?

For a foreigner holding assets in Colombia, the question is how far the market can stay insulated from Brazil’s political volatility. In Latin America, decoupling is never complete.

Peru – A Different Kind of Scoreboard

Peru’s sports pages have their own story today. Universitario beat Deportivo Wanka 3-0 to win the first stage of the Liga Peruana de Vóley, the country’s top volleyball league.

For a foreigner in Lima, the practical advice is simple: a Brazilian election is not the only conversation, so ask about the volleyball.

The Shared Mood

Across the region, there is a strange split-screen feeling. Brazil is a pot about to boil over, while most of its neighbours are trying to keep their own kitchens cool.

The shared mood is watchful, not panicked. Leaders have congratulated Lula, markets are about to deliver their verdict, and ordinary people are going about their Monday, whether that means a football tribute in Mexico, volleyball in Peru, or a business deal in Colombia.

But the undercurrent is unspoken and universal: no one wants another January 8. The memory of Brasília’s sacked buildings in 2023 is still too raw.

Today, the continent is holding its breath, hoping that Brazil’s wounded democracy can walk itself back from the edge.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who won the Brazilian election?

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the October 25 runoff with 51.79% of the vote to Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, with all ballots counted.

Why is Flávio Bolsonaro disputing the result?

He criticised the extension of voting hours on election day and said he would ask for the result to be annulled.

How are Latin American markets reacting?

Brazilian markets have not yet reacted because B3 reopens later today. The real strengthened 1.3% on Friday to R$4.98 per US$, and Argentina is watching for knock-on pressure on its bonds.

01 The world in one read

Global markets enter a week dominated by three major central-bank decisions, with the US Federal Reserve up first on Wednesday. The Fed is widely expected to hold its policy rate at 3.75–4.00%, pausing after September’s quarter-point increase.

The pause masks a live December debate. Preliminary US third-quarter GDP is forecast at 3.2% annualised, nearly a full point above the second quarter, and core inflation remains stuck above 3%.

Oil offered a rare pocket of relief. Brent fell on Monday, retreating from multi-month highs, but stays well above US$100 a barrel.

Asian equities were defensive rather than panicked, with Japan’s Nikkei down about 0.8% and South Korea’s Kospi also lower. Investors are still weighing energy costs against wobbles in technology and artificial-intelligence spending.

Assessment — Hold now, squeeze later risk looms MEDIUM The evidence leans toward a patient Fed this week but a nervous December. A 3.2% growth print and 3.1% core inflation leave policymakers with little room to declare victory, yet they are unlikely to surprise markets with a move absent fresh shocks. The variable to watch is how strongly Chair Jerome Powell pushes back against market pricing for another hike—or lets it survive.

03 The main event — a week of central-bank decisions

The Federal Reserve leads off on Wednesday with a hold widely priced in at 3.75–4.00%, but the decision is not the main uncertainty. The market’s real question is whether policymakers signal that September’s hike was the last or merely a pause before another move.

The European Central Bank follows on Thursday, expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.50%. The Bank of Japan rounds out the week on Friday, with investors watching for any drift toward policy normalisation.

The backdrop for all three is an economy that refuses to buckle under high rates. US growth is forecast to hit 3.2% annualised in the third quarter, and the labour market remains resilient enough to sustain wage pressure.

Oil is the wildcard. If supply fears return and energy costs climb back toward their highs, central banks will face a renewed inflation headache that could tilt the December calculus.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online exchange where users trade real money on outcomes, traders price another Fed rate hike before the end of 2026 at 76.5% (US$1.07 million traded) and a Fed rate cut by the December meeting at 2.5%, as of 00:01 ET on 26 October. These prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

04 Policy and data

The week’s data calendar is packed with signals that will shape the December decision. Durable goods orders for September are due on Tuesday, with the headline number forecast at 0.6% and the core measure excluding transport at 0.6%.

US consumer confidence is expected at 80.5, down from 81.9, while new home sales are seen slipping to 0.66 million. House price data will also land, with the S&P/Case-Shiller index forecast to rise 2.6% year-on-year.

Friday’s surveys set the tone. US business activity stayed strong: the S&P Global manufacturing PMI, a monthly survey of purchasing managers in which 50 separates growth from contraction, was 56.0 (forecast 55.5, previous 55.9), services 57.9 (forecast 58.0, previous 58.8) and the composite 57.6 (forecast 57.6, previous 58.4). University of Michigan consumers expect 4.7% inflation over one year (forecast 4.7%, previous 4.6%) and 3.5% over five years (forecast 3.5%, previous 3.4%).

Europe and Japan were more mixed. The euro-zone composite PMI fell to 51.9 (forecast 52.7, previous 53.1), with services at 51.7 (forecast 52.5, previous 53.0) and manufacturing at 52.4 (forecast 52.7, previous 52.9). Japan’s composite PMI held at 52.3 (forecast 51.9, previous 52.3) while manufacturing slipped to 53.3 (forecast 54.5, previous 54.1). Britain’s composite PMI rose to 53.1 (forecast 51.8, previous 52.0), services to 53.1 (forecast 51.8, previous 52.1) and manufacturing to 52.8 (forecast 51.7, previous 51.9), yet retail sales fell 0.4% (forecast −0.1%, previous +0.7%) and 0.7% excluding fuel (forecast −0.1%, previous +0.9%). Source: RT economic calendar (RT).

Core personal-consumption expenditure inflation, the Fed’s preferred gauge, prints on Thursday at an expected 3.1% year on year. That is far enough above 2% to keep policymakers from declaring the inflation battle won.

In Europe, the ECB’s hold at 2.50% on Thursday will be scrutinised for any hint that policymakers are debating a cut in 2027. For now, sticky services inflation argues for patience.

05 Commodities and currencies

Oil’s retreat from multi-month highs was the main mover in commodities. Brent slipped on Monday but stays well above US$100 a barrel.

The dollar index edged higher, supported by the view that US rates may need to stay elevated into December. The euro held near US$1.12, while the Japanese yen traded near 157 per dollar after edging higher last week.

Gold eased from the US$4,000-an-ounce threshold as the immediate haven bid faded alongside oil. Silver also dropped more than 1%, reflecting the broader pullback in precious metals.

The message from currency markets is one of patience: the dollar is not surging, but it is not weakening either, as traders wait for the Fed’s assessment of growth, inflation and December risk.

06 The Latin American read-through

The external backdrop remains challenging for Latin American economies, even as oil retreats from its highs. Brent well above US$100 a barrel keeps energy import bills elevated for countries such as Chile and Peru, while producers like Brazil and Colombia see a partial offset from export revenues.

The prospect of US rates staying higher for longer is a headwind for regional currencies and sovereign borrowers. A December hike would draw capital toward dollar assets and raise the cost of refinancing dollar-denominated debt.

Domestic policy remains the main driver for Latin American markets this week. Brazil, Mexico and Chile each have local data on the calendar that will shape investor expectations for growth and inflation.

Local data on Friday was mixed. Brazil’s mid-month inflation gauge, the IPCA-15, rose 0.32% in October against a 0.43% forecast (previous 0.70%), taking the annual rate to 4.62% (forecast 4.73%, previous 4.47%). Mexico’s economic activity indicator for August rose 0.6% on the month (forecast 0.3%) and 3.3% on the year (forecast 3.1%). Source: RT economic calendar (RT).

The takeaway for regional investors is caution, not panic. The global tone is defensive, but the absence of a sharp dollar spike or sustained oil shock leaves room for local stories to dominate individual markets.

03 On the B3 radar today — post-election repricing and Gerdau earnings

The domestic data calendar is light but not irrelevant. The FGV consumer confidence number at 08:00 BRT is the earliest opportunity to see whether voters feel better or worse about their own finances after the outcome.

The Central Bank’s Focus survey of economists, also due at 08:30 BRT, is the quiet mover. If economists lift their Selic expectations or push out the easing cycle, that repricing will hit rate-sensitive shares — banks, utilities and homebuilders — within minutes.

04 Copom and the macro backdrop

The Selic is 13.75%, and the next Copom meeting on 3–4 November is now the single most important date on the Brazilian calendar. The committee’s last decision came before the runoff result.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online exchange where users trade real money on outcomes, bettors put no change at the 3–4 November meeting at 60.5%, a 25-basis-point cut at 22.5%, a rise of 50 basis points or more at 6.7%, a 25-basis-point rise at 1.8% and a cut of 50 or more at 1.6% (US$92,979 traded; 26 October, 00:01 ET). These prices are bets, not polls.

Friday’s data pointed to easing price pressure. IBGE, Brazil’s statistics institute, reported mid-month inflation (IPCA-15) of 0.32% in October against a 0.43% forecast (previous 0.70%), and the annual rate reached 4.62% against a 4.73% forecast (previous 4.47%). Across the Atlantic, US activity stayed strong: the S&P Global manufacturing PMI, a survey of purchasing managers in which 50 separates growth from contraction, was 56.0 (forecast 55.5, previous 55.9), services 57.9 (forecast 58.0, previous 58.8) and the composite 57.6 (forecast 57.6, previous 58.4), while University of Michigan consumers expect 4.7% inflation over one year (forecast 4.7%, previous 4.6%) and 3.5% over five years (forecast 3.5%, previous 3.4%). Source: RT economic calendar (RT).

The mechanism is straightforward: a government that signals looser fiscal policy pushes up inflation expectations, which ties the central bank’s hands. If the Focus survey today shows expectations drifting upward, the Copom’s room to cut shrinks, and the yield curve steepens.

This is also why the real matters so much. A weaker currency imports inflation, and a slide through R$5.00 would reinforce the case for holding the Selic flat in November, which would weigh on equities and especially rate-sensitive sectors.

05 Corporate stories to watch today

Gerdau and Metalúrgica Gerdau report third-quarter results after the close, and they matter because steel is a leveraged play on both the domestic economy and the exchange rate. A weaker real helps exporters like Gerdau translate dollar-denominated revenue into stronger local results, even as higher rates squeeze domestic construction demand.

Beyond Gerdau, the post-election tape will separate exporters from domestic demand names.

The currency move is the swing factor today. If the real weakens through R$5.00, exporters with dollar-linked revenue — iron-ore producers, pulp makers, processed-food exporters — should hold up better than banks, retailers and utilities that live and die by domestic rates and consumption.

Earnings season is under way, and today’s Gerdau report is a steer from the heavy industry sector. Its commentary on freight costs and domestic demand will show how heavy industry is coping with high rates.

06 The levels to watch at the open

For the real, R$5.00 is everything. Friday’s close at R$4.98 leaves almost no margin for error.

A clean break above R$5.00 in the first hour of cash trading would open the door to 5.10 and then 5.20, levels that would force a serious conversation about the November Copom decision and possibly December’s meeting too.

For the Ibovespa, 205,000 points is the immediate reference from Friday’s close, but traders will be watching 200,000 as the psychological floor. The index is about 2% below its 52-week high near 209,700, and a post-election sell-off could push it back toward the lower part of its 146,200–209,700 range.

The early session should be framed as a test of whether the market believes Lula’s team can deliver fiscal credibility. If the real holds below R$5.00 and the Ibovespa stabilises around 205,000, the repricing was overdone; if both break, the move has further to run.

07 What to watch

USD/BRL and the R$5.00 line: The first hour of cash trading is the real stress test; a clean break through R$5.00 would extend the move and hit rate-sensitive sectors hard.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Selic?

The Selic is Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, set by the central bank’s Copom committee. It is the main tool for controlling inflation and is currently at 13.75%.

Why does R$5.00 matter for the real?

R$5.00 is a psychological threshold for USD/BRL. A break above it signals that investors are losing confidence in Brazil’s fiscal outlook, which pushes up inflation expectations and rates.

When is the next Copom decision?

The next Copom meeting is on 3–4 November, with the decision due on 4 November. Polymarket bettors currently assign 60.5% to no change and 22.5% to a 25-basis-point cut.

What is the Ibovespa?

The Ibovespa is Brazil’s main stock index, tracking the largest and most traded companies on the B3 exchange in São Paulo. It is the benchmark for Brazilian equity performance.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Monday, 26 October, 12:16 a.m. ET · Source: Brazil’s electoral court (TSE) count; Lula’s victory speech

Lula won the night, and in his victory speech he named his next fight: the tech giants behind the world’s social networks. In his first speech after the Brazil election 2026 runoff, he said social media would have to be regulated.

The 80-year-old president spoke on Sunday night, 25 October, after the count showed him ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator from Rio de Janeiro and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. For readers in the United States, the promise matters because US firms such as Meta, Google and X run big businesses in Latin America’s largest country.

Key Facts The promise Lula, Brazil’s 80-year-old president, said in his victory speech that social media platforms must be regulated.

The count Lula won the runoff with 51.79% of valid votes to Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, says Brazil’s electoral court (TSE).

The target He criticised giant tech companies that, he said, earn billions, pay no tax and tried to sway the vote.

What Lula Actually Said

Lula said platforms must be regulated and that crime in the digital world has to be treated like crime in real life. He called the contest a defeat for denialism, meaning the rejection of facts, and for lies.

He also went after the companies themselves, describing giants that make billions while paying no tax in Brazil and try to manipulate elections. He added that digital communication will take up a very large place in his next government.

How Close Was the Vote?

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE), which runs Brazilian elections, finished counting late on Sunday night. Lula took 51.79% of valid votes (blank and spoiled ballots excluded), or 64,256,232 ballots, against 48.21% for Flávio Bolsonaro.

The court’s formal certification of the result comes later. Our report on the runoff loser’s refusal to concede has the latest on the opposition’s stance.

Why Is Regulation So Divisive in Brazil?

Supporters of rules want clear limits on online fraud and disinformation. Critics fear that rules could turn into censorship of political speech.

Brazil’s courts have already acted. In June 2025 the Supreme Federal Court (STF), Brazil’s top court, ruled that a key article of the Marco Civil, the 2014 internet rights law, was partly unconstitutional. Platforms are now liable in more cases.

What It Means for US Readers

American platforms and their investors face a re-elected president who says digital platforms will be regulated. Any new rule on content or tax would hit their Brazilian operations first.

For now it is a promise, not a bill. Markets and companies will watch whether Lula sends Congress a proposal and how fast.

In plain English, “regulation” could mean rules on illegal content, platform liability or taxation. Lula named crime and tax, but did not say which tools he prefers.

What Is Not Known

Reports of the speech cite no draft law, no tax figure and no timetable. We also do not yet know how Congress would react.

We have not found a detailed answer from Flávio Bolsonaro’s camp. We will update this story when it responds.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Lula promise on social media?

He said digital platforms will have to be regulated and that online crime must be treated like offline crime. He gave no bill or date.

Who won Brazil’s runoff?

Lula took 51.79% of valid votes to Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21% in the TSE count. Formal certification by the court comes later.

World.title: Lula Sets Brazil Vote Record, 64.3 Million

File photo. (Photo: Ricardo Stuckert/PR, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Sunday, 25 October 2026, 11:58 p.m. ET · Source: Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Brazil’s election authority

An 80-year-old president just did something no Brazilian has done: he drew more votes than anyone in the country’s history. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the leftist leader of the Workers’ Party, won 64,256,232 votes in Sunday’s runoff, the second-round vote between the top two candidates.

Key Facts — Record Lula won 64,256,232 votes, the most ever cast for one Brazilian presidential candidate.

— Beat His own 2022 record of 60,345,999 votes, by about 3.9 million.

— Share Lula took 51.79% of valid votes, those cast for a candidate, against 48.21% for senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

— Next The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) formally declares the winner; Flávio Bolsonaro says he will seek annulment.

The record sits on top of a close and bitter race. Our Brazil election results page has the state-by-state count, and our Brazil election 2026 guide explains how the vote works.

Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE, ran the count. Its files show Lula with 64,256,232 votes and Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old conservative senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, with 59,826,041.

How Big Is the Record?

Lula’s old high-water mark was 60,345,999 votes, set in his 2022 runoff win over Jair Bolsonaro. This time he beat it by roughly 3.9 million.

Before 2022 the record was also Lula’s own, about 58.3 million votes in his 2006 runoff win. Jair Bolsonaro, the conservative former president, had won about 57.8 million in 2018.

The loser also set a mark. Flávio Bolsonaro’s 59.8 million votes top every total before 2022 and both of his father’s, and only Lula’s two wins are higher.

Why Do Records Keep Falling?

Brazil’s electorate is large and voting is compulsory for most adults, so turnout stays high. About 158.7 million people were eligible to vote this year.

A bigger roll means bigger totals, so a record count does not by itself signal a landslide. The margin this time was 4.4 million votes, or 3.6 points, close to the 2022 gap of about 2.1 million votes, or 1.8 points.

In Plain English Runoff: a second round held when no candidate wins over half the valid votes in round one.

a second round held when no candidate wins over half the valid votes in round one. Valid votes: ballots cast for a candidate, not blank or spoiled ones; percentages use this base.

ballots cast for a candidate, not blank or spoiled ones; percentages use this base. TSE: the Superior Electoral Court, which runs Brazil’s elections and publishes official results.

What It Means for US Readers

A record vote gives Lula a strong claim to a fresh mandate as he starts a fourth term, which matters for a US investor weighing Brazilian bonds, the real currency and Brazilian companies listed in New York. It does not settle the budget fights or the rival’s court challenge.

Washington deals with the same president on tariffs and trade, so the result points to continuity in Brasília rather than a reset.

What Is Not Known

The electoral court has still to issue its formal declaration of the winner, and we have not seen Flávio Bolsonaro file a court case. We also do not yet have the court’s final turnout and abstention figures.

Our Brazil news desk will update as the court publishes its final bulletin.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Lula win the most votes in Brazilian history?

Yes. His 64,256,232 votes in the 25 October 2026 runoff are the most any candidate has won in a Brazilian presidential election, topping his own 60,345,999 from 2022.

How many votes did Flávio Bolsonaro get?

Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator who lost, won 59,826,041 votes (48.21%). That is more than his father Jair Bolsonaro ever won, but about 4.4 million fewer than Lula.
