World.title: 1am motorcycle stop ends with three traffic charges and $800 bail
World.content:
1am motorcycle stop ends with three traffic charges and $800 bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A late night ride through Orange Walk Town ended with a young man facing three traffic charges.

Officers on patrol early Saturday morning stopped a motorcycle carrying two men on Naranjal Street. The rider told police his licence was at home.

But when officers took him there to check, they found that his driver’s licence had expired more than a year ago, in September 2025. The motorcycle’s licence was also out of date, and its insurance disc had expired at the start of September.

Dathan Raasaun Smith, 24, a labourer of Savannah Street, was taken to the Orange Walk Police Station and formally charged around 2:30am.

The charges are driving an unlicensed motor vehicle, driving without third party risk insurance and driving without a valid driver’s licence.

He was released on $800 police bail.

Police are urging motorists and riders to keep their driver’s licences, vehicle licences and insurance up to date, warning that patrols are continuing day and night.

World.title: No licence, no insurance, no vehicle sticker: Douglas Village rider charged
World.content:
No licence, no insurance, no vehicle sticker: Douglas Village rider charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 19 year old domestic of Douglas Village, Orange Walk District, has been charged with traffic offences.

She is Irainy Yoanie Marin.

Police say that around 8:15am on Friday, October 23, officers on mobile patrol on Douglas Road stopped a black Meilun motorcycle travelling from San Juan Village toward the Philip Goldson Highway.

Marin, the rider, was asked for her driver’s licence but could not produce it. Officers also found no insurance disc or licence sticker on the motorcycle, and she allegedly said she did not have valid insurance or a motor vehicle licence.

She was taken to the Trial Farm Police Sub Station, and the motorcycle was impounded.

Marin was charged with failing to produce a driving permit, using a motor vehicle not covered by third party risk insurance and using an unlicensed motor vehicle. She chose to remain silent when cautioned.

World.title: Belize enjoys another pleasant Sunday with sunshine and little rain
World.content:
Belize enjoys another pleasant Sunday with sunshine and little rain

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize can expect another pleasant day, with mainly fair and mild conditions continuing.

The National Meteorological Service says skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and partly cloudy tonight.

Showers will be isolated, though a few more are possible offshore and over some coastal areas tonight.

Temperatures remain comfortable, with cool nights. Coastal areas will reach 86°F (30°C), with a low of 75°F (24°C). Inland areas will climb to 90°F (32°C), cooling to 68°F (20°C) overnight. The hills will see a high of 78°F (26°C) and a low of 64°F (18°C).

At sea, winds are from the north at 5 to 15 knots, with slight to light chop and waves of 1 to 4 feet.

Similar weather is expected Monday and Monday night.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region in the next 48 hours.

Today’s forecast was issued by forecaster Derrick Rudon.

World.title: Haiti gang crisis raises security concerns for Belize and Caribbean nations
World.content:
Haiti gang crisis raises security concerns for Belize and Caribbean nations

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The escalating gang crisis in Haiti is raising serious security concerns across the Caribbean, including Belize, as a multinational force struggles to restore stability in the troubled CARICOM nation.

The latest concerns follow an ambush involving Salvadoran soldiers serving in Haiti, with four soldiers reported missing following the attack.

The incident marks the first major assault on the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations authorized multinational security mission tasked with confronting heavily armed criminal gangs.

According to Reuters, the mission has approximately 2,000 personnel deployed, significantly below its authorized strength of 5,500.

The force replaced an earlier Kenyan led security mission that struggled with shortages of funding, equipment and personnel.

Belize was among the Caribbean countries that offered support to the earlier international security effort.

Haiti’s deteriorating security situation has become a regional concern because of its potential implications for migration, organized crime and the movement of illegal weapons throughout the Caribbean.

Since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021, armed gangs have expanded their control over large sections of Port au Prince, forcing an estimated 1.4 million to 1.5 million people from their homes.

The crisis comes as Belize examines its own security challenges involving transnational criminal organizations.

Prime Minister John Briceño recently confirmed that Belize is holding preliminary discussions with the United States about possible cooperation under the Shield of the Americas initiative, which focuses on combating drug cartels and organized crime.

While the situations in Belize and Haiti are different, the developments highlight the growing importance of regional security cooperation.

Attention remains focused on the search for the four missing Salvadoran soldiers as the multinational mission faces another major challenge.

World.title: Halo BPO hiring Belizeans for work from home jobs paying up to $10 an hour
World.content:
Halo BPO hiring Belizeans for work from home jobs paying up to $10 an hour

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans looking for an opportunity to work from home still have time to apply for full time employment with Halo BPO.

The company is continuing to recruit outbound sales agents, offering starting pay of $8.50 Belize dollars per hour, increasing to $9.00 after two weeks and $10.00 after 30 days.

Employees will receive weekly payments and work daytime hours from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Belize time.

Halo BPO is particularly interested in applicants with previous experience in appointment setting or home improvement sales.

Candidates must also have a suitable home office setup, including a reliable wired internet connection with minimum download and upload speeds of 40 Mbps.

Other requirements include a webcam, a clear USB headset and a computer with at least a quad core 2.0 GHz processor and 8GB of RAM.

An SSD is preferred, while Chromebooks are not accepted.

Applicants must also have a quiet, professional workspace suitable for handling customer calls.

Interested Belizeans can apply by emailing [email protected], using their full name in the subject line.

World.title: Tough cleaning jobs? Universal Hardware has NorthStar pressure washers starting at $4,614
World.content:
Tough cleaning jobs? Universal Hardware has NorthStar pressure washers starting at $4,614

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): From dirty driveways and concrete surfaces to outdoor equipment and commercial work areas, tough cleaning jobs call for the right tools.

Universal Hardware is highlighting its NorthStar electric pressure washers, offering Belizeans two powerful options for tackling demanding outdoor cleaning tasks.

Customers can choose between a 2,000 PSI model and a 3,000 PSI model, depending on their pressure washing requirements.

The NorthStar 2,000 PSI Electric Pressure Washer, Model 1571102, is priced at $4,614, providing an option for customers who need dedicated electric pressure washing equipment.

Those seeking higher pressure can consider the NorthStar 3,000 PSI Electric Pressure Washer, Model 1571103, priced at $4,978.

That means customers can move from the 2,000 PSI model to the 3,000 PSI option for an additional $364.

Both units feature wheeled designs, allowing users to move the equipment around suitable work areas.

Electric pressure washers can be useful for property maintenance, outdoor cleaning and other applications where pressurized water is appropriate.

For businesses, resorts, contractors and property owners across Belize, investing in suitable cleaning equipment can support regular maintenance and help keep outdoor areas presentable.

Customers interested in either NorthStar model can visit Universal Hardware for more information about availability, specifications and purchasing options.

World.title: Four Belizean students shine in Taiwan art competition with over 60,000 entries
World.content:
Four Belizean students shine in Taiwan art competition with over 60,000 entries

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Four talented Belizean students have brought international recognition to the country after winning awards at the 57th World School Children’s Art Exhibition in Taiwan.

The young artists competed against more than 60,000 entries from 43 countries, earning a silver medal, a bronze medal and two Excellence Awards.

To celebrate their achievements, Taiwan’s Ambassador to Belize, Amino Chi, hosted a special luncheon on October 22, 2026, where he presented medals and certificates to the students on behalf of the competition organizers.

Isabella Emma Waldman of St. Catherine Academy received the Silver Medal, while Sanjana Moolchandani of Belize Elementary School earned the Bronze Medal.

Samar Bathija and Kushan Thadhani, both of Belize Elementary School, received Excellence Awards.

The international award ceremony was held in Taipei on August 16, 2026.

Joining the celebration were St. Catherine Academy Principal Dr. Salome Tillett, Belize Elementary School Principal Mrs. Majiba Sharp, and the students’ proud parents.

The Taiwan Embassy congratulated the young Belizean artists for their outstanding accomplishments on the international stage.

The Embassy is also encouraging more Belizean students to participate in the 58th World School Children’s Art Exhibition in 2027, highlighting the importance of artistic expression and cultural exchange between Belize, Taiwan and the wider world.

World.title: Panton rallies UDP supporters in Corozal and Orange Walk ahead of municipal elections
World.content:
Panton rallies UDP supporters in Corozal and Orange Walk ahead of municipal elections

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Opposition Leader Tracy Panton is highlighting the United Democratic Party’s municipal election preparations following visits to Corozal and Orange Walk.

In a statement, Panton thanked supporters in both districts and reaffirmed her commitment to leading the UDP as it organizes its nine municipal slates.

She said travelling across Belize has provided opportunities to hear directly from residents about their concerns, priorities and expectations.

Panton described her leadership role as both an honour and a responsibility, saying she intends to approach it with humility and determination.

The UDP leader also outlined several areas she wants the party to emphasize, including democratic values, stronger communities, economic opportunities and improvements in living standards.

She argued that political leadership should be measured by its willingness to listen to citizens and deliver results.

Panton placed particular emphasis on community participation, encouraging residents to engage with their neighbours and support initiatives addressing local needs.

Her message also focused on party unity as the UDP continues its municipal preparations.

The Opposition Leader said the party’s supporters in Corozal and Orange Walk have encouraged her to continue meeting communities and promoting the UDP’s agenda.

Panton’s statement did not announce specific municipal policy proposals or identify the individual candidates on the nine slates.

World.title: ‘Bunny’ scores in 100th WSL appearance as points shared in Manchester derby
World.content:
Manchester City's Jamaican striker #09 Khadija Shaw (right) reacts late in the second half during the English Women's Super League football match between Manchester City and Liverpool at Joie Stadium in Manchester, north-west England on May 3, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Manchester City star striker Khadija “Bunny” Shaw scored on her 100th Women’s Super League (WSL) appearance, but Manchester United struck late to seal a derby draw on Sunday.

The Jamaican, who is among the nominees for the 2026 Women’s Ballon d’Or, scored a thunderbolt from the penalty area to give City the lead in the 66th muinute.

However, the Blues were forced to settle for a draw after Elisabeth Terland fired home after reacting first to a long ball into the box in the 89th minute.

It snapped City’s perfect start to the season, however they would be pleased with a draw on the road against their cross-town rivals.

World.title: Port Royal residents furious over ‘unnecessary’ sewage line construction
World.content:
Derek Powell, resident of Polygon Battery in Port Royal

Residents of Polygon Battery Housing Scheme are protesting a new sewage project in the area by the National Water Commission (NWC) which they say has not been clearly communicated to them and is unnecessary.

“They are forcing this sewage system on us which we don’t need. We don’t need it. It is very costly… they are saying that we should meet them on main [road], so we have to [dig] up our driveway, [dig] up everything and come and meet them on the main. That is another cost to us,” said Christopher Farr, who has lived in the community for over 60 years.

Farr explained that there are two areas of the community which sit next to each other and the other is in need of the sewage lines.

“There are two different segments in the scheme. A housing scheme, which was built in the 80s, which is connected to a sewage system. They need it. Because that is the only way to dispose of their waste. And there is the Polygon Battery housing scheme, which consists of around 56 homes, that already have a septic tank in their home,” he said.

Farr explained that community members were told that joining the sewage system was optional at first, which he described as misleading.

“It worked out now in the end that that was a lie. It is mandatory. We must take it. And if it passes our home, we still have to pay for it. So, we are here today to demonstrate that we don’t need it and it should not pass our home,” he said.

Another resident, Derek Powell, also maintained that the project is not necessary. He added that the backyard septic facilities in the community, like his own, are low cost, expressing concern that the new project will be much more expensive

“They are telling us when we went into a meeting, 115 per cent increase on our water bill” he said noting that his current private tank serving a family of four, only costs him $25,000 to clean every three or so years.

Powell maintained that the digging to lay pipes in the community has been prolonged and resulting in reduced road access in the community.

“This is the entrance of the housing scheme. And look at it, over a year and a half and up until now, they haven’t fixed this, but all they are doing is they are digging here, they are digging there and they are doing all sorts of stuff…. And we don’t need that.

Seventy-three-year old Alice Murphy confirmed she already has sewage management facilities attached to her home. The elderly woman also expressed fears of a bill increase in conjunction with the sewage system installation.

“I’m a pensioner. My husband give me his pension when he gets it at end of month time. So what am I going to do? Pay for sewage out on the street and I have my own in here already?” she asked.

“Not with me, I will fight until I die,” Murphy added.

World.title: Jamaica aims to raise minimum gun sentence to 20 years
World.content:
Dr Andrew Holness

Jamaica’s National Security Council (NSC) has recommended that persons convicted of illegal firearm possession face a new minimum sentence of 20 years in prison.

In a press release on Sunday, the NSC said the recommendation is in line with its commitment to refine the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 (Firearms Act) to make it tougher while protecting the innocent and vulnerable.

What’s more, adults who groom children to use, store, transport, or acquire illegal guns will face a new criminal offence under proposed amendments to the Firearms Act, the NSC said, noting that “this is necessary to address the gap whereby gangs seek to recruit and enlist minors in the commission of gun crimes.”

The NSC said it also agreed that further consideration should be given to how cases involving children found with illegal firearms are handled.

“The concerns raised regarding imitation firearms will be clearly addressed to distinguish between toy guns and guns designed to realistically imitate a weapon. The review will also examine matters surrounding firearms with expired licences,” the release stated.

It added that before the new provisions take effect, the Government will provide a gun amnesty and cash buy-back programme, giving anyone holding an illegal gun the opportunity to surrender it.

The Ministry of National Security and Peace has been directed to have the draft legislation ready by the end of November 2026 for wider consultations, according to the release.

Chairman of the NSC, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, said the amendments strengthen the law while keeping it fair.

“We have seen what criminals are capable of, and we will not stand by while they put guns in the hands of our children,” he said. “We are determined to send a strong signal against illegal guns and those who promote them, while making sure the law is fair to the most vulnerable. Make no mistake, this administration is drawing a line in the sand against gun crime, and we are determined to eliminate the gun culture from our society.”

Cocaine Seizures in August 2026

The NSC said it also received a briefing from Commissioner of Police, Dr Kevin Blake, on the intensified effort to interdict and seize illegal drugs entering Jamaica.

The Jamaica Constabulary Force has seized 8,734.37 kilograms of cocaine since the start of the year. That amounts to 74 per cent of the 11,852.01 kilograms seized over the 10-year period between 2016 and 2025, the release noted.

The NSC commended the security forces and the Jamaica Customs Agency (JCA) for their work in keeping the country safe by finding and recovering illegal drugs, weapons, and other contraband.

The NSC noted that, given the effective closure of various drug trafficking routes by US operations in the region, there will be greater attempts to use Jamaica’s geographic location for transshipment.

“It was made clear that we will not allow our country and our sovereign territory to be used for illicit activities,” the release stated, adding that Jamaica will continue to intensify its cooperation with international and regional partners and strengthen maritime, air, and port interdiction efforts.

Dealer and Demonstration Licence Plates

The NSC said it received an update from Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) on its proposed new regime for issuing Dealer and Demonstration Licence Plates, which it said are now being unlawfully used as permission to regularly operate vehicles on public roadways without permanent registration and vehicle identification.

“This facilitates scammers and other criminals in the commission of crimes and provides an avenue to evade taxes,” the release said.

The NSC has directed that the current plates be discontinued and that a new form of temporary vehicle identification be considered for the specific purposes of demonstration or dealer transit.

It was recommended that the new system be electronically enabled to link the plate with the specific vehicle to which it will be temporarily assigned and that the identification plate itself be GPS- and RFID-enabled.

“This will ensure control of the plates issued and enable the police to immediately verify the dealer to whom the identification plate was issued, the particulars of the vehicle assigned to it, and the location of the plate should it be suspected of involvement in an incident,” said the NSC.

The new system will network the TAJ, the Island Traffic Authority (ITA), the JCF, and the JCA, allowing for easier cross-verification.

Sligoville Operation

The NSC said it received a briefing on the police operation in Sligoville and extended condolences to the relatives and colleagues of the brave officers, Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose, who were killed in the line of duty.

The prime minister said the Sligoville incident demonstrates the dangers police face on a daily basis.

“As a Christian nation, we regret the loss of life of any citizen; however, we pay particular honour to those who lose their lives in the line of duty to keep us safe. We also commend the careful actions of the security forces to ensure that the lives of innocent children were spared,” Holness said. “There still exist criminals who will go to the extreme of putting their own families’ and innocent children’s lives in harm’s way to shield themselves.”

The commissioner of police advised that the Sligoville operation was one of many intelligence-driven operations targeting some of the most dangerous criminal terrorists in the country, the NSC said, adding that the police chief noted that these groups are organised, heavily armed, well-resourced, and highly networked. He reportedly said they integrate themselves into communities and oftentimes exert influence over them, enlisting the support of unsuspecting community members.

The commissioner explained that the JCF has a well-developed intelligence and operational system to track and interdict these criminal terrorists.

The NSC directed the JCF to bring forward its planned operations and intensify its push to eradicate these criminal terrorists and their networks from our society.

World.title: Jamaica hit Sri Lanka for six at U15 World Cup
World.content:
File photo (Photo JFF)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica extended their historic run to three wins at the FIFA Under-15 World Cup, beating Sri Lanka 6-0 in Baku, Azerbaijan on Sunday.

This is the first time that Jamaica has registered a win against a non-Concacaf team at a FIFA World Cup since 1998, when the Reggae Boyz beat Japan at the 1998 FIFA Men’s World Cup in France.

The Jamaican team opened their schedule on Saturday with a 9-0 win over the US Virgin Islands and then beat Cuba 1-0 in their first of two games on Sunday.

Jamaica have now recorded three wins in a row for the first time ever at a FIFA World Cup.

They will next face Togo and the Czech Republic on Monday, and if they top their first-round group, will advance to the round of 32 of the competition.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Jamaican DJ Kovert dies at 19 following car crash
World.content:
DJ Kovert gets into his set at an event. The up-and-coming disc jock, real name Matthew Nelson, has died aged 19 after a car crash on Washington Boulevard in St Andrew.

Popular disc jock, DJ Kovert, real name Matthew Nelson, has died.

The 19-year-old passed away at the University of the Hospital of the West Indies on Saturday, following complications from a motor vehicle crash which took place a few days earlier on the Washington Boulevard in St Andrew.

DJ Kovert, who was one of the shining lights in the new generation of music connoisseurs, had been playing music professionally since 2024 when he won the SunCity High School DJ Competition.

A former student at Ardenne High, he was a first-year management studies student at the University of the West Indies, Mona. He also co-promoted a bi-weekly series over the summer called FWD.

News of his passing has rocked the entertainment fraternity. Several of his musical peers took to social media to share their condolences.

In an interview with Observer Online on Saturday night, DJ Russ Buss shared his fondest memory of his late colleague.

“My fondest memory by far of Kovert, was the first time seeing him playing in the SunCity High School DJ competition during the preliminary rounds, and I listened to his transitions and how he played; I knew he would have won,” said Russ Buss. “I was impressed the first time that I saw him play. He reminded me so much of myself when I started playing music, how much he loved it, his humility and he had a lot of manners. He loved the craft and had such a bright future ahead of him.”

DJ Zacky, a close friend of DJ Kovert, shared his condolences and reflected on their friendship in a detailed post on Instagram.

“One DM turned us from strangers to brothers. From practice sessions to site visits, to bookings and even just going out for drinks, you became more than a friend to me. Every Friday, you would call me and say “Wah time yah play tonight”, and once I told you, it was always “Live, me a fwd.” Every room you waked into, you lit it up, and that’s something I’ll never forget,” DJ Zacky wrote, adding “One thing I’ll always remember about you is how you always found the positive in every situation, even when we were late for bookings. No matter what was happening, you always found a way to make the best of it. That’s the kind of person you were, and I’ll truly miss that about you.”

In an emotional post on Instagram, DJ TZ recalled when he learnt about DJ Kovert’s crash.

“I saw you the night of and we did a laugh and a run bare jokes a Ribbiz, to then get a call in the morning seh yuh crash bro. Mnk (Mi nuh know) how fi function rn bro. You was one of the realest, happiest, talented and down to earth niggas I’ve ever met,” the post read. “You was my brother and I got so much love for you gang. I promise to keep your name and legacy alive and to take you with me everywhere I go. I promise to never let you be forgotten and to keep going and to push through bcs ik that is what you would want. Love you family and rest easy.”

Meanwhile, DJ JJ Deadlock wrote on his whatsapp status, “Dawg Kovert sooo humble and jovial. We had this event together and my laptop wasn’t connecting and he easily gave me his laptop to DJ half of my set.”

Others who commented publicly include Fyahman, DJ Hibby, DJ Alpha C and emerging recording artiste Kong Magic.

The circumstances surrounding the fatal crash involving Nelson are still unclear. However, it is understood that Nelson had been driving home in the wee hours Thursday when the incident occurred.

The impact of the crash damaged electrical infrastructure and left sections of Molynes Road and nearby communities without electricity.

World.title: British ‘heirs of slavery’ back reparations
World.content:
(FILES) People calling for slavery reparations, protest outside the entrance of the British High Commission in Kingston, Jamaica on March 22, 2022, during the visit of the Britain's Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. Caribbean nations stepping up their campaign for slavery reparations have won support from an unexpected source -- the descendants of some of Britain's most prominent families to have benefitted from the slave trade. As prime ministers, courtiers and aristocrats, the names of the Gladstone, Lascelles and Trevelyan families were at the heart of the governing elite down the decades. (Photo by Ricardo Makyn / AFP)

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Caribbean nations campaigning for slavery reparations have won support from an unexpected source — the descendants of some of Britain’s most prominent families to have benefitted from the slave trade.

As prime ministers, courtiers and aristocrats, the Gladstone, Lascelles and Trevelyan families were at the heart of the governing elite down the decades.

They accumulated significant wealth from slavery through the ownership of plantations in the West Indies and South America.

Laura Trevelyan, a former BBC journalist, told AFP she had been unaware of her family’s involvement until hearing about an archive listing compensation payments to plantation owners triggered by the British parliament’s abolition of slavery in 1833.

“I was clueless,” she told AFP.

“I looked at the database and saw this small island in the eastern Caribbean called Grenada that various members of the Trevelyan family had claimed compensation for the loss of what was termed their property.”

The revelation spurred Trevelyan, who made a public apology in Grenada in 2023, to co-found the Heirs of Slavery group which supports “reparative justice”.

With other members of her family she has paid voluntary personal reparations of around £100,000 ($133,000) earmarked for educational projects.

“Everybody I met, I asked them ‘should I apologise for what my ancestors did and do you think that I personally should pay reparations?’ and the answer came back a resounding ‘yes’,” she said.

Co-founder Charlie Gladstone, a direct descendant of reforming 19th century prime minister William Gladstone whose father John was one of the largest slave owners in the British West Indies, followed suit by making a public apology in Guyana in 2023.

Another group member is aristocrat David Lascelles, the Earl of Harewood, whose family has close links to the royal family.

A portrait of the actor David Harewood hangs at the family’s stately home, Harewood House in northern England, after it was discovered that his ancestors had worked on Lascelles family sugar plantations in Barbados.

The UK government in September reiterated its rejection of calls for slavery reparations.

Modern British royals have expressed remorse, but like the government have not issued an official apology.

The issue is likely to be raised during a Caribbean tour by King Charles III which begins Tuesday when he travels to the Bahamas, then Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda where he will address the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting.

A Buckingham Palace spokesman said the king would acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery during the trip.

Ahead of the visit, Guyana’s President Irfaan Ali said his country would continue to champion the reparation issue “because slavery was the worst indignity to humankind”.

He called for a “mature” discussion on an apology and reparations, pointing to differing measures from debt relief, to finance for education and healthcare, and even climate adaptation.

The Reparations Commission of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) has called for “monetary compensation” alongside debt cancellation and a full apology as part of its “Ten-Point plan”.

Meanwhile, Britain’s Privy Council — the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories — will next year hear a petition for slavery reparations filed by Jamaica.

The petition asks the court to rule on whether the capture, transport and enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was ever legal under English law, and whether the UK owes the people of Jamaica a “reparatory remedy”.

Not all families who benefitted from slavery, however, have agreed with the Heirs group approach.

Caricom Reparations Commission chair Hilary Beckles has repeatedly spoken out about ex-Conservative Party lawmaker and UK landowner Richard Drax, 68, whose ancestors established Drax Hall Estate in Barbados in the mid-17th century.

Beckles has estimated up to 30,000 slaves died at Drax plantations in Barbados and Jamaica over 200 years.

Drax has remained staunchly opposed to reparations. He has said that while the role his ancestors played in the slave trade was “deeply, deeply regrettable … no-one can be held responsible today for what happened many hundreds of years ago”.

The Draxes are unique in that “they’re the only family that still owns a plantation that was set up in the beginning”, said Paul Lashmar, author of “Drax of Drax Hall: How One British Family Got Rich (and Stayed rich) from Sugar and Slavery”.

But he said it was increasingly difficult to see how Drax’s position could prevail.

“If you are very wealthy and a lot of your wealth comes from those years then it’s not something you can wash your hands of,” he said.

World.title: Heartless!
World.content:
HAVANA, Cuba — A woman carries water containers during a blackout in Havana, on July 7, 2026. Cubans were gradually getting power back on July 7 after the third nationwide power outage since the start of the year, causing mounting despair in the face of an energy collapse precipitated by a US fuel blockade. (Photo: AFP)

Ten former Caricom leaders are urging the global community to support the upcoming United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) resolution that calls for an end to America’s embargo against Cuba, denouncing the long-running sanction as inhumane and contrary to international law.

“The unilateral, coercive actions of the USA against Cuba represent the law of the jungle and can in no way be justified by the Charter of the United Nations or any other source of international law and justice,” the former Caricom heads of State and Government argued in an open letter to all nations of the world dated October 24, 2026.

They pointed out that every year since 1992, the UNGA has been “adopting overwhelmingly” a resolution on this subject. “Yet the USA has been ignoring the clear voice of the international community, the requisites of international law, and the most elemental of civilising principles.”

The 10 leaders are Freundel Stuart, former prime minister of Barbados; Dean Barrow and Said Musa, former prime ministers of Belize; Keith Mitchell and Tillman Thomas, former prime ministers of Grenada; Donald Ramotar, former president of Guyana; Bruce Golding and PJ Patterson, former prime ministers of Jamaica; Kenny Anthony, former prime minister of St Lucia; and Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines.

Noting that the vote is scheduled for October 28, the 10 leaders said they were “strongly and unequivocally” urging all nations to vote in favour of the resolution as the imposition of the embargo is contrary to “every civilised precept of life and living”.

Their appeal came a day after the US Government, in its latest bid to increase pressure on the Cuban Government, urged Cubans to make “discreet” contact with America’s Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).

“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA,” Rubio added.

French news service Agence France Presse (AFP), in its report on the development, said the unusual post appeared to confirm that the CIA is currently active in Cuba after a long history of covert operations, including backing the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.

According to AFP, Rubio’s call was mocked by Cuban officials.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

AFP reported that the CIA later uploaded a video to X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official US installation in person if they can safely travel to one.

For those hoping to contact the CIA online via the cia.gov website, the agency instructed users to access the Internet on a secure network, like a VPN, using a private browser and a ‘burner’ e-mail account unassociated with any personal details.

Those sharing information should be prepared to include their city, job, level of access, and contact information with their message, AFP reported.

For months, US President Donald Trump and other senior officials of his Government have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political, and legal pressure on the Spanish-speaking country.

Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.

“Those beautiful [US military] ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast,” he said. “They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez quickly dismissed Trump’s threats.

“Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination,” he posted on social media.

In another move against the Cuban leadership, Florida’s top prosecutor last week announced an arrest warrant for former President Raul Castro on State murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Castro, 95, is wanted in connection with the 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft from Brothers to the Rescue, an organisation assisting Cubans fleeing to Florida by sea.

“Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier said in a statement.

Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May.

Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action that toppled Venezuela’s then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.

Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has “no legal basis” and was an attempt “to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba”.

The US indictment has also been denounced by China and Russia, which both have close ties with Cuba.

On Wednesday, Beijing urged Washington to cease “all forms of coercion and pressure against Cuba”.

“China has consistently opposed the abuse of judicial measures to exert pressure on Cuba, and firmly supports Cuba in safeguarding its national sovereignty and resisting foreign interference,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference.

“Comrade Raul is a highly respected leader of the Cuban Revolution who enjoys great prestige internationally,” she added.

A day earlier, Russia said in a statement that it “categorically” rejected and “strongly” condemned the Florida arrest warrant, and reaffirmed Moscow’s “unwavering solidarity” with Cuba.

“Bringing a baseless and contrived accusation more than 30 years after the events can only be seen as an act of vengeance by the anti-Cuban lobby in Miami,” Russia’s foreign ministry charged.

In January this year, Trump began imposing a crippling fuel blockade on Cuba, intensifying the island’s severe economic crisis. Washington has since piled more sanctions on Cuba, cutting off nearly all its sources of revenue.

The island of just over nine million people has endured constant power cuts due to the poor state of its ageing thermoelectric plants. That has worsened significantly since the US action in January in its bid to pressure Havana’s communist Government.

A severe lack of fuel makes it difficult to supply Cuba’s power plants and backup generators, which typically run on imported diesel.

In recent weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in outlying provinces they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours.

The cuts have also affected the island’s water supply and mobile phone network, adding to extremely tough general living conditions for residents.

Havana blames the crisis on the array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.

The embargo was first imposed in 1962 by then US President John F Kennedy, who invoked the Trading with the Enemy Act, which allows Washington to restrict trade with countries it considers foes.

Since 1978 every single US leader has renewed the provision annually.

In August this year the US extended the trade embargo by another year, drawing fury from the Cuban Government.

Foreign Minister Rodriguez called the embargo “a genocidal policy” and accused Washington of being “intent on suffocating an entire nation”.

“This extension comes at the cruellest moment of the US offensive against Cuba in recent years,” he said in a post on X.

Trump has claimed that Cuba, located 150 kilometres (90 miles) off Florida’s coast, represents an “extraordinary threat” to US national security.

However, the former Caricom leaders, in their open letter on Saturday, stated that “Cuba is not a threat to any nation or any person on planet Earth”.

They argued that the embargo “continues to be a threat to hemispheric and international peace and security…is a brazen violation of Cuba’s right to sovereignty and independence, [and] derogates from the most elemental human rights of a people established and declared by international law.

“The vote on this UNGA resolution this year is more urgent and important than ever before. In recent months, the US Government has further ramped up its illegal embargo against Cuba in an attempt to starve the Cuban people into submission through the imposition of third-party sanctions against any Government or entity which grants, sells, or transports energy products, including gasoline and diesel, to Cuba. Surely, such US conduct is inhumane, and undoubtedly contrary to international law,” the 10 leaders wrote.

“Accordingly, it is imperative that the blandishments and pressures currently being deployed by the USA to derail and defeat the proposed UNGA resolution must be resisted,” they added.

“Let us all contribute to the healing of the hemispheric fracture between the United States of America and Cuba by supporting the UNGA resolution on October 28, 2026. Let us all stand with Cuba and humanity on this matter,” the leaders said.

World.title: Shake-up ahead for underperforming hospital management
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton is speaking with patients waiting to see a doctor at the Noel Holmes Hospital outpatient area on Friday. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

FORT CHARLOTTE, Hanover — Strong action will be taken against the management teams of non-performing public health institutions warns Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton following a national patient complaints report showing that long wait times remain a primary grievance across the island’s hospital network.

“I am just giving a notice that we are going to be taking stronger action around throughput and the quality of throughput, and Noel Holmes is not going to be an exception. All institutions are going to have that,” stated Tufton during a press conference at the Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover on Friday afternoon.

Before the press briefing, the minister toured the Type-C facility, which is currently being rehabilitated following Hurricane Melissa last October. During the tour, several patients raised concerns about lengthy wait times.

“Coming here and hearing that five people are waiting at an outpatient area from 9:30 or 10:00 this morning until 12:00, and the doctor has not yet seen the patient — the five or six people — not a good thing. Nobody should wait three or four hours and you haven’t seen one patient yet. Sorry. We are going to have to call these things out when they happen,” stated Tufton.

The minister highlighted that staff numbers at Noel Holmes Hospital increased significantly from 189 before the hurricane to 270, including specialist doctors. He stressed that this expanded workforce must translate into enhanced service delivery, improved throughput, and shorter wait times.

Moving forward, the ministry will closely evaluate staff counts against productivity and patient throughput across the entire public health sector.

Tufton added that the recently completed national patient complaints report will be released publicly within three weeks.

“The number one reason why people complain is access to service — timely access to service. And I know that there’s a default mode that says, ‘It’s because we don’t have this,’ or, ‘We don’t have that.’ But if we hire more doctors, the least that can happen is that the doctor must turn up and deal with the patient on time. Patients are not supposed to wait long if you have more doctors working. I can’t put it any plainer,” said Tufton.

Tufton warned institutional and regional leaders that they will be held accountable for administrative and operational failures.

“Hiring more people means greater levels of productivity, more efficient throughput, and less wait time. People see their doctors more on time. Management, leadership, and supervisors must ensure that it happens, and they must be at their posts to ensure that it happens.

“And I’m charging the regions — this regional [acting] director [Deveta McLaren] is on the line now because I’m here in Noel Holmes, but when I go to the other places I do the same thing — they must ensure that their reports reflect that, because we’re ranking institutions now on levels of performance and on complaints. And if you fall below the satisfactory rank, a team is going to come in and they’re going to start with leadership: Are you the suitable person to run this institution or to provide leadership? Because, ultimately, the buck stops with leaders,” warned Tufton.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer what specific administrative actions could be taken, Tufton explained that measures would range from performance warnings to removal from leadership posts.

“It starts with appraisal; it starts with the board. The board is going to put the region under pressure, and the region will have to relate to your parish managers. Parish managers will have to look at the key performance indicators at the level of the institutions, and people will have to be spoken to,” argued Tufton.

He cited a recent example in which a non-performing hospital chief executive officer (CEO) was removed from his post, two weeks ago, following a written directive to the board.

“The board was told to find another place to put him, because he was not providing leadership in the hospital. And we’re going to get more of that. The board has the authority to do it. I appoint the board, and you know, the truth is I appoint or remove them at my discretion. They, ultimately, have responsibility, and they must ask for these reports,” stated Tufton.

To avoid the perception of a totalitarian regime, Tufton said training and technology will be used to provide support to employees.

“Where we need to train and retrain, it has to be a critical part of the culture going forward, and technology is an important thing — using technology to give support. Things like registration, follow-ups, those sorts of things have to be a critical part. It’s not just about the human component; it’s about the ecosystem that you build out around them,” he explained.

World.title: It’s complicated: The status of EU-Canada relations
World.content:
Canada and the EU want a much closer relationship — but they still disagree over what that relationship actually is.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur look ahead to this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal, where leaders are still negotiating the language, the label and the practical deliverables.

Then, Ukraine’s growing financing needs are colliding with the fight over the EU’s next seven-year budget, as some countries resist taking part in another common loan.

And finally, Brussels’ battle over meat-related names takes an unexpected turn — with bacon-flavoured crisps caught in the crossfire.
