World.title: French presidential hopeful Philippe slips in new poll
World.content:
Edouard Philippe listens during a meeting between the Alliance for General News Press and several presidential candidates in Paris on October 14, 2026. | Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP via Getty Images

The former PM lost three points compared to Cluster 17’s survey from last month.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe is losing ground to far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the French presidential race, according to polling conducted exclusively for POLITICO.

The survey, carried out by Cluster 17 between Oct. 19 and Oct. 22, showed Philippe with 16% trailing Mélenchon on 18.5%. Cluster 17’s poll on the presidential election last month had the two tied at 19% apiece.

Both leaders are significantly behind far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, who held her first presidential campaign rally on Sunday. Le Pen’s candidacy does not appear to have been significantly affected by allegations that her protégé Jordan Bardella made antisemitic comments in private as a teenager. Bardella, who was reelected as president of the National Rally at the far-right party’s conference this past weekend, has repeatedly denied the accusations.

World.title: 4 reasons Andy Burnham’s MPs are feeling more cheerful — and the pitfalls ahead
World.content:
Disgruntled Labour MPs warned their new leader must show up, listen to them and accept some disagreement to avoid repeating his predecessor’s mistakes.

POLITICO sets out the four reasons Labour MPs are feeling more chipper under Burnham — but they still see potential pitfalls ahead.

Some of the dozen parliamentarians interviewed by POLITICO for this piece were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the internal party matters.

1) Disagreement is tolerated

MPs reckon Burnham’s administration is more willing to recognize different views within the broad church Labour Party.

Burnham himself told a Parliamentary Labour Party meeting that disagreement is fine as long as MPs speak to him about it, according to Simon Opher — a 2024-intake MP and member of Mainstream, the soft-left faction supported by Burnham when he was Greater Manchester mayor.

“It sounds weird, but that is a remarkable difference from what they had before,” Opher said, claiming he felt a “slight climate of fear” early in his political career.

World.title: SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. La chute de Philippe, relégué derrière Mélenchon
World.content:
La candidate du RN, elle, ne pâtit manifestement pas de la révélation par Mediapart fin septembre d’anciens écrits antisémites attribués à Jordan Bardella, et reste hyperfavorite du premier tour, avec 33% d’intentions de vote lorsque Philippe représente le bloc central, contre 31% dans notre dernière enquête.

A noter : fraîchement auréolé de sa victoire dès le premier round à la primaire du PS et de Place publique, Raphaël Glucksmann, lui, passe de 12% à 13% des intentions de vote, en légère dynamique. Dans le détail, selon Cluster 17, le social-démocrate récolterait 29% des voix des électeurs d’Emmanuel Macron en 2022, ce qui explique en partie pourquoi seuls 49% d’entre eux voteraient Philippe.

“Glucksmann progresse parce que Philippe ne s’adresse pas assez à l’aile sociale-démocrate de l’espace modéré”, note Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de Cluster 17.

Retailleau doublé par Lisnard

Quant au candidat des Républicains, Bruno Retailleau, il ne décolle toujours pas, mais se maintient avec 7,5%-8% des intentions de vote. Il a toutefois une nouvelle raison de s’inquiéter : lorsque David Lisnard, étiqueté Nouvelle Energie, est testé lui aussi, il atteint les 8%, grappillant des points à Le Pen (30,5%), Retailleau (7%), ainsi qu’Eric Zemmour (qui passe de 4% à 3,5%).

La cote du maire de Cannes, pourtant encore méconnu d’une partie des Français, s’explique parce qu’il “répond à une forte demande de libéralisme du centre et même de miléisme des très conservateurs”, commente Jean-Yves Dormagen, en référence au président argentin Javier Milei.

Testée également par Cluster 17, l’hypothèse d’une candidature de Gabriel Attal à la place de celle d’Edouard Philippe ne donnera guère plus d’espoir aux partisans du bloc central : le secrétaire général de Renaissance recueillerait 12% des voix aujourd’hui, contre 13,5% selon le même institut au mois de septembre. Dans ce scénario, Jean-Luc Mélenchon grimperait lui à 19,5% et Raphaël Glucksmann à 14%.



(*) Sondage réalisé du 19 au 22 octobre auprès d’un échantillon de 3 000 personnes, représentatif de la population française âgée de 18 ans et plus grâce à la méthode des quotas. L’enquête a été réalisée via un questionnaire autoadministré en ligne. La marge d’erreur est comprise entre 0,8 et 1,8 point.

World.title: Serbia’s Vučić concedes defeat after tense parliamentary elections
World.content:
As the minutes ticked by after the polls closed at 8 p.m. local time, the Central Election Commission and election observers remained silent instead of publishing their customary exit results. An hour later, Vučić’s abrupt statement was carried simultaneously on all TV channels in Serbia.

The moment the news landed, euphoric residents started streaming into central Belgrade, dancing, hugging and chanting Gotov je! (“He’s finished!”), a refrain popularized a quarter century ago, the last time the country saw this level of voter participation. That October 2000 ballot toppled Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosević following a punishing decade of wars in the Balkans.

“Never again to tyranny in our country!” said the leader of the Student List candidates roster, Ilija Srdanović. “We are moving toward a civilized and better Serbia,” he told journalists in an address at the party’s headquarters.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also released a statement after Vučić’s concession, noting that “today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country’s future” and congratulating the Student List on its victory.

“We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” she added.

While Serbia has been an official EU candidate country since 2012, its candidacy remains frozen over rule-of-law and democracy concerns and Belgrade’s refusal to join EU sanctions on Russia.

World.title: Le Pen casts herself as protector of France as troubles swirl
World.content:
In a speech lasting over an hour, Le Pen told thousands of supporters that she was not aiming for a “revolution” but rather “a real change in power” that would spark a new “Renaissance” in the country.

“We’re not saying: It was better before,” she said. “We say: It was good before and it will be better tomorrow.”

Le Pen also played her usual refrains, promising to restore public order in France, strengthen the country’s borders and expel undocumented migrants if she came to power.

Le Pen and her allies have spent days pushing back against accusations by rivals that the far-right National Rally has helped deepen divisions in France amid the turmoil and disorder sparked by recent student protests. In her address, the four-time presidential candidate refrained from attacking political opponents and pitched her party as the one offering French citizens a brighter future.

“My protective vision will benefit all,” she said.

The eurozone’s second-largest economy is facing a cocktail of crises including cost-of-living protests, difficulties adopting a state budget and a spiraling debt and deficit. The dire situation has spooked the markets, with France’s borrowing costs climbing above 5% last week for the first time since 2002.

World.title: France: The sickest man of Europe
World.content:
France has become the new sick man of Europe just in time for its next presidential election.

After two weekends that saw hundreds of thousands of protesters hit the streets demanding the government increase teacher salaries, fix run-down schools and help subsidize the rapidly rising cost of living, the European Union’s second-biggest economy is being dragged into a vicious cycle of twin fiscal and social crises that are fueling each other.

“France is on the brink of a financial crisis,” former Prime Minister Michel Barnier told POLITICO. “We need to send a signal to the markets.”





Authorities were able to prevent the type of rioting and looting this past weekend that marked the first round of demonstrations Oct. 17-18, but financial markets are spooked. Even before the demonstrations began, investors were dumping French debt or demanding historically high returns because of the government’s failure to significantly cut a stubbornly high budget deficit, bring down €3.5 trillion of debt, jumpstart growth and reform an unsustainable pension system.

The prospect of a presidential runoff next spring featuring far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and her far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is in the mix for second place according to most polls, is further scaring investors. Both candidates want to spend billions to lower the retirement age.

The rioting, for now, is estimated to have cost tens of millions of euros, much of which will be covered by insurance. But the chaos is pouring fuel on an already explosive situation by sending worrying signals to investors, especially if the civil unrest continues. The Yellow Vest protests of 2018 to 2020, which came early in President Emmanuel Macron’s tenure, cost the French economy 0.1% of gross domestic product, with shops reporting losses of €2 billion.

Protesters climb the Column of July monument in Paris Oct. 8, 2026. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images

“It is clear that protests have an impact on markets,” Eric Lombard, who served as economy and finance minister last year, told POLITICO.

Given that current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s proposed budget for 2027 already includes €43 billion in savings, leaving little room for more cuts, the government is faced with an impossible choice: Borrow more money and saddle the next generation with billions of euros in interest payments, or hope the protests die out on their own.

“We have a knife to our throats, and we can feel the drops of blood on our jugular,” said a government minister who was granted anonymity to discuss the current situation.

“We need to show that we’ve heard the outrage. But we have little margin for maneuver given the market situation.”

Playing with fire

Mario Monti, who faced a similar situation as Italian prime minister and managed to avert a financial crisis in 2011 with spending cuts and a pension reform, told POLITICO that “things can go very fast.”

Back then, the spread between Italian and German 10-year bonds — an indicator that measures how risky one country’s debt is compared to historically safe Germany — shot up from around 150 basis points to more than 500 within a few months, Monti recalled. The spread between French and German debt was 169 basis points when markets closed on Friday, while the yield on France’s benchmark 10-year bond hit 5.14% the previous day, the highest level since 2002.





France has long been seen as the EU’s “spoiled child,” Monti said, taking advantage of its political and economic weight to bend or break the bloc’s fiscal rules. But few had thought a country that big and powerful would end up on the front line of a European debt crisis.

While the ability of the European Central Bank to buy government bonds on the secondary market under certain conditions gives it a powerful tool to avert a eurozone crisis, Monti says French voters must recognize that a sovereign debt crisis in their country is no longer the stuff of fiction.

“The major problem is that the public is not concerned enough with this risk,” Monti said. “France is not psychologically ready to view itself as the target of a crisis or even as the starting point of a crisis that could spread.”

That malaise isn’t just economic: Many indicators show France has lost confidence in itself.

A protest on Paris on Oct.24, 2026, bringing together former members of the yellow vests movement, labor unions, high school and university students. Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images

According to a poll last month, 9 out of 10 French people are pessimistic about the future and believe their children will be worse off than themselves. A pan-European study conducted earlier this year found that only half of French respondents feel pride in the democratic system, compared to two-thirds of Germans and close to 70 percent of Britons.

That pessimism has pushed voters toward more extreme candidates like Le Pen — whose economic platform has been panned by some economists as unrealistic and unserious — and Mélenchon, who wants to set French debt “on fire.” According to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls from earlier this month, Le Pen enjoys the support of 34% of voters while Mélenchon has 15% — meaning nearly 50% of the electorate intends to vote for an anti-establishment figure. Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe, arguably the best-placed mainstream figure to take on Le Pen, has tried to sell himself to voters as a candidate of fiscal discipline who is unafraid to address tough truths. But his campaign has struggled to find its footing.

Doom loop

The officials, lawmakers and diplomats POLITICO spoke with all agreed that France was not at risk of a Greece-like scenario forcing the government to stop paying officials and creditors. But it could very well experience a crisis similar to the one in Italy when Monti replaced Silvio Berlusconi in 2011.

“We are not yet a banana republic which risks filing for bankruptcy,” said veteran centrist lawmaker and budget expert Charles de Courson.

But during rioting earlier this month, in front of the shattered window of an already ransacked supermarket in Paris’ hipster 11th arrondissement, a man with no apparent connection to the shop was encouraging passers-by to go in and steal what they needed. A few meters away, the owner of a Chinese restaurant locked the door behind each client to make sure the rioters couldn’t get in.





These are scenes one would expect in a country on the verge of a sovereign debt crisis, not a member of the G7. Watching from Brussels, Washington or New York, diplomats and economists recognize that Paris will likely fail to bring its budget deficit down to 3% of GDP by 2029 as it previously promised to the EU.

De Courson said France has “lost all credibility” with its European partners when it comes to fiscal issues. Lombard, the former economy minister, said “we failed to honor our commitments,” but held out hope that things could change.

“On behalf of the French people, we made commitments to get the finances back on track, but we didn’t keep them. I was very much in favor of honoring my commitments. But collectively, we didn’t do that,” Lombard said. “So we put ourselves in a position of weakness.”

World.title: Canada and Europe want to reshape the global order. But whose vision will prevail?
World.content:
The competing visions will be tested this week when Carney and von der Leyen meet in Montreal for a summit intended to chart a new course for transatlantic relations. Both want to demonstrate they can prosper in a world upended by U.S. President Donald Trump. But they have different ideas about their curious new alliance — and face political resistance that could limit how far the partnership can go.

Von der Leyen’s offer of “associate membership” in the EU surprised officials on both sides of the Atlantic. Four diplomats told POLITICO they were not consulted before she floated the idea in the State of the Union. The officials added that they don’t understand the label, which has yet to be defined. Germany has since led pushback on the plan.

“We’ve definitely put the cart before the horse,” one of the diplomats said. “We’re announcing something and then figuring out how to flesh it out.”

Trump called the membership idea “laughable,” but also threatened “very serious tariffs” should it come to be — a reminder that leaders in pursuit of Washington workarounds must avoid provoking the White House.

The leaders are under pressure to leave Montreal with more than a liberal democratic photo-op. For starters, they need to decide what “associate membership” means — and disarm resistance in the EU capitals blindsided by von der Leyen’s plan.

Canada’s Ambassador to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson told POLITICO last month that people got too hung up on a label that was revealed prematurely. Carney called the Canada-EU relationship an “alliance for the future” when he addressed European lawmakers in Strasbourg.

World.title: Brazil's Lula clinches election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results
World.content:
Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched a re-election victory with a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote.

 

The 81-year-old leftist defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term, staving off a conservative wave that has seen numerous South American countries, such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.

Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro speaks after the presidential runoff in Brasilia, Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Eraldo Peres

The senator is the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country's last election in 2022.

Lula had requested the extension after he complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as "unacceptable" and a "dirty trick".

"It is impossible to recognise the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections," he said in a brief speech in Brasília.

Comeback after first round defeat

After a first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies, declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and revamped their social media strategy.

No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the country's military dictatorship.

The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 percent to 19 percent.

"People went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country," Lula said in his first comments after the win.

Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula's Workers' Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.

Supporters of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva celebrate after he won the presidential runoff in Rio de Janeiro, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Lucas Landau

Lula's campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump's United States.

“Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil,” he said. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard," he said as he addressed his supporters.

In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

Brazilian lawmaker Andre Janones embraces Lula as he delivers a victory speech after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff in Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Andre Penner

Lula heads into a fourth term with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change.

He rose from poverty to become president in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006.

Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges were annulled on procedural grounds.

In his third term, Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime.

Already one of the world's oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.

World.title: Serbia: crowds celebrate in Belgrade after Vučić admits defeat
World.content:
Supporters of the student-backed opposition movement celebrated the announcement, marking a major political turning point after nearly two years of demonstrations against his government.

 

Earlier, election officials had begun counting ballots at polling stations across the capital as voting closed. Preliminary figures released by Serbia's election commission indicated the country's highest parliamentary election turnout in more than three decades, reflecting the scale of public participation in a closely watched contest between the governing party and a broad opposition movement.

The election followed a prolonged wave of protests that began after the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station in November 2024, killing 16 people. The disaster triggered widespread anger over alleged corruption and failures of public oversight, with students emerging as the driving force behind demonstrations that spread across Serbia. Their movement gradually brought together people from different political backgrounds, united in demanding accountability and political change.

Vučić's concession on Sunday brought a dramatic conclusion to the electoral contest, with supporters of the student-led movement gathering in Belgrade to celebrate the defeat of the party that had dominated Serbian politics for years.

World.title: Songs of praise: An emotional Greek-German musical collaboration at Berlin Cathedral
World.content:
German Unity Day may well have been celebrated earlier this month but the sounds of the songs sung to mark the occasion are still reverberating from Berlin to Athens.

 

Some 240 Greeks and Germans joined their voices in a festive service at Berlin Cathedral on Saturday 3 October. The Greek participants were 38 pupils from the Chios Music School, who performed alongside choirs and ensembles from Berlin’s Sing-Akademie (Sing-Akademie zu Berlin).

Together they performed works by Mendelssohn, Poulenc, Britten, Lewandowski and Holst, as well as "Ora kali" by Michalis Adamis and "Messa Latina" by Yannis Christou. The result of this remarkable musical encounter was deeply moving.

The service at Berlin Cathedral χ

Kai-Uwe Jirka, the artistic director of the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin, was the conductor of the concert given at the Berliner Dom:

"Today we celebrate the reunification of the two parts of Germany. For the past three years we have held a ceremony in the cathedral. After the service inside, we go outside with the congregation and we all sing together on the church steps for Europe. There is a special story behind this, because this event for Europe was our own idea. Three years ago, after the service, we came out of the cathedral and there was another event taking place in the Lustgarten, organised by the far-right party in our society.

And we all said that this could not be allowed to happen. We had just come out of the service and we wanted to be together without hatred, without racism. So for three years now we have been reserving this space for our choirs and saying: 'All right, we cannot celebrate only Germany. Because what is Germany without Europe? And what is Europe without Greece?' This year, for me, everything that happened was perfect. We have young people from all over Europe coming together, singing side by side and sending a very strong message for Europe."

The choir at the concert in Berlin cathedral Credit: Peter C Theis

This was not the first collaboration between the Greek choir and the German choral ensembles. As part of the 10th Chios Music Festival last August, more than 50 young choristers from the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin spent a week on the island, giving concerts at various venues across Chios.

Conductor Friederike Stahmer founded the Berlin Sing-Akademie Girls’ Choir 20 years ago. She was on Chios this summer and shared her experience with Euronews:

"What really makes this exchange programme special is that we come together and create music. A short while ago my choir travelled to Chios for the island’s Music Festival. There we learnt some Greek songs, mainly from Chios but also from the wider region. The pupils of the Chios Music School learnt German songs. Of course, at the beginning such musical collaborations are always challenging: the musical style is different, the language is different and you really have to work hard. At the same time you realise that you are learning so much about another musical culture.

The service at the cathedral Euronews

And now it is very rewarding that the Chios Music School is in Berlin and we have the chance to revisit all the repertoire we had already performed on Chios. You can see how it develops and blossoms. And I think it is not only about getting to know one another; creating art together, making music together has an even deeper impact on them. I am sure it will be an unforgettable experience in their lives."

The Chios Music Festival and the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin have set up this special cultural exchange, bringing the island’s Music School together with German choirs, with the support of the Greek-German Youth Foundation (ΕΓΙΝ/DGJW). The Greek group stayed for eight days in the German capital and took part in three concerts in total.

The service at the cathedral Euronews

Olga Holdorff Myriagou and Lefteris Veniadis shared the artistic direction of the highly successful Chios Music Festival:

"For the Chios Music Festival it is very important to offer opportunities to young people, to the new generation, because the choir that is here in Berlin taking part in the exchange programme has many more opportunities than the children on Chios, which lies on the edge of Europe. It is therefore a great chance for the children of Chios to come to Berlin and join such a project. Suddenly we have 100 children on stage. So we want to create opportunities on Chios as well, when the children from Berlin come through this programme, and ensure that they too have high-quality experiences there. We want to bring similarly significant activities to the island, but also to have the chance to take our children abroad, so that they can learn and discover new things, to open their ears," explains Olga Holdorff Myriagou.

Lefteris Veniadis adds: "Through the common language of music, we witnessed a miracle. German children sharing the stage with the children of Chios, singing German and Greek songs. There was, in other words, a kind of osmosis, a common goal. We managed to stage all these concerts as part of the Chios Music Festival in different parts of the island, in wonderful landscapes that took on a new dimension through music. And now something similar is happening in Berlin. We are very pleased with the outcome and the children from Chios are truly impressed by what is taking place here."

Four young people who took part in the exchange programme and sang in the service and the concerts shared their experience with us:

Chrysa Noka - Orfeas Kirythras Euronews

Orfeas Kirythras, who is from the Chios Music School said: "First of all, the experience is absolutely unique. Nothing like this has ever happened before in my life, or anything similar. I believe this exchange is extremely valuable, because we learn to live alongside people from another culture, another mindset, and overall they teach us a great deal. Greeks and Germans share this desire to create, this longing for creativity and for music. We want to build this beautiful thing called music."

Chrysa Noka is also a student at the Chios Music School: "At first I had doubts, but then I agreed to come, because I thought I would never have this experience again. When the children came to Chios, of course we faced quite a few difficulties because of our differences, but in the end we were able to coexist and we adapted our daily lives so that everyone felt comfortable."

All together now on German Unity Day Euronews

Louise Castellani from the Berlin Girls’ Choir noted: "The experience on Chios was so wonderful, because I made many friends there. In the morning we would go to the beach and play volleyball, so it was really fantastic, and here in Berlin it is also just perfect. I enjoy it very much and I hope we can repeat this collaboration next year. We had a great time."

Elsa Kriegenburg from the Berlin Girls’ Choir said: "What brings us together is the common language of music. It makes everything much easier. Singing together creates a very different sense of companionship and community. Communication in general was not that difficult either, because I think that, especially as young people, we all speak English to some extent, so we could really talk, have conversations with one another. So we became friends very quickly. And it is wonderful that we are now meeting again here in Berlin."

Germans and Greeks come together to celebrate German Unity Day Credit: Peter C Theis

After the service ended, the musical encounter continued outside Berlin Cathedral, on the steps overlooking the Lustgarten, with the initiative "Sing for Europe!", where the choirs and the large crowd sang together.

World.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy confirms trilateral talks with Russia and US to take place in November
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the US and Russia is set to take place in November in an attempt to restart stalled peace talks.

 

"We are ready to talk. If it's a territorial issue, it must be addressed at a leadership level. Other issues fall within the remit of the technical groups. All this can therefore be discussed in November," Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukrainian television.

Talk of negotiations with all three sides at the table, aimed at stopping the drawn-out war has done the rounds repeatedly in recent weeks.

The latest announcements came amid intensified diplomatic efforts by US President Donald Trump's administration.

His envoy Steve Witkoff met on Tuesday with Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo, before meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday.

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, center, with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, right, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, 2nd left, and U. S. envoy Steve Witkoff Heiko Junge / NTB

Following the meetings, both Kyiv and Moscow voiced their readiness to resume direct talks mediated by Washington.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to restart the talks after 10 November, Putin's foreign affairs adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told reporters following a meeting in St. Petersburg between the Russian leader and US envoy Steve Witkoff.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, and US special envoy Steve Witkoff shake hands prior to the talks at the Konstantin Palace in St Petersburg, 21/10/2026 Sputnik

Following the meetings, both Kyiv and Moscow voiced their readiness to resume direct talks mediated by Washington.

The talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he supported the push from Washington to restart talks swiftly.

"The agenda is clear: to end the war, bring peace closer, and, as I understand it, prepare everything for a meeting at the leaders’ level,” Zelenskyy said in an audio message issued late Wednesday.

Representatives of the three countries held three rounds of negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February.

However, little progress was reported beyond exchanges of prisoners of war as Moscow and Kyiv stuck to their longstanding basic demands.

World.title: Student List wins Serbian election in political earthquake as Vučić concedes defeat
World.content:
Serbia has entered a new political era. The Student List has won the country's parliamentary election, marking a dramatic breakthrough for a movement that emerged from months of student protests and rapidly transformed itself into the country's most important political force.

 

In a brief statement to the nation, outgoing Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat and declared that the Student List has won the majority in parliament.

Vučić said that “based on the stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost the election,” adding that “the Student List has won and will have between 135 and 140 seats, while we will have around 105.

“No one else has entered parliament. The Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (SVM) has won three seats, the Albanians one, and I think the SDA has also secured a seat,” he added.

The Serbian Progressive Party received around 1.72 million votes, admitted Vučić. The Student List won 2.2 million, giving it a majority of 52% to 32.3 %.

It is still too early to assess the final results and determine whether any other smaller parties have crossed the 3% electoral threshold, but it is clear that this would not affect the final outcome of the election or the identity of the winner.

The result represents far more than a change in the distribution of parliamentary seats. It is a profound rejection of the political model that has dominated Serbia for more than a decade.

From protest movement to political force

The Student List's victory is particularly significant because it was not created as a conventional political party. Its origins lie in the student protests that became a powerful expression of dissatisfaction with the country's political institutions, the government, corruption allegations, media conditions and what many protesters described as a lack of accountability.

What began as a protest movement has therefore achieved something considerably more difficult - it has translated street mobilisation into electoral legitimacy.

The result suggests that the movement managed to attract voters far beyond the university campuses where the protests began. Young people were its most visible supporters, but the electoral coalition appears to have extended to parts of the urban middle class, opposition-minded voters and citizens who had previously been reluctant to support established opposition parties.

A defeat for the old political establishment

For the ruling establishment, the result is a major political setback.

For years, President Aleksandar Vučić and the Serbian Progressive Party dominated Serbian politics through a combination of strong electoral organisation, extensive political influence, control over a large part of the media environment and a highly personalised political strategy centred on Vučić himself.

The election result indicates that this model has reached a critical limit.

What happens next?

The transition from protest movement to government could therefore prove much harder than winning the election for the Student List.

Running a country requires decisions on the economy, foreign policy, relations with the European Union, Kosovo, security, energy, public finances and Serbia's relations with Russia and China. The students will now have to demonstrate that their political legitimacy can be transformed into effective state governance.

What does the result mean for Serbia?

There are several possible consequences.

First, it represents a generational change in Serbian politics. A movement dominated by young people has succeeded in challenging a political establishment that has shaped the country for years.

Second, it could lead to a major institutional reset. The new government is likely to face strong expectations concerning the independence of institutions, the judiciary, corruption, public media and electoral conditions.

Third, Serbia's foreign policy could enter a new phase. The new political leadership will face immediate questions about the country's EU accession process, relations with Brussels and Washington, and its traditionally close relationship with Moscow and Beijing. Whether the Student List seeks a clear pro-European orientation or attempts to maintain a more balanced foreign policy will be closely watched.

Fourth, Aleksandar Vučić's political future becomes uncertain. Even if he remains president, an electoral defeat would fundamentally change the political balance in Serbia. His ability to dominate the political agenda would be significantly reduced, while his party would have to rebuild itself in opposition.

A new political test

The Student List has won the election. But its real political test begins now.

Winning an election requires mobilisation, a powerful message and the ability to unite voters around the desire for change. Governing requires something different: institutions, experienced personnel, economic policy, compromise and the ability to take responsibility for difficult decisions.

For Serbia, the election therefore represents both a political rupture and a moment of uncertainty.

The central question is no longer whether the students can challenge the established political order.

They have already done that.

The question now is whether they can replace it - and what kind of Serbia they intend to build in its place.

World.title: Marine Le Pen launches presidential campaign with vow to restore 'rule of law'
World.content:
Far-right French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen kicked off her campaign before thousands of supporters at her first campaign rally in the city of Orléans.

 

Addressing thousands of supporters of her nationalist, anti-immigration party Rassemblement National RN (National Rally), she said she wanted to offer France "a alteration of course" which, in her words, is "not a revolutionary act but a normal breath of democratic life".

Le Pen is the current frontrunner in the polls, six months ahead of the vote. "No one thinks we are stronger today than we were yesterday, nor that after ten years of Emmanuel Macron we are walking through a field of rose petals," she said.

"Everyone in France agrees with us", Le Pen claimed.

She vowed to preserve France's cultural identity, from its language and traditions to its values and way of life, drawing cheers from supporters waving French flags.

'The rule of law is not the law against the state'

Among her priorities, should she win in May 2027, Le Pen is promising what she calls more security for French citizens. She denounced what she sees as the failings of the justice system under Emmanuel Macron, which she considers far too lax.

"Who can claim there is a rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings, or carry out real raids in front of law-enforcement officers who have been deliberately disarmed, both materially and morally?" she said, referring to the looting and clashes of 17 October on the fringes of protests over the rising cost of living.

"The rule of law is not the law against the state," Marine Le Pen went on, promising "certainty" that cases will be brought and sentences carried out, as well as the expulsion of foreign offenders.

Defending her sovereigntist line, Marine Le Pen also argued for "national priority", saying she wanted to restore "a double border: French and European".

On the international front, without explicitly mentioning Ukraine, she vowed that France "will not send" its young people "to die in reckless or irresponsible military adventures, and even less in wars that are not ours".

Jordan Bardella blames LFI for 'fanning the flames of insurrection'

Leading up to Marine Le Pen's speech, in which she wanted to "rise above the fray", The National Rally's president, Jordan Bardella, introduced her on stage, openly attacking the government and revisiting the week's explosive news.

"The French have seen a power that has fallen, that has given up, that has abdicated even the idea of protecting our compatriots," he said, condemning the violence that broke out on the sidelines of the social movement.

According to the RN president, his party "has appeared as the only option capable of restoring order and bringing back authority". As the crowd gathered at the Orléans convention centre chanted "Macron, resign", he replied: "Don't worry, he won't be long before he is going, it's planned and it's coming soon".

Jordan Bardella also took aim at La France Insoumise (France Unbowed), or LFI, and the party's leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who backs the high school students' movement and the social mobilisation generally, accusing the hard-left party of "fanning the flames of insurrection", which in his view disqualifies LFI "from aspiring to the highest offices of the state".

Start of Jordan Bardella's speech disrupted

His speech was briefly interrupted by members of a Jewish student union who unfurled a banner referencing a French media report alleging he had deleted antisemitic messages from an old Facebook account.

Jordan Bardella then called on people "not to give publicity to the far left, which hates democracy".

"While the security services do their job, I am asking you to sing the Marseillaise," he went on.

The circumstances of the incident were not immediately clear. Later, the Union of French Jewish Students (UEJF) posted a message on X, confirming that activists from the organisation had unfurled the banner, which read: "Bardella re-elected: racism and antisemitism do not bother the RN, quite the opposite."

This protest referred to Mediapart revelations concerning antisemitic messages attributed to Jordan Bardella when he was 18. He rejects the accusations.

Le Pen on the campaign trail, Bardella in charge of the party

The Orléans rally took place the day after the National Rally congress, held under heavy police protection, at which Jordan Bardella was confirmed as party leader.

Bardella, the sole candidate for his post, was re-elected president of the National Rally with 98.98% of the vote. For a time he had been tipped to run for the French presidency himself, if Marine Le Pen's conviction in the case of misuse of funds for European parliamentary assistants had prevented her from standing.

His re-election formalises the division of roles within the duo presented to voters as a "winning ticket": Marine Le Pen will run for office as president of the republic, while Jordan Bardella, strengthened at the helm of the RN, is positioning himself to become her prime minister in the event of victory.

She reiterated this in her speech on Sunday: she wants to form a “national unity” government led by Jordan Bardella.

Another takeaway from the congress: Marine Le Pen has given up chairing the RN group in the National Assembly, in order to focus on the presidential campaign. MP Sébastien Chenu, one of her close allies, is taking over the role.

Jordan Bardella AP Photo/Teresa Suarez

'It is the only party we have not tried yet'

According to the organisers, the rally was attended by 8,500 of the party's supporters.

"I'm here because I vote for Marine Le Pen. I've wanted her to become president for a very long time, because in my view the country is doing very badly today and I think she's the only one who can turn it around," said Karine, a RN supporter, speaking to Euronews before the rally began.

Among her priorities, she lists security, jobs and housing, all issues which she believes "keep the country going". She says she understands "young people's distress" but deplores their "behaviour", criticising the excesses on the sidelines of demonstrations over the cost of living.

Another attendee also stressed security and purchasing power. "We are here to represent our country, France, to represent both the youngest and the oldest," he explains, before summing up his choice: "In any case, it's the only party we haven't tried yet, so we want to try it."

'Some would have preferred you not to come'

"Some would have preferred you not to come," Marine Le Pen wrote on X, addressing her supporters, while welcoming the atmosphere at the Zénith Centre in Orléans.

Elsewhere in the country, the most recent round of protests against the high cost of living, rising fuel prices and lack of funding for education brought between 410,000 and 800,000 people onto the streets. While the demonstrations were largely peaceful, clashes broke out sporadically at the end of the marches, with 1,314 people arrested.

On Saturday morning, a demonstration organised by several trade unions and left-wing parties against the congress peacefully brought together 13,000 people, according to the local council, and 26,000 according to the organisers.

On Sunday, police were carrying out checks on vehicles at the entrance to Orléans. A small unauthorised march, bringing together a few dozen people, tried to reach the convention centre, chanting anti-fascist slogans.

According to the council of the Centre-Val de Loire region and the Loiret county, 3,000 members of the security forces and emergency services were deployed in Orléans over the weekend to maintain order.

Trade unions and yellow vest protesters have pledged to continue their demonstrations in the coming weeks, pointing to a period of heightened tensions in the run-up to the presidential election.

Marine Le Pen, for her part, has accused Emmanuel Macron's government of lacking authority and of "denying reality" in the face of the violence that erupted on 17 October.

World.title: Brazil: long queues and river journeys mark decisive presidential vote
World.content:
Across Brazil, voters made their way to polling stations on Sunday 25 October as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faced Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.

 

In the Amazon rainforest, residents of the isolated Lago do Catalão community travelled by canoe and motorboat to cast their ballots, relying on waterways to access polling facilities.

In Rio de Janeiro's Rocinha favela, long queues formed as residents waited to vote, reflecting the deep divisions surrounding the election.

In Brasília, 59-year-old Cleonice Campos arrived at her polling station holding a small doll resembling President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, keeping it close before casting her ballot in support of the incumbent president.

Brazil's Supreme Court extended voting in the presidential runoff by two hours following complaints that public transport disruptions prevented voters from reaching polling stations.

As voting drew to a close, election officials prepared electronic voting machines and printed electoral rolls. The extended polling period was set to end at 22:00 CET (19:00 Brasília time), with official results expected between 01:30 and 02:00 CET on Monday as vote counting progresses.

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.

World.title: Brazilian leftist President Lula wins reelection against conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro
World.content:
Published 10/26/2026 Published October 26, 2026 Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election

Lula has won a fourth presidential term after a historic upset Image: Brian Snyder/REUTERS

Brazilian leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, electoral authorities said.

Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The campaign was marred by scandals and mudslinging. Sunday’s vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula’s claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.

Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.

In regards to foreign policy in his next term, Lula will have to manage relations with Washington while maintaining his anti-imperialist stance, as the Trump administration increasingly asserts its influence across the region. Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.

Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.

However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.

Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.

The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.

World.title: Serbia election: Vucic concedes defeat to student-led movement
World.content:
In a seismic political shift, Serbia's longtime strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic has conceded defeat to a student-led movement in the country's parliamentary elections.

Serbia's longtime leader, strongman Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat to a student-led movement in the country's parliamentary elections on Sunday in what represents a seismic political shift.

High turnout and growing tension marked a hotly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between the Balkan country's longtime leader and a diverse movement of university students who have led protests against him for almost two years.

The result brings an end to more than a decade of rule by Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

Pre-election polls had suggested a tight race between the SNS and the newly formed, youth-backed Students' List, which emerged from a mass student protest movement.

Vucic: 'It is clear that we lost these elections'

"Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections," Vucic said as he addressed supporters at SNS headquarters in Belgrade.

In his concession speech, Vucic said projections had the youth-backed Students’ List taking between 135 and 140 seats, whereas the SNS was projected to win around 105.

Vucic blamed Serbia's independent media for the loss while also alleging interference from unnamed European countries and the "American deep state."

Celebrations erupted on the streets of the capital as soon as Vucic conceded defeat. Passing cars honked horns and crowds began to party near the election commission's headquarters.

At Students' List headquarters, supporters cried tears of joy, cheering, hugging and chanting — "Victory! Victory!"

What is Serbia's student protest movement

Sunday's result is the culmination of nearly two years of protests after the deadly collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi ‌Sad in 2024.

The disaster killed 16 people and stirred widespread anger over alleged corruption, poor construction standards and a lack of accountability for public infrastructure projects.

Protesters accused the government of allowing corruption and political patronage to undermine public safety, allegations authorities have rejected.

Demonstrations demanding accountability have ultimately snowballed into a movement larger than anything Serbia has experienced since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What began with university students staging blockades and marches soon drew support from teachers, farmers and other segments of Serbian society, turning demands for justice over the disaster into a broader challenge to Vucic's grip on power.

Vucic's tough election challenge

SNS won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics ever since. Vucic himself first came to power as prime minister in 2014 before becoming president in 2017.

After calling snap elections last month, he stepped down as president to run for prime minister.

Vucic and the SNS have run Serbia for more than a decade Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS

His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia's constitution prevents him from serving a third term.

Critics have accused him of concentrating power, undermining independent media and weakening democratic institutions. He and his party deny the allegations.

The student movement has managed to channel the energy of the street protests into an electoral challenge the likes of which neither Vucic and his ruling party nor Serbia's established opposition has ever seen.

​Serbia's election commission put turnout at nearly 70%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.

Serbia vote draws EU attention

The election was closely watched in Europe, where Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated the Students' List on their victory. "We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," von der Leyen said on X.

Vucic maintained close ties with Russia and refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.

The vote comes six months after Peter Magyar's victory in Hungary , when he defeated Vucic's ally, Viktor Orban. Magyar congratulated Serbia’s student-led Students’ List on its victory in a post on X.

Serbia’s bid to join the European Union has been hampered by concerns over democratic standards and the rule of law. But the election result has prompted a positive response from another European, non-EU institution — the Council of Europe.

"The Council of Europe stands ready to work with Serbia’s democratically elected leadership to strengthen human rights, democracy and the rule of law," the organization’s Secretary-General Alain Berset said on X.
