World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Dew could trouble NPL bowlers, but may not decide games
World.content:
Dew could trouble NPL bowlers, but may not decide games

With 21 matches scheduled under lights, including the final and all three playoff games, dew could give batters an advantage. But pitch conditions and team form may matter more than winning the toss.

Hemanta Shrestha/TKP

World.title: Divers search for three missing after boat accident in Saptakoshi river
World.content:
Divers search for three missing after boat accident in Saptakoshi river

Seven divers and teams from Nepal’s Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have resumed the search for three people, including a seven-year-old boy, after a passenger boat suffered mechanical failure on Sunday.

World.title: Pakistan players’ NPL participation in doubt over PCB clearances
World.content: Nayak Paudel covers sports for The Kathmandu Post. He previously worked at the Post (2018–19) and spent over five years at The Rising Nepal. His reporting spans crime, health, education, and social issues.

World.title: Prime Minister Balendra Shah to inaugurate NPL third edition, wishes tournament success
World.content:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah to inaugurate NPL third edition, wishes tournament success

The third edition of the Nepal Premier League begins Monday in Kirtipur, with international stars and a growing commercial footprint raising expectations for the T20 tournament.

World.title: Nepal to expand flood warning systems across six river basins
World.content:
Nepal to expand flood warning systems across six river basins

A new white paper outlines plans to lower water levels in four high-risk glacial lakes and strengthen disaster preparedness as climate change intensifies risks in the Himalayas.

East Rapti river at Sauraha. Wikimedia Commons

World.title: Lula, Brazil’s iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback
World.content:
Lula, Brazil’s iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback

The 80-year-old leftist defied polling expectations and a regional shift to the right, but a deeply conservative Congress and mounting economic pressures threaten to complicate his next term.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate seeking re-election, waves a flag during a closing campaign rally ahead of the presidential runoff, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 24, 2026. Reuters

World.title: Public medical colleges add seats as entrance exams begin on Saturday
World.content:
Public medical colleges add seats as entrance exams begin on Saturday

The Medical Education Commission has added 418 seats for the upcoming academic year, including 50 MBBS places in Geta. Medical reforms campaigner Dr Govinda KC has challenged the decision over concerns about infrastructure and staffing.

World.title: Career judges lose ground as lawyers gain sway in Nepal’s judiciary
World.content:
Career judges lose ground as lawyers gain sway in Nepal’s judiciary

Recent appointments have renewed debate over merit, experience and political influence. Career judges are absent from the Supreme Court and their share of High Court judges is declining.

Former justice Krishna Jung Rayamajhi questions a succession pattern that favours judges from private legal practice. Post File Photo

World.title: Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda dies at 90
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who led Japan from 2007-08 and sought to strengthen ties with China during his brief tenure and after, died Thursday at the age of 90, his son announced Monday.

Further details surrounding his death were not immediately available.

Fukuda, the son of former Japanese leader Takeo Fukuda, became the country’s first second-generation prime minister when he assumed office in September 2007, succeeding Shinzo Abe following his abrupt resignation.

On the diplomatic front, he sought to improve relations with China, hosting then-President Hu Jintao on a state visit in May 2008. The two leaders issued a joint statement pledging to bolster what they called a “mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests.”

Fukuda also chaired the Group of Eight summit in Hokkaido in July of that year, where leaders adopted a global goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by at least 50% by 2050, placing climate change as one of the grouping’s core agenda items.

At home, his administration helped secure legislation providing compensation to people infected with hepatitis C through contaminated blood products, following years of litigation. Fukuda personally apologized to the victims on two separate occasions during his premiership.

He also laid the groundwork for the establishment of the Consumer Affairs Agency, seeking to strengthen consumer protection after a series of food safety scandals. It was eventually formed in 2009 after he left office.

Before becoming prime minister, Fukuda served as chief cabinet secretary under Prime Ministers Yoshiro Mori and Junichiro Koizumi. He was first elected to the Lower House in 1990, representing a constituency in Gunma Prefecture, and retired from politics in 2012.

World.title: U.S. military bans Chinese-made BYD cars from key air base in Okinawa
World.content:
The U.S. military has restricted vehicles made by the Chinese car manufacturer BYD from its sprawling Kadena Air Base in Okinawa Prefecture over security concerns about the vehicles.

The ban, which took effect Monday, currently only affects Kadena — one of the largest U.S. Air Force installations in the region.

The U.S. Forces in Japan did not specifically explain what prompted the move, and officials with the Kadena base did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Installation commanders are responsible for protecting their people, facilities, and assigned missions and may implement lawful, risk-informed security measures necessary to mitigate credible threats,” USFJ spokesperson Col. John Severns said.

The ban comes as the U.S. and other Western countries have been tightening their security messaging following concerns about the smart technology used by Chinese-owned car brands such as BYD, MG and Jaecoo.

In safety advice issued in late September, the Dutch government warned that vehicles’ modern technology — including GPS, microphones, cameras, entertainment systems and Bluetooth connections — could be used for spying by state actors.

Last year, the U.S. also issued a ban on the sale of some Chinese vehicles and related hardware and software if it was deemed they could be a national security risk.

Smart vehicles have raised particular security questions for governments, given the amount of information that app developers, manufacturers and companies can access. This data is valuable to external parties or state actors who could receive the data from companies or obtain it via illegal means like hacking.

In June, the Pentagon added BYD to a blacklist of 188 “Chinese military companies” banning direct procurement or contracting with the firms.

It was not clear whether the BYD ban will be extended to other U.S. bases in Japan.

The Kadena Air Base is a crucial hub for U.S. military operations in the region. The U.S. military’s Typhon midrange missile system — believed capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles as far as 1,600 kilometers — is currently being stored at the base after it was deployed for joint military exercises earlier this year.

The decision to “temporarily” store the weapon there, effectively putting parts of China within striking distance, has prompted outrage in Beijing.

World.title: Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli wins in Texas to move to brink of Formula One title
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli delivered a dominant U.S. Grand Prix victory for Mercedes on Sunday to stand on the brink of becoming Formula One’s youngest-ever champion with four rounds to spare in Mexico next weekend.

The 20-year-old Italian did all he could to put the championship out of reach of his rivals in Texas, but Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate George Russell did just enough to delay the inevitable by finishing fourth and eighth respectively.

Antonelli now needs to score only two points — a ninth-place finish — in Mexico City to be sure of the title even if Russell wins.

World.title: Tomoka Nishiyama to become first woman to enter kishi shogi ranks
World.content:
Tomoka Nishiyama will become the first woman to enter Japan’s regular professional shogi ranks, breaking a century-old barrier in the typically male-dominated game, after announcing Monday morning that she would exercise her newly acquired eligibility.

Nishiyama, 31, who holds four women’s titles, told a news conference in Tokyo that she had decided to become a kishi after considering her options for two weeks.

“I received warm words from many people. I also realized how strongly I wanted to compete against strong players and aim higher,” she said.

Shogi has two separate professional classifications: kishi, which is open to both men and women, and jōryu kishi, which is exclusively for women. No woman had qualified as a kishi since the Japan Shogi Association was established in 1924.

The association introduced a system in 2025 allowing players who have won the prestigious women’s Hakurei title five times to qualify for professional status. Nishiyama won the title for a fifth time on Oct. 10 but had initially held off on deciding whether to exercise her right to play as a kishi.

She will officially become a fourth-dan professional on April 1, 2027.

Nishiyama plans to continue competing in women’s title matches alongside her new professional career.

“The women’s professional title system has a history of more than 50 years. The people who came before me have built that history,” Nishiyama said.

World.title: NFL party goes off without hitch despite unrest in France
World.content:
The Pittsburgh Steelers defeated the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the first NFL regular-season game in Paris on Sunday, in a calm and festive atmosphere, a day after fresh demonstrations drew more than 100,000 people into the French capital.

The nationwide protests largely overshadowed the buildup to the game, with some fan and NFL events canceled over the weekend, mainly due to their location in central Paris.

On Sunday, as Saturday’s rain gave way to sunshine, the mood was peaceful before kickoff around the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, some 10 kilometers north of Paris’ city center and more than 13 km from Porte d’Italie, where Saturday’s protests began in southern Paris.

World.title: Father of woman struck by man who jumped from building seeks murder charge
World.content:
The father of a 23-year-old woman who died in July after being struck by a man who jumped from an apartment building in Nagoya is campaigning for prosecutors to charge the man — who survived — with murder.

Kenji Inaba, 50, of Watarai, Mie Prefecture, says that the 29-year-old man, who was arrested on suspicion of causing death through gross negligence, should be charged with murder based on “dolus eventualis” — the legal concept of recklessness in which a person recognizes the possibility of causing another person’s death but proceeds anyway.

Inaba argues that the man must have been aware of the danger his actions posed to others.

World.title: Unscrupulous businesses preying on older people with dementia
World.content:
Older people with dementia have emerged as a prime target for unscrupulous businesses that pressure them into signing contracts for expensive home renovations via door-to-door sales.

As the number of older people living alone continues to rise in Japan, and the number of those with dementia alongside it, such predatory practices may go undetected unless someone around the victims notices the warning signs.

Experts say it is essential to establish a support system to protect this vulnerable group in the community.

World.title: Yuri Yoshida rallies for first victory on LPGA Tour
World.content:
Yuri Yoshida overcame a four-stroke deficit entering the final round of the BMW Ladies Championship to record a one-shot victory in Haenam-gun, South Korea, on Sunday.

Yoshida recorded an eagle on the par-5 second hole and three straight birdies on Nos. 5-7 to highlight a 4-under-par 68 on Sunday at Pine Beach Golf Links. She finished the tournament at 17-under 271 to capture her first LPGA Tour victory and pocket a first-prize check of $352,500.

“It’s a special moment for me, and actually, I was nervous,” Yoshida said. “But at this moment, I’m really happy.”

Yoshida, 26, became the fourth player from Japan to win this season and the fourth first-time winner on the LPGA Tour.

She benefited from a brilliant shot out of the bunker on the 17th hole, enabling her to make a birdie that proved pivotal.

“Actually, I didn’t have confidence,“ Yoshida said of the shot out of the bunker. “But I thought, just hit, just hit, it’s the perfect distance. It was perfect, yeah.”

Yoshida finished one shot ahead of South Koreans Choi Hye-jin (69 on Sunday) and overnight leader and World No. 3 Haeran Ryu (73). The latter two golfers bogeyed their final holes.

From there, Yoshida finished her round and was greeted by several Japanese players and friends.

Choi failed to capture her first LPGA Tour victory despite entering the final round with at least a share of the lead on five occasions. She has three runner-up finishes this season, including last weekend’s effort in China.

Ryu recorded 15 consecutive pars during her final round before sandwiching bogeys around a birdie over her final three holes.

Ryu, 25, was looking for her sixth title on the LPGA Tour. She won her first two majors this season at the Women’s PGA Championship and the Evian Championship.

Fellow South Koreans Minsol Kim (67) and Kim Hyo-joo (68) finished in a tie for fourth place at 15-under.

Defending champion Kim Sei-uoung Kim of South Korea carded a 70 on Sunday to finish in a tie for 55th place.

This is the second of four events on the fall Asian swing, followed by tournaments in Malaysia and Japan.

World.title: Man falls to death fleeing Hong Kong police raid on suspected drug den
World.content:
A man has died after falling from a building while trying to flee a Hong Kong police raid on a suspected drug den in Yau Ma Tei.

The 42-year-old man, surnamed Kwong, was found unconscious outside 385-387 Reclamation Street at about 9.28pm on Sunday.

He was rushed to Kwong Wah Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said on Monday.

World.title: Man bitten after being chased by 3 dogs on his way to work in Yuen Long
World.content:
A 26-year-old warehouse worker has been injured in Hong Kong after being chased by three dogs and bitten by one of them on his way to work.

A source said police received a report at around 8am on Monday from the victim, surnamed Leung, saying one of the dogs pounced on him as he was walking towards his workplace at a logistics company in Yuen Long’s Kam Pok Road.

Paramedics arrived at the scene and found the victim with minor wounds. He was sent to Pok Oi Hospital for treatment.

World.title: Hong Kong arbitration body eyes Mideast, Africa prospects amid global tensions
World.content:
An international arbitration body in Hong Kong is exploring business opportunities in the Middle East and Africa, citing the city’s neutrality and predictability as key draws for new markets amid rising geopolitical tensions.

Domitille Baizeau, co-chairwoman of the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, said the city had benefited from an overall shift in global business growth from Europe to Asia, with overseas businesses increasingly choosing Hong Kong to arbitrate disputes.

The international commercial arbitration specialist was speaking on the sidelines of the ADR in Asia Conference, an event organised by the centre last week. The conference brought together legal practitioners to discuss the latest developments in alternative dispute resolution and the use of artificial intelligence in the field.

World.title: Head of Hong Kong’s new drug regulator pledges to build trust, push innovation
World.content:
The head of Hong Kong’s new drug regulatory body has pledged to build a fully capable and globally trusted agency that will become a catalyst for medical innovation rather than merely acting as a “miniature version” of existing overseas models.

Dr Li Zili, controller of the Hong Kong Centre for Medical Products Regulation (CMPR), said that while many other places in Asia, such as mainland China, Singapore and Japan, had established regulatory agencies long ago, Hong Kong had a distinctive competitive edge.

“We are not going to be a mini-FDA, nor a miniature version of any regulatory body in the world,” he said, referring to the United States Food and Drug Administration.

World.title: Hong Kong’s pursuit of top university rankings comes at a cost
World.content:
The latest rankings confirm what many in Hong Kong already know: the city’s universities are exceptional. Five institutions continue to sit among the world’s top 100, reflecting decades of investment, academic ambition and hard work.

Yet behind the rankings triumph lies a question that receives far less attention: what happens to the people responsible for that success?

As universities compete ever harder for rankings, grants and prestige, academics face growing pressure to produce results on ever-shorter timelines. If Hong Kong wants to sustain its success, it must look beyond rankings and ask if the risks and rewards of academic achievement are being shared fairly.

World.title: Interpol’s Hong Kong meeting to consider ‘silver notice’ targeting criminal assets
World.content:
Interpol will seek approval at its general assembly in Hong Kong next month for a new “silver notice” system to target criminals’ assets and speed up financial investigations into transnational crime.

Hong Kong’s police chief also pledged to make financial investigations and scams a top priority in discussions with overseas counterparts during Interpol’s annual meeting, which the city is hosting for the first time.

Interpol secretary general Valdecy Urquiza said in an interview in Hong Kong that the global law enforcement organisation would strive to keep technical channels for data exchange open among member states despite growing geopolitical tensions worldwide.

World.title: HK Express passenger injured after power bank overheats on flight to Jeju
World.content:
A traveller was injured after a power bank overheated and emitted smoke aboard an HK Express flight from Hong Kong to South Korea on Sunday, prompting crew members to deploy emergency safety measures before the aircraft landed safely.

The incident occurred on flight UO676 to Jeju, which was carrying 236 passengers and seven crew, prompting an apology from HK Express.

The budget airline, a subsidiary of Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, said the power bank was stored in a bag under a passenger’s seat and began overheating as the aircraft approached Jeju International Airport.

World.title: Hong Kong to boost Huanggang Port capacity after Halloween, concert congestion
World.content:
Hong Kong’s No 2 official has pledged to open extra clearance counters and vehicle lanes at the recently revamped Huanggang Port control point ahead of peak hours, after Halloween crowds and concertgoers created heavy cross-border congestion.

Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, who inspected the Shenzhen Bay and Huanggang ports on Sunday, said he had instructed the Security Bureau to step up advance assessments and passenger flow forecasting.

He added that he had directed the Transport and Logistics Bureau to work with bus and rail operators to keep sufficient vehicles and manpower in reserve for flexible deployment based on demand.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019146/How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.title: How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019146/How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.content:
The drive southwest from Hangzhou, the capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, takes about six hours. The highway passes through tunnel after tunnel, opening onto solar farms terraced into hillsides, villages with white walls and gray-tiled roofs, and transmission towers climbing the ridges. The last tunnel leads into a narrow valley, with clouds hanging low over the mountains.

This is Qingyuan County, which remains relatively remote despite its location in one of China’s richest provinces and improvements in transport infrastructure. Little known beyond its shiitake mushrooms and pencil manufacturing, the county moves to its own rhythm. I arrive at dusk, just as electric moped riders stream in from factories and workshops a few minutes outside town. Here, electric mopeds have a lane of their own. At traffic lights, riders cluster together, their helmets like a patch of colorful mushrooms, then move off as one when the light turns green.

Media portrayals of China often focus on modern metropolises or traditional villages, overlooking places like Qingyuan. Its urban center is a xiancheng, or county town, where schools, hospitals, shops, and cultural and government facilities serve both townspeople and residents of surrounding villages. Qingyuan County as a whole had 141,000 permanent residents in 2023. Across China, some 160 million people lived in similar county towns at the end of 2021. A 2022 national policy recognized their role in connecting cities and the countryside, calling for improved public services, including museums.

County towns have also been largely overlooked in China’s contemporary art scene. For more than a decade, Chinese artists and curators have been working beyond major cities like Beijing and Shanghai. Festivals such as Art Field Nanhai have brought installations to the countryside in the southern Guangdong province. The Bishan Project incorporated art into a “rural revitalization” initiative in a village in Zhejiang’s neighboring Anhui province. Anren, a historic town in the southwestern Sichuan province, hosted three editions of a contemporary art biennale.

These projects have expanded the reach of contemporary art in China. Yet artistic practices in county towns, where urban and rural life intersect, remain underreported. Another problem is the condescending language sometimes used in media coverage. For example, the term xiachen, literally “sinking,” is often used to describe cultural resources flowing from major cities to smaller communities, downplaying the role of local people in shaping art scenes.

The Art Museum of Pond Loach (AMPL) in Qingyuan offers a different perspective, showing how contemporary art institutions and smaller communities can shape one another.

Established in 2023, AMPL takes its name from a small, mud-burrowing freshwater fish. The museum draws on this image to describe its mission: immersing itself in the space between urban and rural life and engaging with the everyday experiences of county-town residents. It seeks to support what its director, Hu Dingyu, describes as “modest yet significant contemporary art.”

A Qingyuan native who left the county as a child and later studied and worked as a curator in the Netherlands, Hu has a complicated relationship with her hometown and resists portraying her return as a nostalgic homecoming or a search for her roots. Instead, she sought to establish a lasting institution where relationships among artists, museum staff, and local residents could develop over time.

That starts with the architecture. AMPL occupies two floors of a ceramics museum founded by a member of Hu’s family. Dedicated to celadon, a type of green-glazed ceramic with strong ties to Zhejiang, the museum shares a building with the local marriage registry and a library reading room.

Hu and her team carved out a space for contemporary art within this setting, and the contrast remains visible. Gray concrete walls, exposed rebar and pipes, and alarm fixtures sit alongside the polished glass cases displaying celadon downstairs. To me, these unfinished surfaces made the gallery feel like a work in progress, reflecting the artistic practices taking shape within and beyond its walls.

AMPL’s development resembles a process of grafting: artistic practices and networks formed elsewhere take root through encounters with local institutions, skills, and ways of life. These local conditions are not simply a backdrop. They are constantly evolving and actively shape what artists and the museum can do.

Indeed, AMPL’s curation, research, and public education programs are all centered around county-town life. It invites artists to spend time in Qingyuan and develop projects in collaboration with local people. Rather than focusing solely on the finished artworks, artists are encouraged to gain inspiration from everyday encounters, including those with local workers.

In one project, a modified “chariot” joined the evening moped traffic. In another, local shops and a long-vanished dance hall became subjects of an exhibition. The museum’s collaborations have also extended into classrooms. Working with artists, AMPL made recordings of contemporary art classes at Hangzhou’s China Academy of Art available to local high school teachers for use in their lessons. Together, these projects have brought artistic practice into familiar settings, from roads and shops to schools.

Local networks are equally important to AMPL’s day-to-day operations. Without a dedicated exhibition installation team, the museum relies on local welders, electricians, and other tradespeople recruited through personal contacts. Since the museum opened, workers who were initially unfamiliar with installing contemporary art have become regular collaborators. These relationships have become part of the museum’s infrastructure.

AMPL’s 2026 exhibition, “Factory Girl,” is perhaps the most convincing evidence of how contemporary art can take root — rather than “sink” — in county-towns. Featuring artist Zheng Que and curated by Nie Xiaoyi, the exhibition explores manufacturing in China’s counties through Zheng’s own experience. Beginning in 2023, she worked at a factory producing Christmas goods in Pan’an, another county in Zhejiang, and filmed herself on the job. Like Qingyuan’s pencils, the factory’s products connected local workers to consumers far beyond the county. Zheng herself was the “factory girl.”

According to Zheng, most workers were women from nearby villages, ranging in age from their 30s to their 70s and 80s. Many were retired and wanted something to keep them occupied. Coworkers were often also neighbors or relatives, connected through overlapping networks of family and acquaintances.

At the opening of “Factory Girl,” I met artists, curators, and other art professionals who had traveled from Shanghai and Hangzhou. Over dinner, we shared loach hotpot, a local specialty featuring the fish that gave AMPL its name, and shiitake mushrooms, all prepared by local residents.

Together, these activities suggest a more reciprocal relationship than the language of xiachen implies. At AMPL, the graft is both architectural and cultural. What matters is how the different elements come together: how space is shared, how local skills are put to use, and how relationships are sustained through repeated collaboration and practical adjustments.

Whether these connections can sustain AMPL in the long term remains uncertain. Resources and networks from major cities will continue to matter, but so will the museum’s ability to give artists time to develop work with local residents and maintain those relationships beyond individual exhibitions. For the graft to take hold, collaboration must become an ongoing practice, giving people in Qingyuan a role in shaping the museum’s future. More broadly, AMPL raises questions about how contemporary art can develop beyond China’s major cities, and the role smaller communities can play in shaping it.

(Header image: The installation “Zheng Que: Factory Girl,” Art Museum of Pond Loach, Qingyuan County, Zhejiang province, 2026. Photo by Luo Shunqi, Han Qian and Cao Danyang. All images courtesy of Jin Yu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.title: China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.content:
Chinese scientists have developed the world’s lightest wireless mesoscope, a miniature microscope weighing just 1 gram that can record 25 times as many neurons in mice as comparable devices.

The device, named Airscope, was unveiled in the prestigious journal Nature on Oct. 19, and developed by a team led by Tsinghua University professor Dai Qionghai and Chinese PLA Medical School professor Dai Pu, in collaboration with researchers from other institutions.

When installed on a mouse’s head, the Airscope can record activity from over 8,500 neurons as it freely explores, climbs, and interacts with other mice.

Previously, microscopes designed to image large areas of the brain at high resolution often required cables or the subject to be restrained, making it difficult to study natural behavior. Meanwhile, head-mounted microscopes that let animals move freely could observe only limited areas.

In contrast, the Airscope combines wireless operation with mesoscopic imaging, allowing scientists to observe large areas of tissue while still distinguishing individual cells. This enables researchers to “understand how large numbers of neurons interact and work together to produce complex functions,” Wu Jiamin, an associate professor in Tsinghua University’s Department of Automation and one of the study’s corresponding authors, said in an article published Tuesday by Tsinghua University.

The device weighs just 1 gram without its battery, more than 30% less than the latest head-mounted mesoscopes, according to the researchers. It has single-cell resolution of 4 to 6 micrometers, and a 6-millimeter field of view compared with typically less than 1 millimeter for conventional head-mounted devices. A magnetically attached battery can be replaced in two seconds.

With the Airscope, the team conducted several experiments that were previously difficult because of cables or equipment weight.

For example, in a simulated natural habitat with ramps, tree hollows, and shelters, mice could explore freely while researchers recorded their cortical activity. The team could also use neural signals to predict which portion of the habitat a mouse was in.

In another experiment, researchers placed two mice at opposite ends of a narrow tube and used their neural activity to predict which would force the other to retreat, achieving over 80% accuracy.

Other experiments included mounting one Airscope on a mouse’s head and another on its back to compare spinal cord and cortical neural activity, as well as tracking mice exploring a large maze in search of water rewards.

The team has also publicly released several datasets collected from their experiments.

Zhang Yuanlong, one of the study’s first authors and an assistant professor at Tsinghua University’s Center for Life Sciences and Artificial Intelligence and Department of Automation, said the team used AI to help optimize the optical design. The technology also uses a 2-megapixel image sensor, whereas previously published wireless systems had not exceeded 1 megapixel, allowing higher resolution.

Dai Qionghai said the Airscope could enable “more precise neural detection” and potentially expand into fields such as immunology and cancer research.

Zhang added that the device could be used to track the progression of Alzheimer’s disease, brain injuries, cardiovascular diseases, depression, and other conditions in animal models, and gain insights into disease mechanisms, prevention, and treatment.

In 2023, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed two head-mounted microscopes using a new optical design: one optimized for a larger field of view, measuring around 4 millimeters and weighing 1.4 grams, and another optimized for lower weight, with a 1-millimeter field of view and weighing just 1 gram. Both devices required wires for power and data collection.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from the WeChat public account of Tsinghua University, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.title: In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.content:
For her vacation to China’s southern province of Hainan during this year’s weeklong National Day holiday, Chang Yajie bought five new pieces of clothing: a beach skirt, a floral halter top, a straw hat, a swimsuit, and a pair of loose rainbow pants.

She wore them all on the trip, relishing taking photos in her new outfit on the resort-laden island’s beaches and posting them to social media.

But when she got home, she stuffed the clothes into her trash can.

Chang, an office worker in Xinxiang, a city in the central Henan province, used to spend thousands of yuan on vacation outfits. Unsuitable for work and out of place in everyday life, they ended up at the back of her closet after her trips.

“You can’t possibly wear a plunging, neon-colored beach dress to a corporate desk job,” the 37-year-old told Sixth Tone. “Spending so much on clothes I might wear only once or twice just isn’t worth it.”

In contrast, the five items she packed in early October had cost a total of just 200 yuan ($28). Known as cipaoyi, or disposable outfits, these clothes typically cost under 50 yuan per item and are designed to be worn once for holidays, photo shoots, or social media posts, and then discarded or resold.

The trend, which took off this National Day, comes amidst fast fashion and influencer-driven consumer culture, as well as the phenomenon of haoyangmao, or buying clothing, wearing it for travel, photoshoots, or events, and then returning it for a full refund.

On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, posts under the topic have drawn over 60 million views. On e-commerce platforms, sellers offer clothing ranging from coats and snowpants for use in the northeastern city of Harbin to red dresses designed for photos in the desert. The trend is particularly popular among young women.

Proponents of disposable outfits argue that they’re an inexpensive way to look and feel good while matching scenery and holidays. But others, including environmental advocates and medical professionals, have raised concerns about their potential impact on the planet and people’s health.

Cutting costs

Despite having always loved dressing up, Chang said her clerical desk job leaves little room for it, so she keeps an understated, practical wardrobe. Disposable outfits, then, are a way to “boost her mood.”

“When I go to work, I just wear whatever helps me blend into the crowd,” she said.

But travel, and embellishing her outfits, have helped her reconnect with a more energetic, youthful version of herself. “After months of the same dull routine, dressing up for a trip feels like a shot of adrenaline,” she said.

Chang wasn’t initially looking for disposable clothes. But as she scrolled online for holiday looks, she found it hard to choose among those that caught her eye. In the end, she opted for cheaper versions of similar styles so she could buy more.

A brand dress can easily cost 300 to 500 yuan, she said. “For the same amount of money, I could buy seven to 10 cheaper outfits — enough to wear a different look each day of the trip.”

Chang said the appeal of disposable outfits lies partly in their novelty, helping her match a destination’s look and feel. The clothes let her try styles she rarely wears in daily life — brightly colored pieces with bold, saturated hues, more revealing cuts, or designs that push the boundaries of her usual wardrobe.

For 20-year-old Wu Xiangmeng, a college student in the southern Guangdong province, disposable outfits help her travel money — saved from her university’s monthly living allowance — go farther, leaving more for train tickets, accommodation, food, and activities. So far, she has visited almost 10 cities across China this way.

Before each trip, she researches her destination to pick disposable outfits that fit the scenery. When she’s done with her clothes, she lists them on secondhand platforms like Xianyu and Xiaohongshu instead of throwing them away, pairing the listings with photos of herself wearing the outfits on holiday to attract buyers.

“I can recoup some of the cost while making room — and saving money — for my next trip,” she said.

Outside impact

Though disposable clothing can be a cost-effective way to dress for specific destinations, Wu said she spends hours finding clothes she considers suitable, shopping, sorting through poor-quality purchases, and returning those that don’t make the cut. “The shopping experience is very draining,” she said.

While preparing for a trip to Hainan’s city of Sanya, for instance, Wu ordered several dresses, only to find the fabric flimsy, ripping at the slightest pull. She ultimately kept only two pieces from the pile and returned the rest.

Zhang Bingquan, who operates a garment factory in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, said disposable outfits cost so little partly because of their simplified designs and production process. With fewer patterns and straightforward sewing techniques, as in beachwear, he said production costs per garment can be kept in the single digits in yuan.

But the low prices have also intensified competition among manufacturers. To cut costs, some factories use lower-quality fabrics, reduce fabric weight and thickness, or take risks by using fabrics and dyes that fail to meet quality standards, he added.

“The biggest health risk with disposable clothing lies in the materials used,” Zhong Jianbo, deputy chief physician of the dermatology department at Hangzhou First People’s Hospital, told local media. “Cheap garments often use low-quality fabrics and dyes that may contain high levels of chemical residues.”

Sun Weiling, a dermatologist at Jiangsu People’s Hospital, told domestic media that disposable clothing is often made from stiff fabrics that can irritate the skin and cause damage, particularly in more delicate areas, such as the underarms, chest, waist, abdomen, and inner thighs.

The trend has also drawn criticism over its environmental costs. China is the world’s largest producer, consumer, and exporter of textiles, and generates vast amounts of textile waste. According to the China Association of Circular Economy, discarded clothing in the country is expected to reach 50 million metric tons a year by 2030, with each person throwing away an average of 16 garments annually.

During this year’s National Day holiday, the volume of textiles collected by Shanghai-based recycling platform Feimayi nearly doubled from the same period last year, Deng Qihua, the company’s head of marketing and sustainable development, told Sixth Tone.

“Some of the clothes we collected still had their original tags attached,” Deng said.

But recycling disposable outfits can be difficult and costly, as they are often made from blends of synthetic fibers, she added. “A garment bought cheaply and worn only a handful of times may therefore leave behind a much longer problem once its owner is ready to discard it,” Deng said.

A growing number of users are noticing the problem. A September commentary by state-run media outlet People’s Daily called on regulators to steer the market toward more sustainable alternatives, such as clothing rental. A Douyin hashtag promoting alternatives to “disposable fashion,” with tips on styling existing clothes and buying clothes with long-term use in mind, has garnered more than 32 million views.

But for many, health and environmental concerns take a back seat to looking good on vacation for minimal cost. Chang, the office worker, said that when she posted pictures of herself in her disposable outfits, friends praised her looks and “girlish charm.”

“At least it helps me feel better about myself,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.title: China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.content:
China has approved its first auditory brainstem implant for clinical use among deaf patients amid a national push to commercialize brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies.

Approved Oct. 19 by China’s National Medical Products Administration, the implant — dubbed Nurotron WH-01A — is classified as a Class III medical device, the highest-risk category under the country’s medical device classification system.

The device was developed by a team led by Wu Hao, a surgeon and professor of otolaryngology at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Ninth People’s Hospital, in collaboration with Zhejiang Nurotron Biotechnology, headquartered in the eastern city of Hangzhou.

It is designed to restore hearing in patients who cannot benefit from conventional cochlear implants because of severe inner-ear malformations or an absent cochlear nerve, which normally carries auditory information from the inner ear to the brain.

Unlike cochlear implants, which stimulate the nerve via the inner ear, the auditory brainstem implant bypasses both the cochlea and the cochlear nerve, delivering electrical impulses directly to the cochlear nucleus, a brainstem structure through which all sound information enters the brain and where sound processing begins.

The system consists of six components, including a stimulator and a receiving coil. Used with Nurotron’s cochlear speech processor, located outside the patient’s body, it converts digital signals into electrical pulses that directly stimulate the cochlear nucleus.

Eligible patients include children aged 2 to 6 with “nonsyndromic deafness,” or deafness without other associated medical conditions or physical abnormalities, as well as those whose deafness was not caused by tumors or who cannot benefit from cochlear implants.

By 2024, the team had completed the implant surgeries and follow-up procedures for its clinical trial. The device achieved an overall treatment effectiveness rate of almost 97% after 12 months of activation, they told domestic media.

The approval comes as China ramps up efforts to advance its BCI industry toward clinical use and commercialization. China’s national development plan, part of its most recent five-year plan (2026–2030), identified BCI as one of six future industries. In July 2025, seven national ministries jointly set guidelines and targets for fostering a globally competitive BCI industry by 2030.

National regulators have also accelerated BCI device approvals for patient populations including those affected by stroke, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and spinal cord injuries. In March, the country approved its first BCI kit, designed to help patients with quadriplegia caused by cervical spinal cord injuries regain limited hand function.

China’s BCI market is expected to exceed 6 billion yuan ($900 million) by 2028, with a compound annual growth rate of roughly 18% between 2024 and 2028, according to domestic research agency CCID Consulting.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Left: Professor Wu Hao’s team during an auditory brainstem implant surgery. Right: The auditory brainstem implant recently approved for market release. From the website of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.title: Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.content:
In 2022, I spoke with Emma, a 22-year-old Chinese student in the UK, about her experiences with dating apps. Recalling one particularly disappointing encounter, she let out a sigh. Emma had matched with a man whose profile explicitly stated that he was looking for a long-term relationship. But the day after their third date, he texted her to say he had only ever wanted casual sex, then ghosted her. Feeling betrayed and emotionally drained, Emma changed her dating profile to say she was “Not Sure” what she wanted.

Emma’s experience was far from unusual. More than two-thirds of the 40 heterosexual Chinese students I interviewed in the UK reported similarly ambiguous dating intentions — findings drawn from a longitudinal study conducted between January 2022 and March 2023 that examined how their experiences with dating apps evolved while studying abroad. Many initially joined dating apps with clear goals, whether to pursue romantic relationships, make friends, or engage in language and cultural exchange. Yet over the course of the study, 27 of the 40 interviewees became less certain about what they wanted, increasingly adopting a “go with the flow” or “I’ll just see what happens” attitude.

For some, this ambiguity opened up new possibilities. For many others, however, it became a way to protect themselves after disappointing dating experiences. Beneath their apparent uncertainty, many still longed for a stable, long-term relationship.

For some young Chinese students arriving in the UK, keeping their dating intentions ambiguous is a deliberate strategy to leave their options open. In China, traditional dating culture places considerable emphasis on long-term commitment and marriage. Expressing vague or noncommittal intentions on Chinese dating platforms can carry a social stigma, with users sometimes labeled zhanan or zhanü, derogatory terms for men and women perceived as dishonest or irresponsible in romantic relationships.

Moving abroad can change these expectations. In the UK, students encounter a dating environment where a wider range of relationship arrangements is socially accepted. Living far from their parents and the social expectations of home also gives them greater freedom to experiment. For some, dating apps offer an opportunity to explore different kinds of relationships without committing to any particular one.

This “go with the flow” mentality was particularly common among postgraduate students enrolled in one-year degree programs. Jenny, a 23-year-old master’s student, explained during our first interview, shortly after arriving in the UK, that she had deliberately avoided setting clear dating goals so she could explore unconventional relationships.

“In China, I never thought about it because I was afraid of facing stigma and judgment,” she recalled. “I want to seize this opportunity to explore different possibilities during this one-year period.”

But not everyone embraced ambiguity out of a desire to experiment. For many other students, particularly women, keeping their intentions vague was a response to negative dating experiences.

After encountering misleading dating profiles and being ghosted without warning, some students became reluctant to invest emotionally in new relationships. Julia, a 23-year-old woman who had joined dating apps hoping to find a long-term partner, described feeling “emotionally paralyzed” after repeatedly meeting men who were only interested in casual sex. She initially had a clear relationship goal, but as she grew increasingly doubtful that she would find the commitment she wanted, she changed her profile to express more ambiguous intentions. By lowering her expectations, she hoped to avoid further disappointment.

Yet the difficulties these students faced in finding long-term relationships were not only about whom they encountered on dating apps. Their status as temporary residents in the UK could also make commitment more complicated. With student visas approaching expiration, many faced uncertainty about where they would live or work after graduation. Investing emotionally in a relationship could feel risky when relocation or a return to China was only months away. Potential partners in the UK might also hesitate to commit to someone who could soon leave the country.

Chou, a 23-year-old student, summed up her approach as “No expectations, no disappointments.” She explained, “Most local daters did not want to form a long-term relationship with me because I’m only here temporarily as an international student. They worried that once I head back to China after graduation, our relationship wouldn’t have a future.” Chou thus adopted ambiguous motivations to cope with the difficulty of forming and maintaining long-term relationships as graduation approached.

Yet perhaps the most surprising finding from my study was that adopting a “go with the flow” approach on dating apps did not necessarily signal a growing preference for casual relationships. In practice, my interviewees experienced different kinds of relationships, with some remaining short-term while others had the potential to develop into longer-term partnerships. Many of them still longed for lasting love. In some cases, that desire became stronger over time, as the initial excitement of exploring different relationships began to fade.

Jack, a 26-year-old student, described this gradual shift. During our first interview, he said he found it exciting to keep his intentions ambiguous because it allowed him to “explore different types of relationships.” But when we spoke again nearly a year later, he had come to understand his desires differently.

“As I kept using dating apps, I started to realize my expectations for long-term relationships had been awakened. Trying different relationships was fun, but it gradually left me feeling empty. I really wanted a serious relationship, but I suppressed that desire because I felt it was impossible to find something long-term on dating apps.”

The word “awakened” is revealing. It suggests that Jack’s desire for long-term commitment had never entirely disappeared. Rather than simply shifting from a preference for casual relationships to serious ones, he gradually came to recognize what mattered most to him.

Eve, a 23-year-old master’s student, captured this tension through a food metaphor. She described her short-term relationships as daican, a Chinese term meaning “meal replacements.” In Chinese internet slang, the term describes a substitute that offers some comfort or satisfaction but cannot fully make up for what someone really wants.

“I feel it’s very difficult to form long-term relationships on dating apps, so I’ll just stick to some ‘meal replacements’ for now to keep me from getting hungry,” she explained. “But a meal replacement cannot replace staple food.” For Eve, these brief connections were not meaningless. They offered companionship and helped ease the loneliness of living abroad. But they were substitutes for what she really wanted. The “staple food” in her metaphor was a stable, long-term relationship.

These experiences were neither entirely positive nor entirely negative. The “meal replacement” strategy could help meet immediate emotional needs. But such relationships rarely satisfied overseas students’ deeper desire for lasting commitment. In this sense, these experiences shouldn’t be taken as defining who they were or what they wanted from intimacy.

Dating apps offer Chinese students abroad new opportunities to explore relationships beyond the expectations they grew up with. But while living overseas may change how they approach dating, it does not necessarily change what they ultimately want. For many, the desire for lasting love remains, even as the uncertainty of their temporary lives abroad shapes what they feel able to pursue.

In line with research ethics, all research participants are given pseudonyms.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019127/At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.title: At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019127/At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.content:
ZHEJIANG, East China — At China’s largest film and television production base, veteran director Zheng Zhongfu was taking his two leads through a confrontation between a prince and his wronged wife.

“In my previous life, you gouged out my heart and left me to die in the wilderness,” he recited, showing them how to deliver the line and where to look. “In this life, I will take back everything that belongs to me.”

Qi Kexin and his wife listened closely. But once the cameras rolled, they caught each other’s eye and burst into laughter, forcing Zheng to call cut. Again.

“The emotion has to land … your gaze has to focus,” he reminded them. “Whatever you do, don’t laugh. Let’s go again.”

Qi, 48, and his wife were tourists at Hengdian World Studios in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, where visitors can pay 388 yuan ($60) per person to star in a short drama of their own. Qi had booked the shoot on a whim after spotting the experience on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

The package includes costumes, makeup, and filming, with studio performers filling the supporting roles. Visitors spend about an hour in makeup and on set, sometimes longer if they add scenes or need additional coaching. Two days later, they receive a finished two-minute drama with a complete storyline.

Earlier tourist shoots required groups of three to five and at least two hours, said Wu Yizhuo, who oversees the service at Hengdian World Studios. “Individual tourists with packed schedules found that hard to accept.” His team developed shorter shoots that a single visitor could book.

Visitors can now choose from nearly 30 scripts written by staff screenwriters, drawing on themes from Chinese social media and the country’s booming ultrashort drama industry, including palace intrigue, martial arts fantasy, and romances featuring domineering CEOs.

Wu’s team asks visitors whether they want to play a hero or a villain. Most choose villains as a way to relieve stress, he said, with “satisfying revenge” stories especially in demand.

Amateur hour

Qi chose a palace intrigue script in which he plays a prince who wants to divorce his wife for another woman. His real-life wife plays the wronged spouse, who turns the tables on him with an emperor’s order and a sword.

After a nervous start, the pair began to settle into their roles as Zheng coached their dialogue and movements. Their sleeve flicks and sword draws became more assured. “You nailed it!” he called from behind the camera after one take.

By the time the shoot wrapped, Qi had a new respect for professional actors. “You have to memorize lines, vary your tone, and add emotion. You can’t attend to everything at once,” he said.

“Actors really have it hard. It truly takes skill,” Qi added. “We’re just playing around — we’re far behind the professionals.”

Zheng had spent years directing trained actors before he began filming tourists in Hengdian this summer. He breaks difficult lines into smaller pieces, sometimes splitting a sentence across three shots to ease the pressure on visitors, and aims to finish filming in about 30 minutes.

Professional crews are serious and not particularly cheerful while filming, Zheng said. With tourists, the focus is on participation and keeping the set lively. “They may not care much about the final film’s quality. The main thing is to come here and be happy.”

Zheng is open to visitors adding scenes or lines, or switching into dialect. “As long as the final film works well, it’s fine,” he said. “The more drama there is, the more fully they perform — and the more they share it on social media.”

On the day Sixth Tone visited Hengdian, Zheng moved straight from Qi’s shoot to his next performer, Zhang Zhongfeng. The 58-year-old farm owner had driven more than 2,000 kilometers from the southwestern Sichuan province with her daughter for the experience. She had never acted and was nervous when she learned her daughter had booked a shoot for her.

Zhang chose palace intrigue, and Zheng tailored a role to her age and temperament. Once filming began, her commanding presence surprised him. Onlookers mistook her for one of the studio performers.

Her daughter, Su Jing, 35, filmed a princess scene at another set the next day. “It’s a bit more complicated than filming yourself with a phone, but much simpler than a big movie — no huge number of lines to memorize, and staff guide you throughout,” she said. “It’s like an upgraded version of travel photography.”

Zheng said the experience was drawing growing numbers of visitors, particularly during holidays. Nearly 3,000 people have taken part since the package launched in July.

Around 2010, Hengdian mainly hosted big-budget films and large TV productions with long shooting schedules, Wu, who oversees the tourist service, recalled. Before one production finished, the next was already booked. “Vertical-screen short dramas have since become more common, while large productions have declined,” he said.

In recent months, cheaper AI production and cuts in platform financing have reduced live-action shoots. In Hengdian, the weekly average number of filming crews reportedly fell nearly 25% year on year in the first half of 2026.

On peak days, Wu’s team handles 30 to 40 groups of tourists. When its regular staff cannot cover the bookings, the studio calls in local part-time workers. Zheng films tourist dramas as a member of one such outsourced team.

Giovana Velasco, a tourist from Peru, first visited Hengdian last year, when the experience wasn’t available, she recalled. After spotting it on Trip.com this year, she booked a shoot and chose to play a rejected daughter seeking revenge.

She rehearsed lines in Chinese, Spanish, and English, battled nerves and laughter, and sometimes relied on body language to stay in character. Her shoot took twice as long as those of Chinese visitors. She is already planning another trip to play a scheming sister and surprise her TikTok followers.

A Shanghai tourist surnamed Xia chose a scene from the 2011 Chinese period drama “Empresses in the Palace” in which her character slaps a maid who has struck her first. She booked the shoot after seeing influencers perform in Hengdian on social media. “Just for fun, out of curiosity,” she joked.

Before she delivered the slap, the director demonstrated how to draw her hand back to make the movement look bigger on camera. The finished film arrived two days later, sooner than she expected. Xia was impressed by the picture quality, the background, and her own styling and makeup.

When she shared it with close friends, many wanted her to take them along to film one themselves. They asked, “Where’s the next episode?”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo and Xiao Chuhan; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A crew films tourists in Hengdian, Zhejiang province, September 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019149/Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.title: Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019149/Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.content:
China has used a domestically developed satellite communication system to make video calls with those in the Arctic for the first time, supporting scientific data transmission, emergency medical response, and other purposes.

The breakthroughs occurred between polar research vessels on the country’s latest Arctic expedition, the country’s Qinling research base in Antarctica, and a base in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, domestic media reported Monday.

The system uses the GW constellation, the country’s first state-backed satellite internet constellation project. The constellation launched its first satellites in December 2024 and plans to deploy almost 13,000 satellites by 2035. It aims to provide broadband services to areas beyond the reach of terrestrial networks through a system of low-orbit satellites operating below 2,000 kilometers above Earth.

The expedition has transmitted and received more than 300 files totaling over 100 gigabytes and held more than 40 video conferences via the system. Connectivity reportedly remained stable in harsh conditions, including extreme cold, high altitudes, strong winds, blowing sand, and ice fog.

The first breakthrough came on Aug. 3, when the research vessel Xuelong, then in the Arctic Ocean, completed a video call with China’s Qinling Station in Antarctica, the country’s highest-latitude communication ever performed using a domestic satellite system.

On Sept. 25, as the Xuelong returned to China, its crew exchanged Mid-Autumn Festival greetings via the satellite system with researchers at the Qinling Station and those aboard the Jidi and Tansuo-3 vessels during their ongoing Arctic expeditions.

A separate video call connected the Jidi, Qinling Station, a test station on the Lhasa River in Xizang, and the North China Sea Bureau of the Ministry of Natural Resources in the eastern Shandong province.

The communication system also reportedly enabled a video consultation with medical experts in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao, who provided remote medical support for a crew member in the Arctic.

Video call lag was no more than one second, according to state media outlet CCTV. After the vessels entered ice-covered waters, files and navigation logs were also transmitted via the GW constellation, with peak one-way speeds of around 30 megabits per second, enough to download a 1 GB file in about 10 minutes.

The event also marked the first time domestically developed buoys had transmitted ocean observation data in real time via Chinese satellites rather than international satellite services, state media outlet People’s Daily reported.

“The tests have improved the ‘information isolation’ faced by polar expeditions … offering practical evidence and experience for fully domestic communications support for China’s polar expeditions and marine equipment,” Zhang Meng, a member of the expedition and an on-site tester with the North China Sea Bureau, told state news agency Xinhua.

Previously, maritime communications along Arctic shipping routes relied mainly on shore-based radio and satellite systems, but coverage was limited and signals were often constrained. Earlier media reports said Chinese polar expeditions had used satellite services including the U.S.-based Iridium and British Inmarsat systems.

China’s latest Arctic expedition departed from the northeastern Liaoning province on July 3. The Xuelong and Xuelong 2 returned to Shanghai on Sept. 29 after completing their missions.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019141/Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.title: Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019141/Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.content:
“Xiaohai, how come your parents still aren’t here? Everyone else’s family has come to help,” a teacher asks a teenage boy preparing for a student-led product sales competition.

“I’m fine, teacher,” the boy says, sweat streaming down his face. “I can do it alone — I believe the aunties and moms out there will help me.” He then makes an at-camera plea, sweat now turned to tears, asking viewers to help him by buying a luxury face cream and saying, “Are children from poor families really not suited for this stage?”

This scene comes as videos featuring the AI-generated teen male character, “Xiaohai,” surge in popularity, with a related hashtag amassing more than 620 million views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Tuesday. The videos, marketed to older women, appear across dozens of accounts and push a range of products, from soy sauce to cosmetics.

But in response to the popularity of Xiaohai videos — in which the teen often relays fictional sob stories, likening them to elderly-targeting scams — other user-made clips portraying him as a greedy, ill-mannered troublemaker, under arrest or admitting to fraud, have also begun to emerge, domestic media reported this week.

In the original Xiaohai videos, the character addresses viewers as “aunties and moms,” asks after their health, and occasionally performs a song before marketing various products.

Many older viewers reportedly believe the AI-generated character is real. In one video in which Xiaohai donates blood, the comment section is flooded with statements that appear to reflect people’s belief that he is real, such as “You’re such a good boy,” and “Why are you so pale? Please take good care of yourself.”

Using the character to sell products has proven lucrative, according to domestic media. A report by state media outlet Shandian News found that content creators producing videos featuring Xiaohai earn up to over a half of total sales, and some creators say they earn at least 1,000 to 2,000 yuan ($140 to $280) a day from videos featuring the AI character.

In contrast, the recent wave of Xiaohai videos shifts the narrative, aiming to paint him in a light that proves he’s not worthy of viewers’ affection and to dissuade them from purchasing his products. In some videos, the boy brags about how much money he’s squeezed out of his devoted followers. In others, he smokes, drinks, insults older women, or flaunts his wealth.

In response, some commenters said they were angry they had bought Xiaohai-backed products. Others interpreted the videos as evidence that Xiaohai had accidentally gotten into trouble or been coerced into lying. “Know that your aunties and moms won’t think badly of you,” reads one comment. “This will pass … I’ll think of something; tell me your address and phone number.”

Xiaohai creates a “sense of intimacy” that can make his appeals persuasive to seniors, Yi Xiaoting, associate dean of the School of Humanities and Public Administration at Shanghai Open University, told Sixth Tone. “That sense of familiarity and intimacy can override the need to verify whether the character is real or whether the story is true,” she said.

Helping older adults navigate AI-generated misinformation means encouraging them to question seemingly trustworthy personas and to verify claims independently, even when the story feels emotionally convincing, Yi added. She also stressed the need for both digital literacy programs for seniors and increased regulation of AI-generated content.

In recent years, regulators and state media have increasingly scrutinized the use of fabricated personas and empathy-driven narratives to sell products online. In 2024, a local court in southwestern China’s Sichuan province convicted eight people for selling products online using false narratives. At last year’s Two Sessions meeting, industry experts called for legislation to curb the misuse of AI-generated deepfakes.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Screenshots of Xiaohai, an AI-generated character. From Weibo)

World.title: Villar’s Vista Land 2025 net income falls 59% as delayed figures surface
World.content:
After months of delay, Vista Land celebrates its higher EBITDA despite a plunge in net income and a P5-billion gap between its Q3 2025 and FY 2025 net income figures

MANILA, Philippines – Billionaire Manny Villar’s Vista Land and Lifescapes (VLL) finally released its long-delayed 2025 earnings figures on Monday, October 26, revealing a steep drop in net income despite higher operating earnings.

Its net income plunged 59% to P3.8 billion from P9.37 billion in 2024. The company, however, led its announcement with earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), which rose 6% to P24.2 billion from P22.82 billion, meeting what it described as “the company’s target for the year.”

Unlike net income, EBITDA excludes interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. This means it can rise even as the bottom line falls if these expenses increase, such as when a company faces substantial borrowing costs.

Vista Land also reported P35.8 billion in consolidated revenue, although gross profit from its residential business, after deducting direct costs, fell 18% to P9.7 billion.

More puzzling is its September 2025 quarterly report, which showed P9.46 billion in net income for the first nine months alone, more than double the P3.8 billion now reported for the full year.

This leaves a more than P5-billion difference, which suggests a substantial fourth-quarter loss, revisions to earlier figures, or some combination of both.

What drove the divergence remains unclear, as VLL issued only a press release with selected figures, rather than its set of full audited financial statements. The company did offer one possible explanation, saying its results “reflect, in part, the recognition of interest expenses that were not capitalized into qualifying assets.”

Instead, Vista Land emphasized that it launched 46 horizontal housing developments worth an estimated P49.6 billion, mainly under its Camella flagship brand. Its reported assets stood at P376.8 billion at year-end.

The earnings release arrives after months of delays in reporting the company’s financials. Vista Land is among six listed companies linked to the Villar family suspended from trading for missed reporting deadlines.

On October 8, Vista Land, Vistamalls, and VistaREIT announced a board approval to release their 2025 audited statements. The disclosures came on the same afternoon Senator Mark Villar moved to the Senate majority, while his sister Camille remained in the minority.

But so far, Monday’s filing is still limited to a press release attached to an SEC Form 17-C, not the complete audited statements or annual report. It does not clear Vista Land to resume trading. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Giovanni ‘Banoy’ Lopez, the new DPWH secretary?
World.content:
LOPEZ. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Transportation Secretary Banoy Lopez inspects the Metro Manila Subway Project’s tunnel boring machine breakthrough on September 23, 2026, connecting the southbound tunnel between the North Avenue and Quezon Avenue Stations.

After serving in the Department of Transportation for nearly a decade, Giovanni 'Banoy' Lopez moves to the Department of Public Works and Highways

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Transportation Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez as chief of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), replacing Secretary Vince Dizon.

Dizon, meanwhile, returns to lead the Department of Transportation.

A certified public accountant and lawyer, Lopez will be tasked to institutionalize reforms in the DPWH, which has been marred by corruption issues, said acting Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano.

Lopez has been serving DOTr for nearly a decade. Based on available public information, he served as assistant secretary for procurement and project implementation and director for legal services in the DOTr in 2017.

He was then appointed as DOTr undersecretary for finance and chief of staff in 2021. In the same year, he became executive director (officer-in-charge) of the Toll Regulatory Board.

In 2022, Lopez became executive director of the Land Transportation Office.

From February to August 2025, he was senior undersecretary for administration, finance, and procurement of DOTr.

Marcos appointed Lopez as DOTr secretary in September 2025, after the post was vacated by Dizon.

Lopez hails from Tuguegarao, Cagayan. He finished high school at the University of Saint Louis Tuguegarao in 1996.

Lopez earned his accountancy degree as cum laude at St. Paul University Philippines. He studied law at San Beda University. – Rappler.com

World.title: Gasoline prices get a rollback, diesel prices rise again on October 27
World.content:
Motorists queue at a gas station in Paco, Manila, to take advantage of a ₱4.30 per liter drop in gasoline prices, on October 20, 2026, while diesel prices rise by ₱2.60 per liter.

Continued tensions and possible escalations in the Middle East conflict continue to put pressure on global supplies

MANILA, Philippines – Gasoline prices are set to ease while diesel prices rise for a second straight week starting Tuesday, October 27.

The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following permitted price adjustments for October 27 to November 2:

Gasoline – rollback of P0.30 per liter

Diesel – increase of to P1.20 per liter

Kerosene – rollback of P0.50 per liter

Photo from Department of Energy briefing.

The adjustments follow last week’s movements, when gasoline prices dropped by P4.30 per liter and kerosene by P1, while diesel increased by P2.60 per liter.

The continued diesel price increases come amid tight international supplies, made worse by renewed attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and commercial vessels in the Middle East. Escalating hostilities involving Yemen’s Houthis have threatened alternative oil export routes, while tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continue to put pressure on global supplies.

Oil prices went up on Friday, October 23, with Brent crude rising 3.14% to $116.72 per barrel, its highest settlement in nearly six months.

Local pump prices remain substantially higher than before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, common Metro Manila prices stood at P56 per liter for RON95 gasoline, P54.70 for RON91, P55 for diesel, and P83.47 for kerosene.

The Philippines imports much of its petroleum requirements as finished products, making domestic prices vulnerable to changes in regional fuel markets, freight costs, and foreign exchange rates.

Meanwhile, excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene remain suspended under Executive Order No. 125, issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in September. The relief does not cover gasoline or diesel. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Newspoint] Duterte’s Frankenstein monster
World.content:
One problem remains intractable and self-compounding, and that problem happens to be the Frankenstein monster Rodrigo Duterte created for us

Lest we lose perspective in our preoccupation with Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, she is the anointed political heir of the man who brought untold horrors upon us when he was president — her own father.

And as though in too much hurry to prove herself deserving of the anointment, and with a sense of impunity that runs in the family, she got herself impeached even before she could go halfway through her term as vice president, the very first national office she has held. And impeachment being a dicey thing, wait till she is acquitted, thus retained in office and re-certified eligible to go for the heights of notoriety achieved by her father — or higher.

Her prosecutors appear confident, however, that she will be stopped. They have decided to pursue only one of the articles of impeachment and drop the other three. They made that decision after their final witness, a financial forensicist, had lent a strong close to their case on that one article — unexplained wealth. If they get her on that, she is removed automatically as vice president and barred from holding public office ever again.

But then again, in a court where senators, instead of professional judges, sit, politics is always a factor, making acquittal a realistic prospect regardless of the quality of the evidence. And how is this for political weight? Sara Duterte is polling the best numbers for the presidential vote in 2028. I confess I don’t quite get it myself, knowing that we need only look back on her father’s time to see what we’re in for if she does win.

Rodrigo Duterte’s presidency (2016-2022) was notorious across the board, but, for our purpose here — a quick, immediately relevant review of his treasonous, murderous, and corrupt regime — I have selected only a few cases, although cases sharply emblematic by themselves.

Our first case is his war on drugs, which took tens of thousands of lives by extrajudicial means and for which he was flown to The Hague, the Netherlands, to face trial before the International Criminal Court for “crimes against humanity.” That war was generally explained away as Duterte’s own sick “final solution,” but it is turning out to be sicker than that. Duterte may have had Hitler’s deeply unprincipled conviction, but, apparently, he was all business too.

Old and mostly hearsay allegations that his war was actually a coverup for his family’s own connection to the drug trade are gaining credence. Bank accounts held jointly by Rodrigo and Sara and submitted in evidence at the impeachment hearings have revealed payments from a drug-trafficking suspect.
