World.title: Tokayev expands Kazakhstan’s logistics capabilities: from Middle Corridor to CASA
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is consistently strengthening the country’s position as a transport and logistics hub in Eurasia.

“Airports, railway stations, bridges, seaports and border infrastructure are being built and modernized. This is important work, and it will continue,” he said at a ceremony marking Republic Day.

One of the areas of this work is the development of transport links with South Asia. Kazakhstan is exploring a new railway route through Uzbekistan and Afghanistan to Pakistan’s seaports, which could complement the country’s existing transport corridors and expand its access to international markets.

On September 30, the ministries of transport of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure signed a memorandum of cooperation on the CASA route project (Kazakhstan - Uzbekistan - Afghanistan - Pakistan). The parties intend to conduct technical and economic studies and assess the feasibility of developing the necessary railway infrastructure. The establishment of a working group to address technical, economic and financial issues is also under consideration.

Under the proposed arrangement, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan could make use of their railway infrastructure and transit potential, while the UAE could contribute its experience in transport infrastructure development, logistics and the implementation of major investment projects.

The cost and implementation timeline for CASA have not yet been determined, as the project remains under study. The route’s prospects will depend on its economic feasibility, the availability of sufficient cargo volumes, financing and transit conditions. Security along the Afghan section and the coordination of transportation terms among all countries along the route will also be important.

Developing the southern route alongside the Middle Corridor could expand Kazakhstan’s transport links with several major markets. The route through Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan could provide access to South Asian markets and Indian Ocean ports, while the Middle Corridor connects Kazakhstan with Europe via the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus. Developing these routes would allow Kazakh exporters to choose the most suitable options based on the geography of their shipments and trade requirements.

Germany has also expressed interest in developing Central Asia’s transport links. The issue was discussed by Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin and German Ambassador Heike Peitsch at a meeting in Astana on October 23. Zhumangarin highlighted the importance of developing the southern route and diversifying transport corridors. According to Peitsch, the development of such routes is of interest not only to Central Asian countries but also to Germany. It was noted that the region could become an important link between European and Asian markets. The discussion covered not only railway connections but also the development of digital communications, gas pipelines and oil pipelines, which would expand opportunities for trade and economic cooperation.

Cooperation between Kazakhstan and Germany received additional momentum following Tokayev’s visit to Germany on September 29-30, 2026. The parties agreed to expand cooperation in industry, energy, critical raw materials and transport. Bilateral trade reached $4.5 billion in 2025, an increase of 13.4%, while German investment in Kazakhstan since 2005 has amounted to $8 billion.

Thus, CASA complements Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop international transport links. Alongside the Middle Corridor, which is oriented toward European markets, the southern route could expand the country’s access to South Asian markets and Indian Ocean ports. As the project is further assessed, key tasks will include evaluating its economic viability, determining financing mechanisms, and coordinating transit conditions. If these issues are resolved, CASA could expand logistics options for Kazakh exporters and strengthen the country’s position in the Eurasian transport system.

World.title: Latvia eyes dairy, meat, food tech exports to Kazakhstan (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Latvia and Kazakhstan are currently discussing potential joint projects aimed at exchanging experience and transferring knowledge in several areas of the agricultural and food sectors, the International Affairs Department of Latvia’s Ministry of Agriculture told Trend.

According to the ministry, these include dairy and livestock production, food processing, aquaculture, veterinary and food safety, agricultural research and innovation, and logistics for agricultural products.

"Latvia remains open to strengthening mutually beneficial cooperation with international partners, with a focus on areas that can generate tangible benefits and opportunities for people and economies and contribute to shared prosperity", the source said.

For Latvian exports, several product categories have particular potential. Latvian companies are exploring opportunities to place dairy products, particularly cheese, on the Kazakh market. Kazakhstan is already an established market for Latvian fish and fish products, providing a basis for further expansion.

Latvian companies have also expressed interest in the Kazakh market for meat and processed meat products, as well as in cooperation in meat processing. There is potential to increase exports of other processed food products with higher added value rather than focusing only on primary agricultural commodities.

Latvian peat products have also been identified as an area with export potential. In addition, opportunities exist for Latvian companies providing agricultural, veterinary, digital and food-processing technologies and expertise.

According to the ministry, in 2025, exports of Latvian-origin agricultural and food products to Kazakhstan amounted to 2.9 million euros and included confectionery (cream), fish products (frozen herring and sprats), chocolate, miscellaneous food preparations (food supplements), preserved fruit (fruit fillings), sugar confectionery and plants.

"The existing presence of Latvian food products on the Kazakh market provides opportunities to further diversify exports and increase the share of higher-value processed food products", the ministry said.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory (26.10.20): President Ilham Aliyev interviewed by Italian Rai 1 TV channel (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

On 26 October President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev was interviewed by the Italian Rai 1 TV channel.

Trend presents the interview:

- Mr. President, good afternoon. Please tell us if this new truce, this new ceasefire will hold. If I am not mistaken, this is the third ceasefire.

- Everything will depend on how Armenia behaves because the first two ceasefires were disrupted by Armenia. After the first ceasefire, which was declared for humanitarian considerations, Armenia violated the ceasefire within 24 hours and barbarically launched a ballistic missile at the city of Ganja at night. As a result of the first shelling, 10 people were killed and many were wounded. Then they hit Ganja again, and also at night. There were even more victims. So we had to answer. As for the second truce, we have a chronology of Armenia's violations of the ceasefire. They violated it literally two minutes after the appointed hour of the truce. Today, at 8 o'clock, a new truce came into force. Now it is 10 o'clock in the morning in Baku. At about 3-4 minutes after the ceasefire entered into force at 8 o'clock, several shells were fired at the city of Tartar again. We are not reacting to this. We hope this was an accident, but if this continues, we will be forced to respond adequately.

- Mr. President, what actually caused the outbreak of hostilities at the end of September? Why did this happen?

- There was a series of events of political and military nature. Armenia's main goal was to disrupt the process of negotiations in every possible way. The new government of Armenia has repeatedly stated that the fundamental principles are unacceptable for it, that it is not going to return a single centimeter of the occupied territories, which contradicts the fundamental principles. The prime minister stated that we should negotiate not with Armenia but with the so-called leaders of Nagorno-Karabakh, which is unacceptable both for us and for the OSCE Minsk Group. He also stated that 'Karabakh is Armenia, full stop', thereby completely undermining the negotiations. In the past year, there were practically no negotiations, and in order to shift the blame on us, Armenia made three sabotage attempts – in July on the border, in August when they sent a sabotage group, and in September when they shelled our cities. They probably thought that we would show restraint again, but that did not happen. We answered them in a manner that they are now regretting it.

- On what conditions will you agree to stop the hostilities then? You have repeatedly spoken about the need for a constructive approach on the part of Armenia. What should a constructive approach be like?

- A constructive approach should be that they must publicly declare, through the prime minister, that they accept the fundamental principles. The fundamental principles envisage the return of seven districts located around the Nagorno-Karabakh autonomous region to Azerbaijan and the return of Azerbaijani refugees to the territory of Nagorno-Karabakh, including the ancient Azerbaijani city of Shusha. These approaches are, in principle, based on four UN Security Council resolutions, which require practically the same. But when the Armenian prime minister says that not a single centimeter of land will be given to us, when the Armenian defense minister says that Armenia will start a new war for new territories and when aggression is carried out against us, this is not a constructive approach, of course. He must say that yes, the occupied territories will be returned to Azerbaijan, that the Azerbaijanis will return to Nagorno-Karabakh, including Shusha, and then, of course, we will come to an agreement very quickly.

-Mr. President, there is one very controversial issue. Some countries, not only Armenia, but also France, have somehow accused you and Turkey of sending thousands of mercenaries, jihadists from Syria to Karabakh via Turkey. How will you respond to such accusations, and how will you respond to the accusations that speak of the presence of Turkish troops and Turkish military aircraft on the territory of Azerbaijan?

- I have already answered this question many times and I will answer it again. First, such unfounded accusations were brought against us by only two countries – France and Russia. France said that through the President, Russia through the head of the Foreign Intelligence Service. These charges were brought against us immediately after the outbreak of hostilities. Although almost a month has already passed, not a single piece of evidence, no proof was provided to us. In fact, I will say this for the first time – I asked the French side for the heads of relevant agencies to meet, discuss the issue and provide us with evidence. Nothing was presented to us. Therefore, these are all insinuations. All this is an attempt to cast a shadow on Azerbaijan. I regret that such unfounded accusations come from the co-chair countries, which are supposed to be objective. After all, we do not talk every day about how many weapons are supplied from Russia to Armenia. We do not talk about the fact that Armenia would not have lasted a day in the occupied territories without external assistance. Political support, military support, moral support – all this comes from countries that are supposed to stay neutral. Therefore, we strongly reject these insinuations. It is not necessary. We have 100,000 soldiers of the regular army. If necessary, we will announce overall mobilization, which, by the way, we have not done unlike Armenia. Therefore, this is all lies and slander. As for the participation of Turkish troops in operations, this is also a lie. There is not a single piece of evidence. The fact that Turkish F-16s are on the territory of Azerbaijan was a result of our joint military exercises on the eve of the conflict. We do not talk about how many Russian MIG-29s and Su-30s are on the territory of Armenia. We do not talk about the fact that 5,000 Russian troops are located at the base in Armenia in Gumru and, according to our data, there are periodical supplies of the Armenian armed forces from there. These are facts, in contrast to what is being said about us. Therefore, I suggest that those who want to accuse us first deal with themselves and then make such hasty conclusions based on false information.

- Mr. President, my last question more or less also concerns our country, Italy. You probably know that in Europe there are many successful examples of a peaceful settlement of territorial disputes or separatism. We have one of such examples in Italy. It is Alto Adige/Südtirol. Don't you think that Italy could help you with its experience in resolving the status of Karabakh? Moreover, Italy has very good, close and strong political and cultural relations with you and also with Armenia.

- Yes, I believe that Italy can play a very important role in the settlement of the conflict. I must say that when the Minsk Group was formed, a very long time ago, almost 30 years ago, it was the Italian representative, the Italian diplomat who was the leader of this Minsk Group. That was before the institution of co-chairs was established. After the institution of the co-chairs was created, the Minsk Group as a group of countries did not produce any results because the co-chairs took this activity into their monopoly. We know what this has led to. For 28 years, there has been no progress, no results, only promises, only bureaucratic procedures. In essence, it seems to us today that the activities of the co-chairs were aimed at freezing the conflict, not at resolving it. As for the model that exists in Italy, we have studied it. We also studied the model of the Aland Islands and other successful autonomy experiences. Azerbaijan, unlike Armenia, is a multiethnic state. In Armenia, as you probably know, 99 percent of the population are Armenians. Therefore, this is a very positive experience of self-government which could be applied in our case. In fact, as far as I know, such proposals were made in the mid-1990s. Even groups of representatives of non-governmental organizations and political scientists have visited your country, the region you are talking about, and the Aland Islands. But Armenia has always categorically rejected this. They believed that they would be able to occupy our territories forever relying on military, political and economic support from leading countries of the world, but they made a gross miscalculation. We are proving our case on the battlefield today. We are implementing UN Security Council resolutions and are restoring international law.

- Mr. President, the very last question: at what level will we be in this conflict in one year? Or will it already be resolved by then?

- You know, I communicate with representatives of foreign media almost every day during this month, and in my addresses to the Azerbaijani people I always clearly state our position. We see the future of the Karabakh region – not only the upper part of it but also the plain because Karabakh is a large part of Azerbaijan – as a prosperous and peaceful territory where Azerbaijanis, who must return there, and the Armenians who now live there will live in peace. Our position is this. I believe that this can be achieved with mutual goodwill of the parties. After all, thousands of Armenians live in Baku and other cities of Azerbaijan today. The Azerbaijanis and Armenians have joint businesses in Russia and Georgia. There are mixed families. Therefore, I think that reconciliation is possible. The Armenian leadership should simply abandon its aggressive policy. And if this happens, with our investments and our experience of rebuilding the country, we can turn this region into one of the most prosperous regions in the world. But for this to happen, the consequences of the war must be eliminated. The occupation must be eliminated, the Azerbaijanis must return to the lands where they have lived for centuries, and live in harmony with the Armenian population. It will not be easy and it will take time. But we know how countries were reconciled after World War II, when European countries were at war – the current neighbors, and many people were killed. But this should not sit in the memory all the time and produce hatred, which is what Armenian ideologists are doing today. Goodwill must be shown. If that happens, what I am saying will happen. If not, we will return these lands anyway. And the current state of affairs on the battlefield is showing that. We will return them at any cost. Either peacefully or war, but we will return them. Therefore, I think the Armenian leadership should seriously think about it and take the right step.

- Thank you very much, Mr. President, and as they say in Italian, Bono Fortuno!

- Thank you, all the best to you too. Thank you!

- Goodbye!

- Goodbye!

World.title: Federal MP Luke Gosling's breach of bail charge dropped by prosecution
World.content:
A breach of bail charge against Luke Gosling has been dropped by prosecutors, with the federal MP continuing to deny assault allegations against him.

During a short hearing in the Darwin Local Court this afternoon, prosecutor Jo Poole said the one breach of bail charge against Mr Gosling was being withdrawn, with no further details provided.

A further two charges of assaulting Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly remain against Mr Gosling, although they were not mentioned in court today.

Luke Gosling is accused of assaulting David Connolly at a Thai festival in Darwin in July. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Mr Gosling's bail conditions ban him from coming within 50 metres of NT Government House and require him to give Mr Connolly's office 48 hours' notice before attending an event where the two may be present.

The NT administrator serves as the Crown's representative in the Territory, in a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.

Mr Gosling's lawyer, Marty Aust SC, issued a statement after today's court hearing, saying the dropped breach of bail charge was "only the first step, but a significant one, in the successful defence of all charges".

Marty Aust has welcomed the withdrawal of the charge. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

"Mr Gosling thanks the community for its ongoing support," he said.

"Mr Gosling continues to deny all allegations and remains steadfast in his position.

"However, he is unable to provide any further comment while the matter remains before the court."

World.title: Patients removed from Canberra health waitlists via letter
World.content:
When Liz Allen's daughter was seven years old, she suffered an anaphylactic response while helping to peel prawns for a Christmas meal.

She's since had allergic reactions to other unidentified allergens, some of which have involved trips to the emergency department.

In January 2024, Ms Allen said her daughter was referred to Canberra Health Services' paediatric allergy clinic because it was "the best, most comprehensive place" to determine what was going on.

But in mid-October, after almost three years of waiting, she received a letter stating that her daughter had been removed from the waitlist because her condition "no longer meets the requirement for a specialist appointment".

"It is stressful because … it could be life threatening," Ms Allen said.

"Not knowing the source of the allergy is of great concern.

" We have waited on this list patiently in the belief that she would get the medical treatment she needs. "

Liz Allen says her daughter had been on the paediatric allergy clinic's waitlist for over two years when she was removed. (ABC News)

Ms Allen said she received no other communication from Canberra Health Services (CHS) before the letter arrived.

"There was certainly no communication about further information, particularly around her [current] health," she said.

" Each new reaction [she has] occurs about every six months. It is getting more and more of a concern for us as she gets older. "

'Your referral has been closed'

The letter from CHS explained that there were more than 65,000 people on outpatient waiting lists, and that the wait for the allergy centre was more than six years long for some patients.

Loading Instagram content

"To deliver an effective service, the criteria we use to decide which patients can be seen at the clinic has recently been reviewed and updated by our clinicians," the letter stated.

" Our team has reviewed the information your doctor sent us against the new criteria, and your referral no longer meets the criteria for a specialist appointment with CHS, and your referral has been closed. "

Ms Allen said it was a "kick in the guts" to have to "start all over again", particularly given their referring doctor had since retired.

"We feel like as family, we are in nowhere land trying to navigate this issue," she said.

A post on social media about her experience attracted dozens of comments from other Canberrans who had received similar letters.

"How is it that the criteria has changed so that even an anaphylactic … response does not make a child eligible for such a service?," she said.

"I do worry about this whole system that appears to be crumbling.

"And that doesn't bode well for families trying to raise healthy children."

CHS 'systematically working through' wait lists

CHS chief operating officer Alison Derritt told 666 ABC Canberra Breakfast that they were "systematically working through" more than 40 outpatient waiting lists as part of a review of specialist and outpatient services.

"There will be more reviews to occur. We are working service by service," she said.

"We need to work through all 40-odd services to understand their waitlists and go through them."

CEO Alison Derrett says Canberra Health Services is trying to focus on higher-category patients. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

She said the current criteria for the paediatric allergy service was "those under 16 with a severe and complex food allergy, and primarily with the history of anaphylaxis".

"Now we do need to talk to [Liz Allen] ... and certainly happy to understand her particular situation," she said.

" But what we're trying to do is focus on those patients that are at the top categories or top of the new categories and be able to see them in a timely way. "

Ms Derritt said that some patients removed from waitlists would need to look at being "seen elsewhere", and one "alternate" would be to go to a private clinic.

She also said some patients needing a "lower category service" may be able to access other local services without needing to travel interstate.

"If someone has got communication or a letter from us and you consider that we've not fully appreciated the situation or there's additional information that you think that we've missed, we're very happy to talk through that with our patients and families," she said.

'Honour original waiting lists': Opposition

Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton says the government should "walk back" removing patients from waitlists. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton has criticised CHS's process, and accused the government of trying to make waitlists look better.

"We understand that they're going through a process of review, but we don't believe that process of review should mean weeding out everyone on the waiting list and starting from scratch," he said.

Mr Parton said he would move a motion in the ACT Legislative Assembly this week, calling on the government to "honour the original waiting lists".

"It doesn't matter which way you look at this situation, it's diabolically bad," he said.

"I don't know how the government's going to defend its position because I think it's indefensible.

"And I would hope that the motion that I run tomorrow will give the government the ability to walk back from this and actually genuinely look after the people who need looking after."

World.title: Our favourite one-pot pastas for busy weeknights
World.content:
Busy weeknights call for easy meals that don't require much clean up.

We've compiled our favourite one-pot dishes to satisfy the whole family.

A wide and deep pan works best for this recipe, to help everything cook evenly. (ABC News: Julia Busuttil Nishimura)

Dinner on the table in less than 30 minutes is more than possible with this one-pot pasta — in fact, it's guaranteed.

The pasta soaks up all the flavours as it cooks, and it also creates an irresistibly creamy sauce, thanks to the starchiness of the pasta.

Perfect for busy weeknights, Lina's baked chicken and pesto gnocchi is packed with flavour. (ABC Everyday: Lina Jebeile)

This simple recipe cuts out the need to pre-boil the pasta.

Simply sear the chicken, toss in a pack of store-bought gnocchi, remaining ingredients and bake.

For even less prep, use chicken tenderloins instead of breast fillets.

Topped with pesto, this is a flavour-packed dinner that's easy to make. (ABC News: Zain Ayub)

This easy lemon orzo is packed with lots of spring vegetables, from asparagus to sugar snap peas. And it can be tweaked to your liking.

You can omit vegetables you don't enjoy and add whatever needs using up in your fridge.

This red wine pasta topped with sage, brown butter and walnuts is an easy vegetarian one pot meal. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Inspired by the Italian dish known as spaghetti all'ubriaco, or "drunken" pasta, this is a one-pot dish in which the pasta is cooked in a red wine bath, which enables the fruity sweetness to permeate each strand of pasta.

The brown butter is the triumphant finish to this beautiful currant-hued dish, with the crispy sage and walnuts bringing irresistible earthy, nutty notes.

World.title: Former RAAF pilot was living 'double life' before wife's death, court hears
World.content:
A former RAAF pilot accused of murdering his wife at their Queensland home embarked on a "campaign to make her death appear like a tragic accident", the Brisbane Supreme Court has heard.

On the first day of Robert John Crawford's trial for the alleged murder of his wife Frances Crawford, the court heard he was a "master manipulator", "adulterer and philanderer" who loved money so much he "killed for it".

The former RAAF squadron leader is accused of strangling his wife, and or causing blunt force trauma to her head at their Upper Lockyer home in late July 2024.

The Crown alleged Mr Crawford then manipulated the scene to try and make it appear like she fell while moving their ride-on mower one evening.

On Monday, the court was shown a photo of the mother-of-three's body where it was found beside the mower, which was tipped on its side, next to a retaining wall at their semi-rural property.

Accused was 'interested in other women'

According to the prosecution, a "perfect storm" was brewing in the lead up to the alleged murder.

The prosecution said this meant Mr Crawford was due to lose out financially in a divorce settlement, prompted by his infidelity over many years.

Psychologist Frances Crawford died at her Upper Lockyer home in July 2024. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

"Mr Crawford was interested in other women and not committed to his marriage," Crown Prosecutor Chris Cook said.

"He wanted to retain possession and occupancy of their house at Upper Lockyer."

He said Mr Crawford had not wanted to split his lucrative superannuation with his wife in any settlement, and did not like conditions imposed on him during a period the couple were separated and attending counselling, while seeing if they could reconcile the marriage.

The week after Frances Crawford's alleged murder, her husband was due to undergo a "looming" polygraph test and was about to be "booted" out of the couples $2.6 million home, the court heard.

Prosecution to call up to 50 witnesses

Robert John Crawford has been on bail for more than two years. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

Mr Crawford has pleaded not guilty to one charge of domestic violence murder.

He has been on bail for more than two years as he awaited the trial, which is set down to run for about three weeks.

The jury heard the Crown planned to call nearly 50 witnesses, including the couple's children, Frances Crawford's siblings and friends, first responders, and various forensic, DNA and ecological experts.

A number of Mr Crawford's former RAAF colleagues, and the women he allegedly had relationships and affairs with in the years before his wife's death are also expected to give evidence.

The court heard that Frances Crawford was a devout Christian committed to her marriage. (Supplied)

Before her alleged murder in 2024, Frances Crawford worked part time as a psychologist in Toowoomba.

The court heard that she was a devout Christian, and despite wanting "to be loved by her husband" and "live happily ever after like a fairy tale", she instead felt "unsafe" in her marriage.

A number of her loved ones attended court for the first day of the trial, with some to speak as witnesses, while others sat in the public gallery in support of the mother-of-three.

The trial continues.

World.title: Jumping castle inquest looks to NASA dust devil researcher
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the Hillcrest jumping castle tragedy is expected to hear evidence from a US dust devil expert who has previously worked with NASA, a hearing has been told.

The inquest into the deaths of the six children from Hillcrest Primary School in northern Tasmania in 2021 started last month in Devonport.

It ran for four days and is due to resume in November and February.

A case management hearing in Hobart today heard Maree Norton SC, the counsel assisting the coroner, is "looking to engage" Dr Ralph Lorenz, a planetary scientist and aerospace engineer, to provide evidence regarding the nature of dust devils.

Ralph Lorenz's fieldwork has included researching dust devils. (Planetary.org)

Ms Norton told the court Dr Lorenz had studied dust devils for over two decades, extensively researching "pressure and wind fields in terrestrial settings", as well as the effects of dust devils on NASA spacecraft on Mars.

She said the scientist was "yet to be formally engaged" for the inquest but, "based on preliminary discussions", he would be able to give his opinion on pressure drops, the effect of the "dust devil vortex", and the interaction between the "dust devil and the castle structure".

Six children — Addison Stewart, Chace Harrison, Jye Sheehan, Jalailah Jayne-Maree Jones, Peter Dodt and Zane Mellor — died, and three of their classmates were seriously injured, when a freak wind gust, or dust devil, lifted a jumping castle across the school oval at an end-of-year celebration in 2021.

The six victims of the Hillcrest jumping castle tragedy, from top left: Chace Harrison, Jalailah Jayne-Maree Jones, Zane Mellor. From lower left: Addison Stewart, Jye Sheehan, Peter Dodt. (ABC News/Supplied)

Reinflation of jumping castle to be postponed

Ms Norton also told the court that further testing proposed by a structural engineering expert, which would involve reinflating the jumping castle, would be postponed.

Another case management hearing held earlier this month heard the test would check what would have happened had the jumping castle been anchored to the ground in a different way and whether current Australian safety standards need to be updated.

The school was inundated with tributes after the tragedy. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

She said Dr Lorenz's expert opinion could influence the test methodology, and the test would only proceed once his opinion was received.

Coroner Olivia McTaggart told the court Dr Lorenz "is likely to be able to provide high-level expertise".

"It is going to assist me considerably to have Dr Lorenz provide an opinion in relation to critical matters which go directly to the heart of my function; being how these deaths occurred," Ms McTaggart said.

The court also heard the schedule for next week's hearing block, which will take place in Devonport at both the Paranaple Centre and the Magistrates Court.

Evidence will be heard from Devonport detective Kim Steven, who was present at the Hillcrest oval on the day of the incident, a worker who assisted in the set-up and operation of inflatable devices on the day, an IT expert and various medical witnesses.

The inquest resumes next Tuesday, November 3.

World.title: Amateur prospector finds $150,000 gold nugget in outback
World.content:
Sounds of excitement fill the air as an amateur prospector digs his hands into red, rocky dirt.

What he comes up with is something he hopes isn't "a painted rock", but instead a gold nugget worth about $150,000.

He had been digging for several days on Mount Stuart station near Tibooburra, in the north-western corner of New South Wales.

But he said the discovery was one of persistence, after having nearly walked past the nugget.

Loading...

'The machine was squealing'

The lucky prospector, who wishes to remain anonymous, has been fossicking for years and is familiar with coming up empty.

"You dig lots of rubbish … lots of lead bullets, old timer's nails, horseshoes, everything," he said.

Metal scraps are the most common find for prospectors. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

He was finishing up a day of searching in mid-October, when he stumbled across a signal with his metal detector, the Gold Monster 2000.

"It wasn't a loud signal for the size of the piece that it is [but] once I got down to 100 [millimetres] or something like that, the machine was squealing," the prospector said.

"It might have been on the first or second scrape I just seen this bright yellow dot in the centre of the hole."

A lucky Broken Hill prospector has dug up a gold nugget worth around $150,000. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

The gold nugget specked with quartz weighs over 1,200 grams, with testing showing around 940 grams is pure gold.

On spot price, it is worth between $150,000 to $160,000.

But with plans to sell the nugget to a collector, the price could be pushed as high as $200,000, according to the prospector, who has nicknamed his precious find the "Tibooburra Spud".

Prospecting a popular pastime

In his 20-odd years selling prospecting supplies in Broken Hill, Greg Spangler has only seen one other person find a gold nugget which weighs over a kilogram.

It is more typical to find gold flakes or smaller nuggets weighing only a few ounces.

"We have a fictitious club [called] the Ounce Club … but not many people [are] in the 'Kilo Club'," Mr Spangler said.

Greg Spangler from Broken Hill Prospecting Supplies says more people are taking up prospecting as a hobby. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Despite the rarity of discovering a nugget worth six figures, Mr Spangler believes a surge in gold prices has drawn more people to the hobby.

"It's got a lot of people interested," Mr Spangler said.

Gold prices soared to new heights this year, peaking in January at almost $8,000 per troy ounce (or 31.1 grams). While the price has since dropped, it's still sitting favourably at about $5,700 per troy ounce.

The nugget has been affectionately named the "Tibooburra Spud" by the prospector who found it. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Beyond the chance of an instant boost to your retirement fund, Mr Spangler said there were other benefits to the hobby, including exercise, fresh air and a bit of quiet.

"You get up in the morning, you're the first one to see the sunrise … it's very peaceful," he said.

"Just another pastime you can involve the whole family in."

More gold in Tibooburra

Gold prospecting around Tibooburra, which dates back to the late 1880s, is a major drawcard for many tourists.

Today, fossicking on the Tibooburra Common, an area surrounding the remote township, is currently banned while Native Title permissions are being pursued.

But at least two stations in the region, Mount Stuart and Gumvale, allow fossicking for a fee.

The lucky prospector found his $150,000 nugget with the Gold Monster 2000. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

And Mr Spangler said for anyone looking to have a go, there could be plenty more gold to be found.

"[It could] keep going forever and ever, because every time it rains, other people find gold where they didn't before," he said.

As for the prospector, he has just one tip for would-be fossickers: "Just keep walking, keep swinging [and] keep digging every target."

World.title: Three-game Bledisloe Cup series looms as new deal struck
World.content:
The Wallabies are set to play two Bledisloe Cup Tests at the MCG in a matter of years, fuelling hopes that one of rugby union's biggest rivalries could be permanently returning to a three-game series.

Rugby Australia struck a multi-year deal with the Victorian government which secures Melbourne to host the Wallabies and New Zealand in the Rugby Championship in 2027 and an additional Bledisloe Cup Test in 2029.

It comes as Lang Park in Brisbane is set to stage the first Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test next April, which sets up a three-match series between the bitter rivals for the first time since 2021.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

Whether a three-game series would persist beyond next year has been a hot question exercising pundits.

But Monday's announcement of an additional Test in Melbourne in 2029 will very much boost optimism that a permanent three-game Bledisloe Cup series could return.

That is because Brisbane has also secured the rights for the 2029 Anzac Day Test along with the 2031 instalment.

RA officials were coy on whether the announcement was a signal for a return to full-time three-Test series, and were unsure if 2028 would be similar to 2027 considering no Anzac Day Test has been announced.

An extra Bledisloe Cup Test would favour the Wallabies, who haven't held the trophy since 2002 and have been unable to win both Tests since it became a two-game duel in 2022.

In 2026, they were utterly humiliated by the All Blacks, conceding a mammoth 93 points across the two games, which dealt coach Les Kiss a harsh reality check ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallabies admit they 'faced the music' It was brutal and confronting, but the Wallabies knew they had to face the reality of Saturday night's defeat to the All Blacks sooner rather than later.

Regardless of the three-Test speculation, having a Bledisloe Cup Test at the MCG next July is set to be a stellar moment for the sport in Australia as it ramps up preparations for the World Cup.

The Wallabies last played the All Blacks at the MCG in 2023, where a crowd of 83,944 filled the historic ground, which was the largest rugby attendance in more than 20 years at the time.

Last year, 90,307 watched the Australians' second Test against the British & Irish Lions, breaking the Lions' all-time crowd record.

"The Melbourne Cricket Ground is one of the world's great stadiums — and a jewel in Australia's sporting crown — and the Wallabies are proud to be hosting the All Blacks at the iconic venue in 2027," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have played only four previous Test matches at the MCG, and this Bledisloe Cup encounter will mark 30 years since both teams took to the hallowed turf for the first time.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have won two Tests apiece at the 'G and another enthralling contest awaits next year."

Australia will also meet the All Blacks at least one more time in 2027 when they face off in their second Pool A match of the Rugby World Cup at Sydney's Olympic stadium.

World.title: Second death increases call for action on health system in 'crisis'
World.content:
Tasmania's health system is in "crisis" after the second death of a patient involving a delayed ambulance this month, Labor and the Greens say.

On Saturday, a man in the west coast town of Zeehan sought help after complaining of chest pain and breathing difficulties.

The call was categorised as a "priority 1" case requiring immediate assistance, but the local ambulance station was not staffed due to unfilled leave.

Paramedics in the nearby towns of Queenstown and Strahan were also unavailable because they were already attending to other cases.

A Burnie crew was then assigned, but by the time it arrived 78 minutes later, the man had died.

The Health Department said a "comprehensive investigation" has been launched into the circumstances surrounding the Zeehan death.

It comes after another tragedy about two weeks earlier when a Hobart family made two calls to Triple Zero (000) over the space of 25 minutes.

The first call was triaged as a non-urgent matter, but the man's condition deteriorated, and by the time they called again, it was escalated to a priority 1 case.

However, it took a further 25 minutes to dispatch an ambulance because none were available.

The man in Zeehan called Triple Zero and was categorised as requiring immediate assistance. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

According to a union, they were either responding to other cases or were ramped at the Royal Hobart Hospital because the emergency department was at capacity.

The man's family ended up driving him to the hospital, but by the time they got there, he was in cardiac arrest and later died.

The Health Department has referred the Hobart death to the coroner and is continuing to undertake its own investigation.

"If any immediate findings or opportunities for improvement are identified during the review process, appropriate actions will be implemented before the investigation is finalised," it said.

"The investigation includes the patient's entire care pathway, including emergency call handling, clinical prioritisation, resourcing, and any broader health system factors."

Greens health spokesperson Cecily Rosol said the deaths highlighted a system under extreme strain.

"The Tasmanian health system is no longer at breaking point, it's broken," Ms Rosol said in a statement.

"Medical professionals have been warning for far too long that Tasmanians would lose their lives because of the worsening state of the health system.

"They presented the Liberals with solutions, but the Government have failed to act.

"We should never have reached this awful crisis point."

Cecily Rosol says the Tasmanian health system is broken. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Eleven per cent of paramedic shifts unfilled

Ambulance Tasmania operates 51 stations across the state, including some that are staffed entirely by paramedics, and others that rely partly or fully on volunteers.

The station at Zeehan, which was unstaffed on Saturday, usually has a single paramedic rostered on day shift and on call out-of-hours, with support from volunteers.

The Health Department said attempts were made to fill the vacant shift through backfilling, including overtime and the use of volunteers.

It said there were ongoing efforts to recruit more paramedics to the region, but the remoteness of the area created challenges.

Tasmania's Health Department says the remoteness of the west coast has made it challenging to recruit more paramedics to the area. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

During a budget estimates hearing in June, Health Department secretary Dale Webster told the Greens about 11 per cent of paramedic shifts had been unfilled since July last year.

The Greens and Labor have urged the government not to proceed with plans to find $700 million worth of savings in the health budget.

"Our health system is in crisis," Labor leader Josh Willie said.

"It cannot withstand further cuts.

" Things will only get worse. "

Josh Willie says the state's health system cannot withstand further budget cuts. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Mr Willie said the government needed to ensure enough staff were available in regional areas.

"There are clearly staff issues in regional areas where paramedics aren't available if there's an emergency," Mr Willie said.

" I think many Tasmanians would be extremely concerned about these two deaths and what might happen in the future if this isn't addressed. "

The Tasmanian Health Department has been asked to find $700 million in savings. (ABC News: James Dunlevie)

Lessons to be learned, premier says

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the investigations into the two deaths would identify any issues that need to be addressed.

"All health professionals do their very best to respond to the needs and care of Tasmanians, particularly of course in emergency situations," Mr Rockliff said.

" And so we do need to ensure this and other incidents are thoroughly investigated to prevent them happening again. "

Jeremy Rockliff says says the investigations into the two deaths will identify any issues that need to be addressed. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Rockliff noted the government's transfer of care policy had reduced the amount of time ambulances are stuck at hospitals by 30,000 hours since it started.

But he said the government was open to further changes to improve the system.

"We need to learn from the outcomes and invest in key actions, whether that be an investment of resources or indeed an investment in finding other ways to support regional crews and ensure that our transfer of care policy is as best as it possibly could be."

The Australian Medical Association last week called for an independent commission of inquiry to find holistic solutions to what it described as a "perpetual crisis".

The call was dismissed by Health Minister Bridget Archer, who said it would cost more than $30 million and not help any patients.

World.title: ASX rebounds to end on a high; CSL names new chair
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX rebounds to end on a high; CSL names new chair Staff writers Updated October 26, 2026 — 4:51pm ,first published October 26, 2026 — 5:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian sharemarket has rebounded after an early fall to close in the green, with materials and energy stocks posting gains thanks to a rise in oil prices over the weekend. The S&P/ASX 200 gained 14.7 points or 0.17 per cent, to 8809 on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.33¢. Wall Street lost ground on Friday as oil prices hit their highest mark in four years. Bloomberg The gains were largely thanks to advancing energy and materials stocks off the back of a rise in oil prices. Earlier in the day, Brent crude advanced above $US116 a barrel while West Texas Intermediate rose above $US102 before retreating slightly in the afternoon. The gains were linked to fears the US would restart its war with Iran, with President Donald Trump telling Fox News it was “getting to be decision time” on whether he would make a deal with Tehran or “finish it off”. Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said if rationality existed, the US would not attempt an attack.



Woodside Energy rose 1 per cent and Santos added 1.3 per cent. Among the refiners, Ampol advanced 0.3 per cent and Viva Energy surged 3.2 per cent. Meanwhile, miners BHP and Fortescue added 1.3 per cent and 2.4 per cent respectively. Related Article AI AI darling NextDC announces board and pay purge after Melbourne power disaster Gold miners also reported gains, with Northern Star gaining 2.1 per cent and Evolution rising 1.6 per cent as the gold price steadied at about $US4000 ($5690) per ounce. Technology stocks fell early, following their Wall Street peers, but rebounded as the day progressed. WiseTech grew 1.7 per cent, Xero rose 1.4 per cent and TechnologyOne added 1.7 per cent. Embattled AI company NextDC slumped 2.5 per cent as it announced its chairman, Douglas Flynn, would stand for re-election at its annual meeting with investors next month but retire once a replacement is in place, and chief executive Craig Scroggie will forfeit millions in bonuses. Pharmaceutical giant CSL has named its interim chief executive, Gordon Naylor, as its next chair, replacing Brian McNamee, who will end his decades-long association with the Australian pharmaceutical giant.



Naylor will take over as chair on March 31. He will hand over chief executive duties to Deborah Waterhouse in February. Related Article Exclusive

Retail ASIC won’t sue Super Retail board over scandal that led to CEO’s sacking, says company McNamee, as CEO, helped steer the company’s transformation from a government agency into one of Australia’s largest listed companies, but it has struggled with a string of downgrades over the past year which sent its shares sharply lower. CSL shares ended the day down 1.6 per cent. On Wall Street on Friday, the S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent as the index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain. Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher.



The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology, and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive. “Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note. The latest round of corporate earnings is being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon. Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent.



American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite reporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade. Related Article Casinos Judgment day looms for Star casino as court decides size of fine JPMorganChase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent. While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent. European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit.



Treasury yields in the US edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late on Thursday. Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the US. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects the US central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily towards another rate hike in December. Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Gina Rinehart takes fight for Perth helipad at Hancock HQ to tribunal
World.content:
NationalWAGina Rinehart Gina Rinehart takes fight for Perth helipad at Hancock HQ to tribunal Heather McNeill October 26, 2026 — 4:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gina Rinehart’s company Hancock Prospecting has taken its fight to build a helipad atop its West Perth headquarters to the State Administrative Tribunal after it was knocked back by the local council. The City of Perth grounded plans for the helipad at the Ord Street building in December, despite two councillors backing the idea of a helicopter landing in the city precinct, and the lord mayor describing Rinehart as an “amazing Australian”. Gina Rinehart is continuing to fight to put a helipad atop her new West Perth head office. Opposition to the helipad stemmed from concerns over noise, whether it was conducive with the area’s existing planning scheme, and whether allowing the CBD’s first private-use helipad would set an undesirable precedent. The area, in West Perth, is an office and residential precinct, with the City of Perth flagging nearby sites could accommodate more residents in the future.



But Ord Street Holdings counsel Grant Donaldson, KC, in his opening statement in SAT on Monday, argued the helipad would only be used in “daylight hours” between midday and 7pm up to 12 times a year for “occasional corporate transport”. “That’s 144 minutes per annum, that equates to the sound of an electric kettle boiling for six minutes, once every fortnight, between the hours of noon and 7pm,” he said. “This case boils down to what negative impact is this use going to have on the objects of the current or new scheme?” The mining giant has previously likened Perth to Tokyo and New York as a “global city”, saying “rooftop helipads are commonplace across the world’s leading cities, and our proposal would elevate Perth’s status”. But City of Perth barrister Tim Houweling said the fundamental issue in the case was noise.



Neighbouring buildings have also objected to the helipad. Related Article Planning and development Gina Rinehart circles around in fresh bid for helipad at Hancock headquarters The Child and Adolescent Health Service made a submission to the City of Perth stating that sudden, intermittent helicopter noise could interrupt testing of children with conditions including autism, sensory issues, ADHD or anxiety. The submission also raised concerns that its roof is old and made of asbestos, and helicopter downwash could disrupt the asbestos dust that has settled. After the council initially refused the helipad application, Hancock Prospecting lodged a revised development plan outlining a new flight path, in a bid to get the request over the line.



Previous plans had the helicopter approaching from the east or west of the eye-popping five-storey headquarters, in a route that would have seen it come down over the inner-city suburb of Subiaco or a mix of residential and office buildings in West Perth. Instead, the new flight path has the eight-seat Bell 429 helicopter approaching the building from the south-west, tracking Thomas Street on the outer fringe of Perth’s CBD botanic garden Kings Park, before turning and descending once it reaches Ord Street. A Hancock Prospecting spokesperson said the company’s original application was “developed with expert input and independent technical analysis which confirmed the helipad and flight path can operate safely and appropriately”. “However, as part of our extensive good faith efforts to reach agreement with the City of Perth, we have proposed an amended flight path and further reduced the proposed operating timeframes,” they said.



SAT judge Henry Jackson is presiding over the appeal, and will make a ruling on the helipad at the conclusion of the two-day trial which will hear from acoustic and planning experts. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: AFLW ladder with one round to play; ‘Difficult decision’: Dons sack inaugural coach
World.content:
Essendon will replace inaugural AFLW coach Natalie Wood next season after informing her that her contract would not be renewed for 2027 after the team’s 1-10 record this season.

Wood was informed on Tuesday about the decision, but players were only told after Sunday’s five-point loss to Hawthorn.

Bombers coach Natalie Wood leads her side on Sunday. AFL Photos

Wood is still planning to coach the final round game next Sunday against fellow strugglers Collingwood.

The Dons will be the third AFLW club seeking a coach, joining St Kilda and expansion club Tasmania Devils.

“The club is not offering me a contract as of next year,” Wood said post game on Sunday.

“It’s been a topic of conversation and a lot of questions with our poor performances this year

“It’s a disappointing end, as clearly I would have liked, like the last couple of years, to have better performances on the field.”

The Dons have struggled with injuries and form this season, but Wood was heartened by the club locking in several future leaders to new contracts but they will look for a new coach.

“We have fallen short of what we wanted on field. We believe a change is the right step,” Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said.

“Natalie has handled this with real integrity, and her commitment to coaching out the season says a lot about her and how much she cares about the players.

“We thank Natalie for everything she has given the club over five seasons, and we wish her all the best for the next step in her football journey.”

Wood was the first female coach to reach 50 games while leading the team for five seasons since they entered the competition.

“[I] just continued on with the week as normal,” Wood said.

“We had two amazing players in Alex Morcom and Maddi Gay having their 50th and 75th game today, so really important celebrations, and we also had Amelia Radford announce her retirement.

Hayley McLaughlin of the Hawks kicks for goal against Essendon on Sunday. AFL Photos via Getty Images

“I would prefer no one ever knows, and I’d just disappear off into the sunset without any discussion or interview, but I was particularly aware this week of not wanting to get in the way of those three players.

“We really wanted to beat Hawthorn today. I thought we put up a really good fight, it was an ugly game of footy, tricky conditions. But always forefront of my mind is playing group first – so I thought it was best to hold off until today.

“Aysha (Ward, AFLW general manager) is heavily pregnant and is going on leave in two or three weeks, so I think the club is keen on getting a start in searching for their new coach.”

Wood said it was hard leading the AFLW side while Essendon as a club has faced so many leadership changes in recent seasons.

“Am I disappointed it’s fallen out this way? It depends how narrow of a view I have of it. Sometimes,” Wood said.

“I remember in my job interview, we were discussing about the wants of the role. [At the time], no female coach had lasted longer than two years, and I was not wanting to step into a senior coaching role without being well prepared and supported to have a career that’s longer than two years,” Wood said.

“To be the first female coach to coach 50 games, I’m really proud of that. To build a team from ground-up, as one of the last expansion teams and the season coming forward, it was a mad rush.

“At the same time, the club’s had a lot of instability. There’s been four CEOs, three presidents, three men’s senior captains and three senior coaches, so to build a culture within a program while the instability of the club – and it’s in a good spot now – it’s been hard at times while there’s been so much change in structure and leadership.

“When I look back to the start of the season and we had so many players sign long-term contracts, players who are really important to the program going forward - we’ve built a culture and place where players really want to be. I’ve done something right.”

The Hawks scored a vital win in their quest to make the top eight, winning by five points in rain-soaked conditions at the club’s new base in Dingley.

The Bombers were brave but couldn’t find the last goal they needed to get the win.

With AAP

World.title: Tassie, Vic gold output clears Kaiser Reef debt as cash hits $40M
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Tassie, Vic gold output clears Kaiser Reef debt as cash hits $40M Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 26, 2026 — 4:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Dual-asset gold producer Kaiser Reef has wiped a key debt from its books after a solid September quarter, a move expected to unchain about $600,000 a month in operating cash flow. The company banked 6263 ounces of gold during the period, boosting its cash and bullion balance to a healthy $40 million and allowing it to fully repay the senior secured gold loan used to acquire its flagship Henty gold mine in Tasmania. Kaiser Reef is advancing a two-pronged strategy at its producing Henty gold mine in Tasmania (pictured) and the high-grade Maldon gold project in Victoria. Production from the company’s two Australian assets continued to build momentum during the period, with total gold output rising to 6263 ounces from 6000 ounces in the prior quarter. The cornerstone Henty mine churned out 5692 ounces of gold and a further 5259 ounces of silver, while its Maldon project in Victoria chipped in another 572 ounces of gold. Impressively, the Maldon operation has now lifted its output for three consecutive quarters, jumping 65 per cent since March. ‘We head into the December quarter with a fully funded balance sheet and clear operational priorities at both assets.’ Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas



Total production generated an underlying cash flow of $5.6 million for the quarter, which more than covered $2.8 million in debt and deferred payments, allowing Kaiser to increase its net cash and bullion position by a hefty $2.8 million. The strong financial position enabled the company to make a final delivery of 104 ounces of gold in October, wiping the slate clean on the 1872-ounce Auramet gold loan. With that facility retired, Kaiser’s only remaining gold delivery obligation is a deferred payment to Catalyst Metals as part of the Henty acquisition, requiring 50 ounces per month through to October 2030. However, the company says repaying the principal acquisition loan from the mine’s own cash flow is an important milestone. Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas said: “Kaiser delivered 6263oz of gold across Henty and Maldon during the quarter, while increasing cash and bullion to A$40 million, paying down debt and advancing Maldon. We have completely repaid the Auramet gold loan, on schedule, with the final delivery made in October. The gold loan helped us acquire Henty, and repaying it from Henty’s own cash flow is an important milestone for Kaiser.” The impressive quarterly report further underscores a remarkable full-year turnaround for Kaiser, which swung from a $20.24 million statutory loss in FY2025 to a $16.8 million after-tax profit in FY2026, backed by an impressive $44.7 million cash inflow from operations. The Henty mine, nestled in Tasmania’s richly endowed Mount Read Volcanics belt alongside the legendary Rosebery and Mount Lyell operations, remains the company’s gold-producing workhorse. A recent resource and reserve update effectively offset mining depletion, maintaining the mine’s ore reserve at 198,000 ounces of gold and its overall resource at 429,000 ounces. In a shrewd move to sweat its assets, the company is also working with fellow ASX-lister Flynn Gold to process its ore through Henty’s 300,000-tonne-per-annum processing plant. As part of the expansion plan, Kaiser has applied to increase its tailings capacity by two million tonnes.



While Henty provides the cash flow, Kaiser’s Maldon operation in Victoria’s fabled Golden Triangle offers a significant high-grade growth opportunity. The project, with a strong track record of producing 1.75 million ounces at a staggering 28 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, is anchored by the fully permitted 200,000-tonne-per-annum Porcupine Flats processing facility. Its Union Hill deposit hosts an inferred resource of 187,000 ounces grading a solid 4.44g/t gold, with site stockpiles adding a further 11,700 ounces. All up, the company’s global resource stands at 5.53 million tonnes grading 3.46g/t gold for 615,000 ounces. With FY27 total production targeted at around 32,000 ounces and no hedging in place, the gold producer appears well positioned to capture more upside should the bullion price remain steady. Another major milestone for the quarter was the start of underground development at the Union Hill mine. The new development will provide access for underground diamond drilling to test the northern extensions of existing workings at Maldon’s Eaglehawk, Linscott’s, Ladies and Sailors Reefs targets. The underground push adds another dimension to a busy surface exploration campaign aimed at building a pipeline of fresh drill targets. Recent infill soil sampling has outlined strong, continuous gold and arsenic anomalies across multiple structures, with some promising trends extending over 1.5 kilometres of strike. This work has been bolstered by a helicopter-borne magnetic and radiometric survey, providing a clearer picture of the structural architecture, with a surface diamond drilling campaign also ongoing. With the Henty operation humming along and paying the bills, Kaiser appears to be in an enviable position of being largely debt-free and sitting on a sizeable cash pile as it methodically advances exploration across one of Victoria’s most celebrated high-grade goldfields. With no hedging in place and a production target of 32,000 ounces for FY27, the company looks to be fully exposed to any upside in the gold price. As drill rods turn on both surface and underground hotspots at Maldon, punters will likely be watching closely for the results to start flowing. World.title: Push for early train times to get FIFO workers to Perth Airport
World.content:
PoliticsWAAirports Push for early train times to get FIFO workers to Perth Airport Hamish Hastie October 26, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Perth Airport boss Jason Waters is “confident” the state government will tinker with its train timetable to better cater the Airport Line for fly-in, fly-out workers. FIFO workers considering public transport for their flight days have long complained the Airport Line service does not run early enough to catch the morning peak of FIFO flights, which runs from about 4am to 8am. An artist’s impression of Perth Airport’s “One Airport” terminal, with the new third runway pictured to the left. The earliest train to the Airport Central station arrives at 5.27am, but for most intrastate flights, check in closes 30 minutes before the flight time – making it nearly impossible to catch a 6am flight using the train. Asked about a FIFO service at a press conference on Monday, Waters said he was in constant communication with the government in relation to both road and rail.



“I’m certain that as the airport grows and the needs of passengers become more clear and understood, I’m confident that we’ll see the availability of train follow suit,” he said. In the past, the WA government has been reluctant to extend train operating hours, because it would shorten maintenance windows on the city’s rail network. At the same press conference on Monday, Premier Roger Cook said Transport Minister Rita Saffioti was always reviewing timetables to make sure they served the community “That’s why you’ve seen millions of people shifting onto rail, taking part in the expansion of Metronet as paying passengers,” he said. According to the latest Public Transport Authority annual report, boardings on the Airport line increased 11 per cent from 2024-25 to 2025-26, rising from 5.62 million boardings to 6.23 million.



Airport transformation spurs warning for travellers Perth Airport will want to see as many people as possible coming to the airport on public transport as it gears up for one of the biggest transformations in the airport’s history. Construction will begin in the coming months on $5 billion worth of work, including a third runway and new terminal which will bring Qantas’ extensive Perth operations under the same roof as all other carriers at Terminal 1. At the same time, another carpark and a new hotel will be built near Terminal 1, prompting a warning from Waters that “the journey ahead is going to be tricky.” “We’re going to be bringing thousands of construction workers onto the terminal site, and that means there are going to be delays and challenges for passengers but we’re going to remain open 24/7 through the entire construction period,” he said.



“Don’t get caught out last minute because from here on in, over the next five or six years, there’s going to be a lot happening at Perth Airport.” Related Article Traveller letters To catch an earlier flight, I asked for a downgrade. Qantas refused Waters revealed only 4 per cent of passengers to Perth Airport used the train to come or go from the airport, driven in part because there was no train servicing the Qantas terminals. However, he said once the airport was all under one roof the Airport Line would be a much more attractive option. “The construction of the one airport model gives us the ability to really go to the people of Perth and Western Australia with a proposition that says use the train because we’re all in one place now,” he said.



Speaking on the 40th anniversary of the opening of Terminal 1, Waters said the airport upgrades were expected to be completed by 2031 and the timing and cost was still on target, but work was still being done on the final time and cost. Perth Airport will be competing with mining, defence and the state government for materials and labour. More than $25 billion worth of work is under way at Henderson to prepare for AUKUS, billions are being spent on grid upgrades, and renewable energy projects and tens of thousands of homes are being built. Waters wasn’t worried about the competition in the state’s already hot construction sector. “I think it’s actually exciting times for Western Australia. The AUKUS investment, the ongoing investment the state government’s making, as well as Perth Airport, it’s all part of what makes the package of Western Australia great,” he said.



“What is important is that in the background we are having conversations to ensure that we schedule things in a way that enable it all to be achieved in a sensible manner. So I’m not asking that anything be slowed down.” Cook said the Office of Major Infrastructure Delivery was working with big constructors to work out timings of project to avoid labor and materials constraints. “There’s timing around concrete, timing around rebar and other steel products to make sure that they can all work in concert with each other,” he said.

World.content:
